body.text: yadyubhayātmaka sa dharmastadāpyanaikāntika eva / ato 'hetukameva [niḥsvabhāvatvamiti] ye pratividadhati tadapyasambaddhameva / yato hyanena tāvat sadasadubhayadharmāṇāṃ paramārthatvasādhane hetorasambhavatvavocyate yuktijñaiḥ na tu niḥsvabhāvatādisāmānyadharmāṇāṃ lakṣaṇasādhane [sambhavatvamiti], yadi tathaiva syāttadā paraparikalpitānāmīśvarādīnāmapi niḥsvabhāvatvasādhane kathaṃ nāma te sarve codyā nābatariṣyantītī?
body.translated_text: If that <s>dharma</s> is of both natures [existent and non-existent], then it would simply be inconclusive. Hence, those who counter that essencelessness [of all dharmas] is without a reason — that too is simply incoherent. For what is stated here by the logicians is that a reason is impossible for establishing the ultimate reality of dharmas having the properties of existence, non-existence, or both — not that [a reason] is impossible for establishing general characteristics such as essencelessness.

body.text: tad yathā īśvarādiṣu sāmarthyavyāpyavastutvaniṣedhārthaṃ vastusvabhāve samāropaṃ ca nisedhārthaṃ asaddharmā na bhavantyasambaddhāḥ / evameva paramārthataḥ kāryakārāṇādivastudharmeṣu vyāpakaniṣedhena samāropaniṣedhaṃ sādhayituṃ kathaṃ nāsmāsu sādhyasādhanasambandhaḥ / anyathā praśānādayo 'śakyaniṣedhābhaveyuḥ, yato hi vastusati svabhāve na tathā kartuṃ śakyate / yadi asatā asambaddhatayā asāmarthaṃ tadā kutra sāmarthyaṃ syāt / paramarthato 'sadvastuni na bhavati kaścana sambandho nāma / yato hi vyāpakaniṣedhena vyāpyanivṛttistāvarnnirdeśamātrameva / yathā sadvastuni dharmadharmibhāvādisarvāṇi vastujātāni kalpitānīti vyavasthāpyante tathā asadvastunyapi kathaṃ tāni naiva vyavasthāpyante?
body.translated_text: Just as, for the purpose of negating entity-nature pervaded by capacity in [entities like] <s>Īśvara</s> (God) and the like, and for the purpose of negating superimposition upon entity-nature, the properties of non-entities are not unconnected — so too, in negating superimposition through the negation of the pervader in the entity-properties of cause and effect and the like in the ultimate sense, how can there be no connection between the object to be proved and the means of proof in our [system]? Otherwise, peacefulness and the like would be impossible to negate, since when the entity has real nature, it cannot be made so. If, due to being non-existent, there is incapacity through non-connection, then where would capacity exist? In an ultimately non-existent entity, there is no connection whatsoever. For the cessation of the pervaded through the negation of the pervader is merely an indication. Just as, in existing entities, all categories of things — such as property and property-bearer — are established as constructed, why are they not likewise established even in non-existent entities?

body.text: api ca, yadā ko 'pi kadācidapi svalakṣaṇatayā bhāvatvena paramārthato naiva sidhyati, tadā vastulakṣaṇasya tathābhūtatvāt tadabhāvo 'pyasiddha eva, paramārthatastatra sadasadubhayadharmatvena kasyāpi hetorasambhavāt / atasteṣāṃ prativādo vā parīkṣaṇaṃ vā kathaṃ yujyeta, sarveṣāṃ vastūnāṃ māyādivat sadasadubhayadharmātītatvāt / sattvasya tadabhāvasya cāpi hetorānukūlyena vādiprativādinoryathāprasiddhatvena te prasiddhayavinābhūtā evoktāḥ / atasteṣu dharmadharmitvaṃ viruddhatvaṃ vyāpyavyāpakatvaṃ svabhāvaḥ kāryatvādīni ca yathā ābhāsante tathaiva sarvā api vyavasthā aviruddhā eva / kaiścid vidvadbhiryadi darśanasyāsya dharmadharmiviruddhādyādhāreṇa prativādaḥ kriyate tadā tatra paramārthavyavahāranayānavabodha eva kāranaṃ bhavatīti / ato 'navamardanīyametaditi grāhyam /
body.translated_text: Moreover, when nothing whatsoever is ever established as an entity by its own characteristic in the ultimate, then, since the characteristic of an entity is of such a nature, its non-existence too is itself unestablished — since in the ultimate, no reason is possible for anything as having the nature of existence, non-existence, or both. Therefore, how would debate or examination be appropriate for them, since all entities, like illusions and the like, transcend the properties of existence, non-existence, and both? Since existence, its absence, and also the [relevant] reason — through their compatibility, as established respectively for the proponent and opponent — they are spoken of as simply inseparable from what is established. Therefore, in those [entities], the property-bearer relationship, contradiction, pervaded-pervader relationship, own-nature, effect-nature, and the like — all establishments are simply non-contradictory, just as they appear. If some learned persons make a counter-argument against this view based on property, property-bearer, contradiction, and the like, then the cause is simply the failure to understand the methods of ultimate and conventional discourse. Therefore, this should be accepted as irrefutable.

body.text: tadapi na śabdamātreṇa sidhyatīti yaduktaṃ tanna duṣanamanabhyupagamāt / na vayamapi śabdamātreṇa śūnyatāṃ sādhayāmaḥ /
body.translated_text: As for the statement 'that too is not established merely by words' — that is not a valid objection, since we do not accept [it]. We too do not establish emptiness merely by words.

body.text:
68
[25] na ca prasaṅgamātreṇa, api tu samyakprāmāṇenaiveti / ityevaṃ yadi vastuṣu paramārthasvabhāva eko bhavati tadā prakāradvayameva tatra bhavet hetupratyayāpekṣitatvāt sarveṣām, utpadyamānasvabhāvatayā anityatvācca / yathātra sautrāntikayogācārāṇāmaikamatyam, svabhāvena siddhatvādāśritantarbhūtaṃ vā tairthikaparikalpātmādivat / na ca nityānityayoranyoparihārasthitalakṣaṇatvāt tṛtīīnā kācana gatiḥ / svabhāve 'smin ubhayamapi prakādvayaṃ paramārthatayā na sambhavati, sādhakapramāṇābhāvād bādhakasambhavācca / yadi pratyakṣamanumānaṃ vā tatra sādhakapramāṇaṃ tadā vastusvabhāva eva pūrvaṃ tāvadubhābhyāṃ na siddhaḥ, sa tu[vastusvabhāvaḥ] tadaiva syāt, kintu kāryakāraṇabhāva eva tāvat pratyakṣeṇa na paramārthataḥ siddhaḥ / so 'pi tāvadindriyapratyakṣeṇa svasaṃvedanapratyakṣeṇa vā sidhyati, yato hi nārvāgdarśino mānasapratyakṣaṃ vyavaharanti, nāpi ca tanmānasapratyakṣaṃ kutrāpi sidhyatīti tatrāmāṇyamaṅgīkriyate /
body.translated_text: [25] Nor merely by <s>prasaṅga</s> (reductio ad absurdum), but through correct <s>pramāṇa</s> (valid means of knowledge) itself. Thus, if entities have a single ultimate own-nature, then there would be exactly two modes — dependence on causes and conditions for all, and impermanence due to having the nature of arising. As the <s>Sautrāntikas</s> and <s>Yogācāras</s> are in agreement on this, since [things] are established by their own nature, the inherent is subsumed —

body.text: tatra kecidindriyapramāṇena na sidhyatīti bruvate, pṛthagarthaviṣayitvena nirdiṣṭatvāttasya, kintu kāryakāranabhūtasya tasyānyārthasya paramārthato jñānagrāhyatvaṃ naiva yujyate / vijñāne svapratibhāsa iva yo hi jñānetarasvabhāvo 'nyāvabhāsaḥ [pratīyate], sa naiva [jñānād] anyaḥ / anyānanyau hi parasparaviruddhau / atastadākāreṇa jñānenānyasya pratītiriti yaducyate, tadapi nopapadyate, atiprasaṅgāt /
body.translated_text: There, some say it is not established through sensory <s>pramāṇa</s> (perception), since it has been indicated as having different objects individually. However, the perceptual graspability in the ultimate of that other object which is the cause and effect [relation] is simply not tenable. For just as in consciousness there is the appearance of its own reflection, whatever other-nature appears, the appearance of the nature of something other than cognition — that is simply not other [than cognition]. For otherness and non-otherness —

body.text: yadyevaṃ tadā ghaṭādayaḥ, ye 'nyaprakārānanuvidhāya prādurbhavanti, te 'pi sarve parasparaṃ gṛhītasvabhāvā eva / yo 'pi tadākārastajjñānākārameveti viśeṣābhidhāne satyapi vijñānasadṛśyenaivānyāvabodhaḥ saṃjāyate, na ghaṭamātrādinetyevaṃ viśeṣo nāsti / vijñānasvabhāvatve 'pi teṣāṃ svasvabhāvasthitatvādanyeṣvakiñcitkaratvameva / yadi nāsti viśeṣastadārthakriyārthinaḥ svato vastvanudhānena samprayujyate, tathāpi pratiniyatārthakriyāsvabhāvaḥ kutrāpi na sidhyati, atiprasaṅgāt /
body.translated_text: If so, then pots and the like, which manifest by following other forms, would all also have their own-nature grasped mutually. Even when the specification is made that 'the form of that [object] is the form of that cognition itself,' the cognition of the other arises merely through similarity to consciousness, not through the pot alone and the like — thus there is no distinction. Even when they have the nature of consciousness, their abiding in their own nature —

body.text: nāṭayacandramalladarśanavad yugapadanekadarśanena tadvijñāneṣvapi parasparasāmyaṃ syāt, jñānasvabhāvasāmyena ca teṣāmapi parasparaṃ pratyakṣatvaṃ prasajyeta / tadudbhūtatve satīti viśeṣāntaropādāne 'pi anyārthasya pratyakṣatvena pratyatirasambhavaiva, yato hi abhyupagamamātreṇopacaritatvād viśeṣo na prasidhyatīti /
body.translated_text: Like seeing the moon in theater, or wrestlers simultaneously — through simultaneous multiple perception, there would be mutual similarity among those cognitions too; and due to the similarity of cognitive nature, their mutual direct perceptibility would follow as an absurd consequence. Even in specifying a further distinction such as 'when it has arisen from that' — it is simply impossible that the other object would be directly perceptible, since the distinction is merely nominal through stipulation alone.

body.text: anayacca, anyārtho yadi pratyakṣatvena prasidhyati tadā jñānaviśeṣastāvattatsadṛśastadudbhūto vā sādhanīyaḥ / kathaṃ jñānenānyārtho gṛhyata ityevaṃ vicāryamāṇe 'nyārtho yadi pratyakṣato 'siddhastadā kathaṃ tāvadasiddhena svabhāvabiśeṣeṇa siddhā mārgaviśeṣāḥ setsyanta iti yāvat /
body.translated_text: Moreover, if the other object is established as directly perceptible, then either a specific cognition similar to it, or one arisen from it, must be proved. When one examines 'how is the other object grasped by cognition?' — if the other object is not established through direct perception, then how could specific paths be established through an unestablished specific own-nature? — and so forth.

body.text: tadvijñānakṣaṇikatvasyāpi samanantarapratyayārthānubalenopapannatvād yathā jñānāni pūrvakṣaṇasāpekṣatayā samudbhavanti tathā janmāntarāṇyapi sambhavanti / ataḥ pūrvavartināṃ paravartijñānagrāhyatvaprasaṅgasya nivṛtirduṣkaraiva /
body.translated_text: Moreover, since the momentariness of that cognition is also established through the force of the immediately preceding condition and the object, just as cognitions arise in dependence on the preceding moment, so too do [cognitions in] other lives arise. Therefore, the cessation of the absurd consequence that preceding [cognitions] are graspable by subsequent cognitions is difficult indeed.

body.text: api ca, ye tāvadavayavyādibāhyavastūnāṃ pratyakṣatvamāmananti, svasiddhāntānusāraṃ ca yathā taddarśanopacāraṃ kurvanti tathā pratyakṣatayāvabhāso nāstyeva / kadācidapyavayavinastadākāragrāhijñāne pratyakṣānubhavo na bhavatī / sarvadaiva pāṇyādyanekāvayavasamūhākārajñānameva pratyakṣatayānubhūyate /
body.translated_text: Moreover, those who claim that external composite objects (<s>avayavin</s>) and the like are directly perceptible, and who, according to their own doctrine, explain how the perception of those [objects] is figurative — for them, there is simply no appearance as directly perceptible [in that way]. Never is there a direct experience in the cognition grasping the form of the composite. Always, only the cognition of the form of an aggregate of many parts — hands and the like — is experienced as direct perception.

body.text: nīlādyavayavino guṇeṣu sadityākārakaṃ jñānaṃ naivānubhūyate, ādhārasyāpratyakṣatve tadguṇādimātrāṇāṃ grahaṇāsambhavāt / ariṣṭanīlākṣapītākṣatimirādyapahatanetreṣu dūrasamīpasthita ekasminnapi vastuni vibhinnāni viṣamākārāṇi jñānānyutpadyante, ato bāhyāvayaviviṣayakaṃ kalpanājālaṃ citte nāstyeva vidyamānam, tathātve tasya pṛthaggrahaṇaprasaṅgāt / atastadātve tatsvabhāvaguṇādyutpattiḥ sarvathāsatī eva / viruddhadharmāṇāmapi guṇānāṃ yadyekatvaṃ tadā bhinnasattākānāmapyekatvaprasaṅgaḥ /
body.translated_text: The cognition with the form 'exists' regarding qualities such as blue and the like of the composite is never experienced, since when the substrate is not directly perceptible, the grasping of its qualities alone is impossible. In those whose eyes are affected by <s>ariṣṭa</s> (bad omen), blue-eye [disease], yellow-eye [disease], <s>timira</s> (eye disease), and the like, different and disparate cognitions arise regarding even a single object placed near or far. Therefore, the web of construction regarding external composite objects simply does not exist in the mind.

body.text: bādhakābhāvād guṇādīnāṃ sarveṣāṃ dharmāṇāṃ pratyakṣatvaprasaṅgaḥ / svapnādiṣu tathānīlādiguvatāmarthāntarāṇāṃ vidyamānatve 'pi nīlādyābhāsijñānānāṃ pṛthaganubhavo bhrānta evaṃ, na cākāravaśena arthāntaragrahaṇavyavasthā yuktimatī / ye khalu paramāṇvātmakalīādyarthānāṃ pratyakṣatvamāmanvate teṣvapi tāvat samānadoṣatāprasaṅgaḥ, niravayavānāṃ sūkṣmapadārthanāṃ bhinnākāreṣu jñāneṣu pṛthaganubhavābhāvāt / samūhaviṣayāṇi tāni jñānānyabhyupeatāni, svapnādivacca tāni sthūlāvabhāsīnyanubhūtāni / na samavāyibhinnaḥ samavāyaḥ samasti, nāpi samavāyakalpanayā tadupacāraḥ sambhavati /
body.translated_text: Due to the absence of an invalidating cognition, the absurd consequence follows that all <s>dharmas</s> — qualities and the like — would be directly perceptible. Even when, as in dreams and the like, other objects different from blue and the like exist, the separate experience of cognitions appearing as blue and the like is simply erroneous. The establishment of grasping other objects based on [cognitive] forms is not reasonable. Even for those who claim the direct perceptibility of objects such as atoms and the like —

body.text: yadi sañcitānekavastugrahaṇāt sthūleṣu bhrāntirupajāyate, tadā tadānīntanajñānasya aprāmāṇyaprasaṅgaḥ, bhrāntatvāditi / yadi sā sthūlabhrāntiścittenopakalpitā, tadābhivyaktau anābhāsatāprasaṅgaḥ, kalpanāviṣayāṇāṃ sarvadā aspaṣṭāvabhāsanāt / yadi tānīndrayajñānāntargatāni tadā paramāṇunāṃ sarvadāgrahaṇaprasaṅgaḥ, sarvadā tadākārajñānānutpatteḥ /
body.translated_text: If, from the grasping of many accumulated things, error arises regarding gross [objects], then the absurd consequence follows that the cognition at that time would be non-valid (<s>aprāmāṇya</s>), due to being erroneous. If that gross-object error is constructed by the mind, then the absurd consequence follows that at [the time of] manifestation there would be non-appearance, since objects of construction always appear unclearly. If they are contained within the sensory cognition, then the absurd consequence follows that atoms would always be ungrasped —

body.text: yasthūle bhrāntaṃ tattathāgrahaṇataḥ pūrvamapi na [abhrāntaṃ] sidhyati, ārambhe utpattāveva sthūle bhrāntatvābhyupagamāt / purataḥ pramāṇairyadi pramāṇyaṃ sidhyati tadā yā sthule bhrāntiḥ sā grahaṇapūrvikaivaikā sidhyati, yadi na tathā sidhyati tadā sā bhrāntirgṛhītetyeva na sambhavati / svapnādiṣvanyapramāṇāni na gṛhyante, tathāpi sthūle bhrāntistu [tatra] dṛṣṭaiva, atastasyāstatpūrvakatvaṃ na yujyate / marubhūmau laghvapi vastujātaṃ mahadityavalokyate / tatra dūrādūrabhedena spaṣṭāṣpaṣṭāvabhāsabhedo 'pi naiva bhavati, tasyaikavastutvena tatra tādṛśākārā naiva sambhavantīti /
body.translated_text: That which is erroneous regarding the gross — since it [was never] non-erroneous even before [the grasping] — is not established [as non-erroneous] previously either, since error regarding the gross is accepted at the very beginning, at the time of arising. If validity is established beforehand through <s>pramāṇas</s>, then the error regarding the gross is established as one preceded by grasping; if it is not so established, then it is simply impossible that 'that error has been grasped.' In dreams and the like —

body.text: api ca, yādyākārā yāthātathyenābhyupagamyante tadā yathā vividhānāṃ rekhādīnāṃ vistārastathā jñānākārāṇāmapi ākāravat pṛthaktvam prasajyeta / siddhāntavaividhyasthāpanārtham anekajñānānāmutpādamavagacchato vijñānasya viṣayeṣu yathā prasārastathābhāso 'sambhāva eva / ekajñānenābhinnasvabhāvatvād ākārāṇāmapyekasvabhāvatāprasaṅgaḥ / yadi [ākārāḥ] bhinnāstadā arthasadṛśjñānena teṣāṃ grahaṇaṃ nopapadyate, bhinnārthatvāt / tadgrahaṇārthaṃ satyāmapyanyānyākārakalpanāyāmākārāṇāmanavasthāprasaṅgaḥ, anyānyākāraṇāṃ kadācidapyunubhavābhāvāt / yadi te 'līkāstadā tattvānyatvavicāro 'upyasambhavī / tadānayā dṛṣṭayā tadvaśenānyārthavyavasthānaṃ sarvathāyuktam, asamyaktvāt / grāhyākāro 'pi hi prajñāptireva syāt /
body.translated_text: Moreover, if the forms [of cognition] are accepted as veridical, then just as various lines and the like have extension, so too the absurd consequence of the separateness of cognitive forms — like [real] forms — would follow. For the purpose of establishing doctrinal diversity, for consciousness that cognizes the arising of multiple cognitions, the appearance corresponding to the extent of objects is simply impossible. Through a single cognition, due to the undifferentiated nature of the forms —

body.text: api ca, yadi jñānasādṛśayaṃ sarvātmanā bhavati, tadā arthānusāriṇo 'pi jñānasya ajñānasvabhāvatvaṃ syāt, paracittābhijñasya yogino 'pi sarāgattvādiprasaṅgaḥ, sarāgādīnāṃ paracittādīnāṃ parigrahaṇāt / ekadeśenāpi na sādṛśyaṃ [yujyate], ekasmin sāvayavatvaprasaṅgāt / yadi viparyaye hyupacārat karturekadeśa eva tadā sarvatra vastusādṛśyasambhāvanayā sarvajñātṛtvaṃ syāt / sādṛśyamapi prajñaptireva strānna tu paramārtham / ataḥ sādṛśyena jñānetarasvabhāvagrahaṇaṃ na [sarvathā] yujyate 'sambhavāt /
body.translated_text: Moreover, if the similarity of cognition exists in every respect, then even object-following cognition would have the nature of non-cognition; and for a <s>yogī</s> possessing knowledge of others' minds, the absurd consequence of being passionate and the like would follow, due to apprehending the minds of others that are passionate and the like. Nor is similarity in one part [tenable], since the absurd consequence of having parts in a single [cognition] would follow. If in the opposite case, through the figurative usage of the agent —

body.text: tatsādṛśyate 'pi na tatpratyakṣatvena grahaṇaṃ yujyate, viṣayasya hetutve tadanubhavakāle sāmīpyābhāvāt / sāmipye 'pi naiva tadgrahaṇam, ātmasthasādṛśyagrahaṇapravaṇatvājjñānasya, aparasya arthasthākārasya tadānīmanavabhāsāt / avabhāse 'pi tadviruddhatvaṃ tulyaparīkṣaṇīyam / yadi sa eva [anubhavaḥ] tadarthākārānubhavatvena gṛhyata iti cet? kalpanāmātramevaitat / naiva tāvanmātreṇa vastunastādṛśaḥ svabhāv san, atiprasaṅgāt / 'agnirmāṇavakaḥ [bāhmaṇavaṭuḥ]' iti kṛte 'pyupacāre naiva [tamin] dāhapākādiḥ prayujyate / ākāreṇānyārthavyavasthāne 'pyanumānamevaitannaiva hi tatpratyakṣam /
body.translated_text: Even given that similarity, the grasping of it as direct perception is not tenable, since, when the object is the cause, at the time of its experience there is no proximity. Even with proximity, there is no grasping of it, since cognition is inclined toward grasping the similarity residing in itself, and the form residing in the other object does not appear at that time. Even if it does appear, its being contradictory to that [cognition] is equally subject to examination. If that itself [is the experience] —

body.text: pratyetavyā arthāntarāḥ sāmīpye 'pi na [jñāna]ākāravyāptā bhavanti, arthāntarābhāve 'pi svapnādiṣu tathākārasambhavāt / atyantaparokṣatvādarthāntarāṇāṃ te [arthāntarāḥ] tadīyajñānākāravantaḥ santīti naiva sidhyati / hetutvaṃ tāvanna kevalam sākārakāryasyotpādanaṃ nāma, svakīyavijñānānāṃ cakṣurādidvārā bhrāntatvāt, śabdādijñānāntaraṃ cakṣurvijñānotpādena śabdādyābhāsicakṣurvijñānotpādasambhavācca / atastāvatkālikāvabhāsijñāanenārthāntaragrahaṇaṃ naiva yujyate / nāpyanābhāsibhiḥ. teṣu bhedābhāvāt / tadā yadi sāmīpyād vijñānenārthāntaragrahaṇaṃ bhavatīti kalpyate tadā sarvāṇyapi vijñānāni sarvasamīpaviṣayakāṇi syuḥ sarveṣu tatsattāyā bhedābhāvāt / phalataḥ sarvaiḥ sarvadarśanaṃ syāt / śrotrādijñānānyapi rupādiviṣayakāṇi syuḥ sāmīpye bhedābhāvāttadānīm / tataśca 'idaṃ nīlaṃ pītamidam' iti vibhāgo naiva syāt, kasyacanāpi vibhāgaviśesyānabhyupagamāt / yadyabhyupagamyata iti tadā tatsādṛśyamabhyupagataṃ syāt /
body.translated_text: External objects to be cognized, even when proximate, are not pervaded by the form of cognition, because in dreams and the like, such forms occur even without external objects. Due to the extreme remoteness of external objects, it is simply not established that they possess the cognitive form of their [corresponding] knowledge. Causal capacity is not merely the production of an effect possessing form, since one's own cognitions are erroneous through the gates of the eye and other [senses], and because even through the arising of visual consciousness after auditory and other cognitions, the arising of visual consciousness appearing as sound etc. is possible. Therefore, the grasping of external objects through a cognition that has a momentary appearance is simply not justified. Nor [can it be grasped] through [cognitions] without appearance, since there is no differentiation among them. If it is then supposed that the grasping of external objects by consciousness occurs through proximity, then all cognitions would have all proximate objects as their domain, since there is no difference in the existence of that [proximity] in all cases. In effect, everything would be perceived by all. Even auditory and other cognitions would have forms and the like as their objects, since there is no difference in proximity at that time. And consequently, the distinction 'this is blue, this is yellow' would simply not exist, since the qualifier of distinction is not accepted for any [cognition]. If it is accepted, then it would amount to accepting a similarity.

body.text: kalpanāsvarūpamātre jñānābhinnātmake sādṛśyātiriktatayā na kaścanāpi bhedo bhaviturmahati, taddoṣāṇāmabhihitatvāt / sāmīpyavaśājjñānasya yadi nārthāntarādanubhavastadā kathamiti praśne tadutpattyaiveti vaktavyaṃ syāt / tathāvidhamabhidhānaṃ naiva yuktam, jñānakāle viṣayasyābhāvāt, abhāvagrahaṇāyogāt samakālikakāryaṇabhāvāsyāyujyamānatvācca / kasyāpyevaṃvidhābhyupagamābhāvāditi /
body.translated_text: In [cognition that is] merely the essential nature of conceptual construction, non-different from cognition in its self, no differentiation whatsoever beyond similarity can exist, since the faults of that [position] have been stated. If, through the force of proximity, there is no experience from external objects for cognition, then in response to the question 'how then?', one would have to say 'through its arising alone.' Such a statement is simply not justified, because at the time of cognition the object does not exist, because the grasping of non-existence is not possible, and because the non-existence of simultaneous causal efficacy is untenable. Because no one accepts such [a position].

body.text: cakṣurindriyādīnāmapi taddhetutvād grāhyatvaprasaṅgaḥ / tulyaikasāmagrīpratibaddhau deśakālāveva vijñānena gṛhyete nānyad, yadyevaṃ parikalpyeta tadāpi cakṣurādigrāhyatvaprasaṅgaḥ duṣparihāraḥ / viṣayatvābhāvādevendriyaṃ na gṛhyata iti cennaitāvatā tadaviṣāyatvam , viṣayalakṣaṇasya satvāt / grāhyatvamapi na viṣayasvabhāvetarat / ataḥ aviṣayatvānnāsti tadviṣaya iti kathamiva vaktuṃ śakyate / tadevaṃ nirākāreṇa tāvajjñānena nārthāntaragrahaṇaṃ yujyate, nāpi tadanyena sākāreṇa [jñānena], vyavasthāyā evābhāvāt /
body.translated_text: There is also the absurd consequence that even the eye-faculty and the like would be graspable objects, since they too are causes of that [cognition]. If it is supposed that only the place and time bound to the same single aggregate are grasped by consciousness and nothing else — even then, the absurd consequence that the eye-faculty and the like are graspable is difficult to avoid. If [one says] the sense-faculty is not grasped because it is not an object — that much does not establish its non-objecthood, since the characteristic of objecthood exists [in it]. Being graspable is also not other than the nature of objecthood. Therefore, how can one say 'it is not its object because it is not an object'? Thus, neither by formless cognition is the grasping of external objects justified, nor by form-bearing [cognition] of another kind, since there is simply no basis for determination.

body.text: yadyevaṃ tarhi śrotravijñānenāpi rupādigrahaṇaṃ syāt / arthāntarāṇāṃ parokṣatve naivānyākāro 'pi sidhyati / yasmādarthāntaragrāhaka ākārāntaro 'pi nāsti, tasmāt kāryakāraṇātmako 'pi nākārāntaraḥ sidhyati / ataḥ paramārthato na pratyakṣataḥ kāryakāraṇabhāvasiddhiḥ / ata eva paramārthataḥ -
body.translated_text: If this is so, then even auditory cognition would grasp forms and the like. When external objects are remote, no other form is established either. Since there is no other form that grasps external objects, no other form of the nature of cause and effect is established either. Therefore, ultimately, the establishment of cause-and-effect relations through perception [is not possible]. For this very reason, ultimately:

children.translated_text: "Through the perception of the two — that which is free from that [external object] and its form —
the determination of the cause-and-effect relation is made."

body.text: iti yaduktaṃ tadapyasiddham sākārabuddhayā arthāntaraparicchedābhāvāt kāryakāraṇabhāvaniśrcāyakapramāṇābhāve, sati jñānadvayābhāvakathane nāsti kimapi bādhakam, anayā tāvad yuktyā sarveṣāṃ dharmāṇāṃ cittamātratākāyapramukhatvāt /
body.translated_text: What is stated there is also not established, because there is no determination of external objects through form-bearing cognition. When there is no <s>pramāṇa</s> (means of valid knowledge) that determines the cause-and-effect relation, in stating the absence of the two types of cognition, there is no invalidation whatsoever — by this very reasoning, since all <s>dharmas</s> are primarily of the nature of mind-only (<s>cittamātratā</s>).

body.text: tatpratyakṣe 'rthāntarāyoge 'pi tajjñānaṃ svasaṃvedanapratyakṣagamyameva, tadapi ca kāryakāraṇabhūtamevetiḥ, kāryakāranabhāvastu pratyakṣasiddha iti cennaiva tad yuktimat, yathā tathatā tathānubhavābhāvād, yathā cānubhavastathā tathātāyā abhāvāt / evaṃ yadi vijñānasya grāhyagrāhakākārarahitatve 'pi tasya vastusattvamabhyupagamyate tadā tatra tathānubhūterabhāvaḥ, sarvasya grāhyagrāhakākārajñānasyaiva sarvadānubhūteḥ / yadyevaṃ na syāttadā sarvasyaiva tathatādarśanaṃ syāditi / tajjñānamapi yathānubhūyate na tathā sthitaṃ bhavati, ekasmin svarūpadvayavirodhāt / yadi bhrāntatvāt tattathā jñānamiti cet? kā nāma bhrāntiḥ? yadi jñānaṃ tadā naiva sā pratyakṣam, abhrāntalakṣaṇatvāt pratyakṣasya, tattu svayaṃ svato bhrāntamiti /
body.translated_text: If [one argues:] 'Even without the application of external objects in that perception, that cognition is accessible through the direct perception of self-cognition (<s>svasaṃvedana-pratyakṣa</s>), and that too is of the nature of cause and effect — therefore the cause-and-effect relation is established through direct perception' — that is simply not logically sound. Because it is not experienced as it actually is, and because that actual nature does not exist as it is experienced. Thus, if the entity-existence of consciousness is accepted even when it is devoid of the forms of grasped and grasper, then the experience of its actual nature is absent there, since all experience is always of cognition in the form of grasped and grasper alone. If this were not so, then everyone would see reality. That cognition too, as it is experienced, does not abide as such, because of the contradiction of two natures in one thing. If [one says] 'that cognition is thus because it is erroneous' — then what indeed is this error? If it is cognition, then it is simply not direct perception, because direct perception has the characteristic of being non-erroneous; and that [erroneous cognition] is itself erroneous from itself.

body.text: dvayātmake ca tatsvabhāvāvabhāsādadvayasvabhāvahāniprasaṅgaḥ, dvayādvayayoḥ parasparavirodhāt / arthāntarasya bhrāntatve 'pi paryantasvasaṃvedyatvānna tenādvayajñānam / yadi pratyakṣaṃ kalpanāsvabhāvaṃ tadā na tat svalakṣaṇaviṣayakam, kalpanāyāḥ samānyalakṣaṇaviṣayatvāt /
body.translated_text: Moreover, when the nature of duality appears in that which is of dual nature, there is the absurd consequence of losing its non-dual nature, because duality and non-duality are mutually contradictory. Even though external objects are erroneous, because [consciousness] is ultimately self-cognized, non-dual knowledge does not [arise] through that. If direct perception is of the nature of conceptual construction, then it does not have a particular (<s>svalakṣaṇa</s>) as its object, because conceptual construction has a universal (<s>sāmānyalakṣaṇa</s>) as its object.

body.text: api ca, yaḥ kalpanāsvabhāva ucyate, tena svatastadātmano 'bhivyaktirucyate, grāhyagrāhakākāro 'pi svata evābhivyajyate, ataḥ kalpanāsvabhāva evaiṣaḥ / yadi sa [grāhyagrāhakākāraḥ] mithyā tadā tadabhinnaḥ kalpanāsvabhāvo 'pi tathaiva mithyā, tathātve kathaṃ sa pratyakṣapramāṇena bhāvasvabhāvaḥ prasidhyet /
body.translated_text: Moreover, what is called 'of the nature of conceptual construction' — by that, the self-manifestation of its own nature from itself is stated. The form of grasped and grasper too is self-manifested from itself; therefore, this is indeed of the nature of conceptual construction. If that [grasped-grasper form] is false, then the nature of conceptual construction, being non-different from it, is likewise false. If so, how could it be established through the <s>pramāṇa</s> of direct perception as having the nature of a [real] entity?

body.text: yadi viśeṣo [viśeṣyaḥ] mithyā tadā kalpanāsvabhāvasya sāmānyasya vastutā asambhavinī, anyavyavacchedena sāmānyaṃ viśeṣeṣu vyavahriyate / tadevaṃ tattvajñānasya yathāvadanubhavābhāvānnaiva tasya svasaṃvedanapratyakṣatvaṃ yuktam / svasaṃvedanapratyakṣatve 'pi na hi tena jñānena kāryakāraṇabhāvasiddhiḥ, ekātmyena kāryakāraṇātmakasya dvayasvabhāvasya virodhāt / apekṣāviśeṣeṇa tayoḥ svabhāvaḥ parikalpyeta tathāpyarthāntaratvādapekṣāyāḥ svasaṃvedanapratyakṣābhāve sā naiva sidhyati / phalatastadapekṣayā vyavasthitasya tatsvabhāvasyāpi pratyakṣatvaṃ na yuktiyuktam / kāryātmakasya kāraṇātmakasya ca svabhāvasya arthāntarabhūtaṃ jñānamapi bhinnaṃ bhinnam, ato hyekasmin jñāne nobhayoranubhavaḥ bhinnakālatvāt /
body.translated_text: If the particular (<s>viśeṣa</s>) is false, then the reality of the universal (<s>sāmānya</s>), which is the nature of conceptual construction, is impossible, since the universal is applied to particulars through exclusion from others. Thus, since there is no experience of reality-knowledge as it truly is, its being [accessible through] the direct perception of self-cognition is simply not justified. Even if it were [accessible through] self-cognition, the establishment of the cause-and-effect relation through that cognition [is not possible], because the dual nature of what is of the nature of cause and effect contradicts [its having a] unitary essence. If one were to suppose that the nature of both is constructed through a specific dependency — even so, since the dependency is an external object, in the absence of self-cognition's direct perception [of it], it is simply not established. In effect, even the perceptibility of the nature established in dependence on that is not logically justified. The cognition that is of the nature of effect and the cognition that is of the nature of cause are each different, being distinct external objects. Therefore, in one cognition, there is no experience of both, because they occur at different times.

body.text: yadyekasmin jñāne nānubhavastadā na kenāpi sambandhagrahaṇam / ekajñānāvabhāse 'pi 'idaṃ kāraṇaṃ kāryaṃ cedam' iti pratyakṣe na śakyamubhayoḥ sattāsambandhagrahaṇam, nirvikalpakatvāttasya / sambandhagrahaṇābhāve naiva tāvat kāryakāraṇabhāvagrahaṇ, anyathā hyatiprasaṅgaḥ syāt / tatpṛṣṭhabhāvinā niścayākarṣiṇā jñānenāpi paramārthatastad dvayaṃ naiva yujyate, tena tadanubhavasyābhāvāt / anyānubhavasyānyena niścayo 'pi naiva śakyate kartum, atiprasaṅgādeva / ekasantāne ekānubhavasya prajñaptirapi naiva yuktimatī, ekasantāne prajñaptasya vastūno hyasattvāt / bhinnasantāne 'pi parasparānubhavasya tāvadasattvam / niścāyakajñānakāle tāvat kāryaṃ kāraṇaṃ cāpyatītam, ataḥ svasaṃvedanapratyakṣeṇāpi na kāryakāraṇābhāvaḥ prasidhyatīti /
body.translated_text: If there is no experience in a single cognition, then no one grasps the relation. Even if both appear in a single cognition, the grasping of the existential relation of the two as 'this is the cause and this is the effect' is not possible in direct perception, because it is non-conceptual (<s>nirvikalpaka</s>). In the absence of grasping the relation, there is simply no grasping of the cause-and-effect relation; otherwise there would be over-extension (<s>atiprasaṅga</s>). Even through the subsequent determining cognition that draws certainty, that duality is not justified ultimately, because there is no experience of it through that [determining cognition]. The determination of one thing through another's experience is also simply impossible, due to over-extension. Even the designation [of cause and effect] within a single mind-stream is not logically justified, because the entity designated within a single mind-stream does not exist. Even in different mind-streams, mutual experience simply does not exist. At the time of the determining cognition, both the effect and the cause have already passed. Therefore, even through the direct perception of self-cognition, the cause-and-effect relation is not established.

body.text: yadi pratyakṣeṇa kāryakāraṇabhāvo nānubhūyate kathaṃ tadā smṛtisvabhāvo 'pyutpadyeteti cenna, svapnādiṣvarthānubhavābhāve 'pi smṛtisambhavāt / na ca paramārthatastatsvabhāve 'rthāntarānubhavaḥ sidhyati, yathoktaṃ prāk / itthaṃ pratyakṣeṇa tāvanna tasya [kāryakāranabhāvasya] siddhiḥ /
body.translated_text: If cause-and-effect relation is not experienced through direct perception, then how can even the nature of memory arise? — this is not [a valid objection], because memory arises even in dreams and the like without the experience of [real] objects. And ultimately, the experience of external objects having that nature is not established, as stated previously. Thus, the establishment of that [cause-and-effect relation] through direct perception is simply not [possible].

body.text: nānumānenāpi, yathoktanayena pratyakṣeṇānubhūyamānasya kasyacid dharmasyābhāvāt / ataḥ kastāvat tatsavabhāvatvenaṃ sādhyeta / hetavo 'pi sarve svabhāvāsiddhā āśrayāsiddhāśca / dṛṣṭāntadharmyapyasiddhaḥ, sarvaviruddhatvāt tulyaparīkṣaṇīyatvācca /
body.translated_text: Nor through inference either, because of the absence of any <s>dharma</s> experienced by direct perception in the manner stated. Therefore, what could be established as having that nature? All reasons too are unestablished in nature and unestablished in basis. The example-subject (<s>dṛṣṭānta-dharmin</s>) too is unestablished, because of being contradicted by everything and being equally subject to examination.

body.text: api ca, kāryahetunāpi sa vastutvena sādhayituṃ na śakyate, anyo 'nyāśrayadoṣaprasakteḥ / [tathāhi -] kāryakāraṇabhāvasiddhau kāryahetoḥsiddhiḥ, kāryahetośca siddhauḥ karyakāraṇabhāvasiddhiriti suspaṣṭamanyo 'nyāśrayadoṣaḥ / dharmiṇo 'siddhau ca kutaḥ svabhāvahetorapi pravṛttiḥ / dharmiṇaḥ siddhāvapi paramārthataḥ kāryakāraṇabhāvasiddhaye nāstyeva kutrāpi hetovyārptiḥ, sarvatra viruddhatvāt tulyaparīkṣaṇīyatvācca /
body.translated_text: Moreover, that [cause-and-effect relation] cannot be established as a real entity through the causal reason (<s>kārya-hetu</s>) either, because of the attachment of the fault of mutual dependence (<s>anyonyāśraya</s>). [Namely:] the establishment of the cause-and-effect relation [requires] the establishment of the causal reason, and the establishment of the causal reason [requires] the establishment of the cause-and-effect relation — thus the fault of mutual dependence is perfectly clear. And when the subject (<s>dharmin</s>) is unestablished, from where would even the essential-nature reason (<s>svabhāva-hetu</s>) operate? Even when the subject is established, for establishing the cause-and-effect relation ultimately there is simply no pervasion (<s>vyāpti</s>) of the reason anywhere, because of being contradicted everywhere and being equally subject to examination.

body.text: yadi kāryakāraṇabhāvasiddhaye 'asmin satīdaṃ bhavatī'tyucyate, tadāpyetad bhrāntameva / taddhetukāle cāśeṣajagato vidyamānatvād 'asmin satī'ti tasya kāraṇatā naiva sarvathā sambhāvyate / santatāvevānyavyatirekasambhavāttasyāmeva kāryasattvasya hetutvam, na kṣaṇikatve, yadyevamucyate tathāpi paramārthakāryakāraṇabhāvasādhanasyaivātrāvasthitatvānnaiva tad yujyate / kṣaṇikatvavyatirekeṇa paramārthataḥ santaterasiddhatvāt /
body.translated_text: If for establishing the cause-and-effect relation one says 'when this exists, that arises' — even that is simply erroneous. Because at the time of that cause, the entire world exists; hence 'when this exists' — its being the cause is not possible in any way. If it is said that the causal capacity belongs only to the series (<s>santāna</s>), due to the possibility of exclusion of others only within the series, and not to momentariness — even so, since the establishment of the ultimate cause-and-effect relation is precisely what is at stake here, it is not justified. Because the series is not established ultimately apart from momentariness.

body.text: kasyāpi kāryakṣaṇasya sattvaṃ kasyāpi karaṇakṣaṇasattvād yadi kalpyate tadā tatsamakālaṃ sarvasattvāntargaśeṣavidyamānakṣaṇānāmapi sattvaṃ syāt / yathā tatsvahetukṣaṇā vidyamānāḥ, yadi dṛśyante, na vidyamānā yadi na dṛśyante, tathaiva taddhetukṣāsamākālaṃ sarvasattvāntargatāśeṣakṣaṇā vidyamānā yadi dṛśyante, na vidyamānā yadi na dṛśyante / evaṃ sati teṣāṃ kathaṃ na hetutvam /
body.translated_text: If the existence of a particular moment of the effect is supposed from the existence of a particular moment of the cause, then simultaneously, the existence of all moments contained within all sentient beings would also [be established]. Just as the moments of its own cause are either existent if perceived, or not existent if not perceived — in the same way, simultaneously with the moment of that cause, all moments contained within all sentient beings either exist if perceived, or do not exist if not perceived. This being so, how are they not causes [too]?

body.text: api ca, 'yadasti tat sat' ityuktau tacchabdena yadyanyo hetubhūto dharmītyevaṃ gṛhyate tadā so 'pi paramārthataḥ pratyakṣe naiva sidhyati,yathoktaṃ prāk /
body.translated_text: Moreover, in the statement 'what exists is real' — if the word 'that' is taken as referring to another [entity] serving as the subject that is the cause, then that too is simply not established in direct perception ultimately, as stated previously.

body.text: nānumānenāpi dharminaḥ sattvasiddhiḥ sambhāvyate, sarveṣāmapi sattvasādhakānāṃ hetūnāṃ doṣatrayānatikrāntatvāt / yadi dharmī tāvadasiddhastadā sato dharmasya hetutvaṃ naiva sambhavi nāpi cāsato dharmasya yaktam, viruddhatvāt / ubhayadharmastu tāvad bhrānta eva, asapakṣe 'pi sattvāt / naitebhyo bhinnāḥ sādhanākārāḥ / yadi dharmī tāvadasiddhastadāparasyāpi sattvaṃ naiva sidhyati, tadapekṣitatvāt / kāryasiddhirapi tathaivasambhavinī / nātra svabhāvahetunā kāryakāranabhāvasiddhiḥ / nāpyanupalabdheḥ, pratiṣedhasādhakatvāttāsāṃ sarvāsām /
body.translated_text: Nor can the establishment of the existence of the subject be envisaged through inference, because all reasons establishing existence do not transcend the three faults [of being unestablished, contradictory, or inconclusive]. If the subject is indeed unestablished, then the causal capacity of an existent property is simply not possible; nor is that of a non-existent property justified, because of contradiction. But a property of both natures is simply erroneous, since it obtains even in the dissimilar class (<s>asapakṣa</s>). No means of proof are different from these. If the subject is unestablished, then the existence of the other [entity] too is not established, since it depends on that. The establishment of the effect too is likewise impossible. Here, the cause-and-effect relation is not established through the essential-nature reason. Nor through non-apprehension (<s>anupalabdhi</s>), because all of those [non-apprehensions] are provers of negation.

body.text: kāryakāraṇabhāvasiddhistāvat pratyakṣato 'nupalabdheti yaduktaṃ, tatrāpyunupalabdhiśabdastāvat taditarasya upalabdhātmakapratyakṣasyābhiprāyeṇa prajujyate, nānumānamabhipretya yathā tadapramāṇaṃ tathoktatvāt /
body.translated_text: Regarding the statement that the establishment of the cause-and-effect relation is not apprehended through direct perception — there too, the word 'non-apprehension' is employed with the intention of direct perception, whose nature is apprehension of the other [entity], not intending inference, since that has been stated to not be a <s>pramāṇa</s> [in this context].

body.text: api ca, yā khalu upalabdhilakṣaṇaprāptasyānupalabdhiḥ sā samupalabdhiphalā, īdṛśonānvayena yā karyakāraṇabhāvasiddhiḥ tatrāpi paramārthataḥ sandehaḥ / kiṃ tattvataḥ sadityataḥ sat atavā adṛśyānāṃ piśācādīnāṃ samīpavartitvāt athavā dūredeśasthitasya vastvantarasya samīpavartino balādevaṃvidhaḥ samdehaḥ / upalabdhilakṣaṇaprāptasyānupalabdhyā deśāntarāt tadāgamanasya pūrvato vā tatsattvasya niṣedhaḥ kriyate, nānyaphalasyeti /
body.translated_text: Moreover, the non-apprehension of what has attained the characteristic of apprehension has its result in [the establishment of] apprehension. Regarding the establishment of the cause-and-effect relation through such reasoning — even there, doubt remains ultimately. Is it [truly] existent, and therefore existent? Or due to the proximity of unseen beings such as <s>piśācas</s> (demons) and the like? Or does such doubt [arise] due to the force of the proximity of some other entity situated in a distant place? Through the non-apprehension of what has attained the characteristic of apprehension, the negation of its coming from another place, or of its prior existence, is made — and not of any other result.

body.text: yadi tat sattadā tatsattvaṃ yādṛcchikaṃ syāt / dūradeśasthacandradīnāmapi cakṣurvijñānahetutvābhyupagamāt / ye cānye tatsamarthahetavaḥ teṣāṃ nivṛttau tatphalasyāpi nivṛttau vyatirekena yā tatsiddhiruktā, sāpi paramārthato naiva sandehavigatā, piśācādīnāṃ dūradeśasthitānāmapyanyeṣāṃ sattve 'pi tadasattvasandehāt / yadi tadasattvaṃ tatrāpi yādṛcchikatvaṃ sambhavati, yathā mātṛvivāhasaṃskāravati deśe janmādānam yatra ca nāsti mātṛvivāhastatrāsat / tatsamarthakāraṇāntarāṇi santītyevaṃ viśeṣābhāvānna syāt sandeha iti cet? na, teṣāṃ sāmārthyaviśesyāsiddhatvāt, avasaraprāptatvācca tattvasiddheriti /
body.translated_text: If it exists, then its existence would be random (<s>yādṛcchika</s>), since even distant objects like the moon and others are accepted as causes of visual consciousness. And regarding those other competent causes — when they cease, the cessation of their effects too — the establishment through exclusion (<s>vyatireka</s>) [of that relation] is also not free from doubt ultimately, because even when <s>piśācas</s> and other distant beings and others exist, there is doubt about their non-existence. If their non-existence [is established] — even there, randomness is possible, just as in a country where the custom of maternal marriage exists, birth occurs, and where there is no maternal marriage, it does not. If [one says] 'there is no doubt because other competent causes exist, and there is no difference' — no, because the specific capacity of those [causes] is not established, and the establishment of [their] reality has reached an impasse.

body.text: kāryakāraṇayoḥ sandehe sati tannaiyatyārthaṃ yadyapi tatkāraṇaṃ samarthaṃ tathāpi prajñākṣetre viśeṣatastadasiddhivacanāni kathaṃ vidvadbhirnirākriyantām / anvayavyatirekau vyatīricya vastuni tatsiddhiniścāyakahetūnāmabhāvāt tatrānavasthādoṣaḥ syāt / yadi tat sattadā tatsattvaṃ sādhayituṃ śakyate, kintu sahakārivastūnāṃ pṛthaksvabhāva iva anyebhyastadutpattyāśaṅkā kathaṃ nivarteta / nāpyadarśanamātreṇa tadabhāvaniścayo yujyate, atiprasaṅgāt /
body.translated_text: When there is doubt about the causal relation, even though a cause is capable [of producing] that [effect] for the purpose of [establishing] its invariable connection — still, how can the statements of its non-establishment be rejected by the learned, especially in the field of wisdom? Since, apart from positive and negative concomitance (<s>anvaya</s> and <s>vyatireka</s>), there are no reasons that ascertain the establishment of that [relation] in the real thing, the fault of infinite regress (<s>anavasthā</s>) would arise there. If that [cause] exists, then its existence can be proved; but how could the suspicion that [the effect] arises from other [causes] be dispelled, just as cooperative factors (<s>sahakārin</s>) have distinct intrinsic natures? Nor is the certainty of its non-existence tenable merely from non-observation, due to the fault of over-extension (<s>atiprasaṅga</s>).

body.text: nārvagdarśināṃ parebhya utpattiniścayasya spaṣṭaṃ darśanaṃ bhavatīti / yadi parebhyo 'pi tadutpattistadā na bhaved hetubhedād bheda iti cet? na, tathā sati svabhāvavailakṣaṇyādisahakāripratyayebhyo 'pyanutpattiprasaṅgaḥ / yadi pṛthak tadviśeṣeṣveva te sahakāripratyayā upayujyante, na tu kāryamātre iti cet? na, paramārthato viśeṣāṇāmapṛthaktvāt / yadi tadaṃśenāpi [kāryāṇi] utpādyānīti cet? na, naikasmin aṃśabhedaḥ sambhavatīti /
body.translated_text: Those of limited vision have no clear observation of the certainty that [something] arises from other [causes]. If [you say] that if it arises from others too, then there would be no difference due to the difference in causes — no, for in that case, the absurd consequence of non-arising even from cooperative conditions such as the distinctive features of intrinsic nature and the like would follow. If [you say] that those cooperative conditions are employed separately only for those particular features, not for the mere effect — no, because in the ultimate, the particular features are not separate. If [you say] that [effects] are to be produced even through a portion of that — no, because a division into portions is not possible in a single [entity].

body.text: yadi viśeṣasya pṛthagviśeṣe upacaryamāṇatvāt sa tattvānyatvābhyāṃ cintayituṃ na yujyata iti vyāharanto naiva viśeṣān vyāharanti, prājñaptikasya kadācidapi hetāvayujyamānatvāt samūhamātreṇaiva tāvadutpattirvibhaktiścāpi vidhīyate, na tvekaikeneti cet, tadapi naiva yujyate, na ca kāyaṃ vyatiricya samūho bhavati / ataḥ ekaikaḥ samūha eva hetutvenābhyupagamyate / phalataḥ paramārthataḥ kāryakāraṇabhāvasiddhau nāsti kimapi pramāṇam, kāryakāraṇabhāvasya sāṃvṛtikatvāt / ata ācāryaiḥ kāryakāraṇabhāvo yathāprasiddhi siddha ityuktaḥ / ataḥ sa naivāsti paramārthenetyabhyupeyam / ityevaṃ paramārthato 'nityasvabhāvam sādhayituṃ nāsti kimapi pramāṇam, paraparikalpitaśabdānāmapramāṇatvāt, pramāṇasya caitatpramāṇadvayasaṃgṛhitatvāt / nityasvabhāvamapi tāvat paramārthataḥ sādhayituṃ nāsti pramāṇam, pratyakṣeṇaivaṃ tāvattadasiddhatvāt, pūrvavatteṣāṃ sākāranirākārajñānabhyāmapi grahaṇasyānupapannatvat /
body.translated_text: If, because the particular feature is figuratively applied to a distinct particular, it is said to be improper to think of it as either identical with or different [from the entity] — those who speak thus do not speak of particular features at all, since what is merely designated (<s>prājñaptika</s>) can never serve as a cause. If [you say] arising and division are ordained for the mere aggregate alone, not for individual [elements] — that too is not tenable, for there is no aggregate apart from the individual [elements]. Therefore, each individual [element] within the aggregate is accepted as the cause. Consequently, there is no valid means of knowledge (<s>pramāṇa</s>) for establishing the causal relation in the ultimate, since the causal relation is merely conventional (<s>sāṃvṛtika</s>). Therefore, the masters said that the causal relation is established as commonly known. Therefore, it should be accepted that [the causal relation] does not exist in the ultimate. Thus, there is no valid means of knowledge for proving an impermanent nature in the ultimate, since the words fabricated by opponents are not valid means of knowledge, and [all] valid cognition is included within these two types of valid cognition. Nor is there any valid means of knowledge for proving a permanent nature in the ultimate, since perception does not thus establish it, and, as before, their apprehension through cognitions with and without aspects is untenable.

body.text: ātmādinityavastūnyapi yathā svasiddhanteṣu vijñapyante tathā pratyakṣajñāne naivāvabhāsante / pratyakṣajñānaviṣayatve sanmātratvena teṣāṃ sattvam / tathā sati sarvadā sattvaprasaṅgaḥ / na cātra parāpekṣā yujyate, anādheyātiśayatvād apekṣāyā ayogāt, ahetukānāṃ ca viṣayatvānupapannatvat /
body.translated_text: Permanent entities such as the self (<s>Ātman</s>) and the like — as they are proclaimed in one's own doctrines — do not appear as such in perceptual cognition. If they were objects of perceptual cognition, they would exist merely as existents. In that case, the absurd consequence of their always existing would follow. And no dependence on [other factors] is tenable here, because [a permanent entity] cannot receive additional capacity, and because being an object is untenable for uncaused [entities].

body.text: tadvijñānane vijñeyasvabhāvatvād viṣayatvopacāre 'pi tadvijñānasya tadvnnityatvaprasaṅgaḥ / tasya [vijñānasya] vijñeyasvabhāvānusaraṇāt saḥ [vijñeyaḥ] api tad [vijñānaṃ] anusarati, anyathā tena jñeyasvabhāvānusaraṇamapi na kṛtaṃ syāt, tadvijñeyasya tadapekṣitatvāt /
body.translated_text: Even when 'object-ness' is figuratively attributed because [the entity has] the nature of what is to be known by that cognition, the absurd consequence of the cognition itself being permanent like that [permanent entity] would follow. Since that [cognition] follows the nature of the knowable, that [knowable] too follows that [cognition]; otherwise, the following of the nature of the knowable by it [cognition] would not have been accomplished, because that knowable depends on that [cognition].

body.text: nānumānenāpi tat sidhyati, kenāpi hetunā saha tasyāsambaddhatvāt / ataḥ kāryahetustāvadasambhavī / tataḥ kramayaupadyābhyāṃ kasyāpi phalasyānutpādāt / apratyakṣārthasya kimapi sahakārikāṇatvena na parigṛhyate / kāryakāraṇabhāvastāvadanvayavyatirekābhyāṃ spaṣṭamavagamyate / ata ātmādīnāṃ sukhādiphalena saha kutrāpyanvayo na sidhyati avikalakāraṇatvena na tataḥ kādācitkasukhotpatiriti / vyatireko 'pi tāvānnāstyeva, nityatvādavyatireka eva / nāpi svabhāvahetostatsattvasiddhiḥ sambhavati, ādhāradharmiṇo 'siddhatvāt tatsattāsādhakahetoḥ pūrvavaddoṣatrayānatikrāntatvācca / ye tāvad rupādayaḥ prasiddhadharmiṇaste 'pi paramārthato 'siddhā eva / kādācitkatvātteṣāṃ vyavahāreṇāpi nityasyāpekṣā durupapādaiva / anupalabdhyāpi tāvannaiva tatsattvasiddhiḥ pratiṣedhasiddhau samarthatvāt pratiṣedhamātraṃ sā sādhayatīti /
body.translated_text: Nor can that [permanent nature] be established through inference, because it has no connection with any reason whatsoever. Therefore, the reason of effect is first of all impossible — since no result is produced through succession or simultaneity. Nothing is accepted as a cooperative cause for what is not perceptible. The causal relation is clearly understood through positive and negative concomitance. Therefore, nowhere is the positive concomitance of the self and the like with a result such as pleasure and the like established — since [the self], not being an unimpeded cause, does not [explain] the occasional arising of pleasure. Nor does negative concomitance exist, because due to [the self's alleged] permanence, there is invariably no withdrawal [of the self]. Nor can the establishment of its existence through the reason of intrinsic nature succeed, because the supporting subject (<s>dharmin</s>) is not established, and because the reason that proves its existence does not transcend the three faults as before. Form and the like, which are well-known subjects, are also not established in the ultimate. Due to their occasional nature, even conventionally, the dependence on the permanent [entity] is difficult to establish. Nor can non-apprehension establish its existence, because [non-apprehension] is capable only of establishing negation — it proves merely negation.

body.text: api ca, svabhāvānupalabdhirapi tāvannaiva sambhavinī, abhāvavyavahārasādhanaparatvāttasyāḥ / indriyairagrāhyārthena sahaviruddhayorvyāpyavyāpakayoḥkāryakāraṇayoścāsiddhatvād viruddhopalabdhirapi tāvannaiva sambhavinī / pramāṇadvayamatiricya nāsti pramāṇāntaramityanyatra prasādhitatvāt / phalataḥ vastusvabhāvaparīkṣaṇārthaṃ nāsti kimapi sādhakaṃ pramāṇamiti / ataḥ prekṣāvadbhiḥ paramārthataḥ sattvena sa naiva vyavaharttavyaḥ / tatra tāvadayaṃ payogaḥ - yasya paramārthaḥ sādhane nasti kimapi pramāṇam, kalpanānirmitatvāttasya tathaiva samyaktāyā grahaṇaṃ naiva karttavyam, yathāśyāmatvādiguṇaviśiṣṭasya vandhyāputrasyeti /
body.translated_text: Moreover, the non-apprehension of intrinsic nature (<s>svabhāvānupalabdhi</s>) too is simply not applicable, since it is aimed at establishing the convention of non-existence. Since the contradiction, the pervaded-pervader [relation], and the cause-effect [relation] between what is not grasped by the senses and [the permanent entity] are not established, the apprehension of what is contradictory (<s>viruddhopalabdhi</s>) too is simply not applicable. Since it has been established elsewhere that there is no valid means of knowledge beyond the two types of valid cognition — consequently, there is no valid means of knowledge that can serve as proof for examining the intrinsic nature of [permanent] entities. Therefore, the discerning should not treat it as existent in the ultimate. Here the formal argument: That for which there is no valid means of knowledge as proof in the ultimate, being a fabrication of conceptual construction — it should not be grasped as genuinely [real], just as the son of a barren woman endowed with qualities such as dark complexion and the like.

body.text: uparyuktayorubhayoḥ samyaksvabhāvayoḥ prasiddhayarthaṃ nāsti kimapi pramāṇam / vyāpakānupalabdhestāvat pratiṣedhamātraphalatvāt, prekṣāvatāṃ sadvyavahārasya ca pramāṇavyāptatvāt / nāsti hetorasiddhatvamiti yaduktaṃ tat pūrvaṃ vistareṇa vicāritam /
body.translated_text: For establishing both of the above-mentioned correct natures [i.e., both permanent and impermanent], there is no valid means of knowledge whatsoever. Since the non-apprehension of the pervader yields only negation as its result, and since the convention of existence for the discerning is pervaded by valid cognition. The statement that there is no unestablished-ness of the reason — that was examined in detail previously.

body.text: vyāpyavyāpakabhāvānupapatteḥ kalpanāyogaprasaṅganivṛttestu bādhakapramāṇābhāvānnāstyanaikāntikatvamapi / sapakṣe sattvānnāsti hetorviruddhatvamapi / sadasadvyavahārayoḥ pramāṇavyāptatvābhyupagatatve bhāvasiddhireva [nūnaṃ] syāt, tādṛśasya khalu vyāpyavyāpakabhāvasya kutrāpyanvayaṃ vihāya vyatirekamātrena siddherasambhavāt /
body.translated_text: Since the pervaded-pervader relation is untenable, and since the <s>prasaṅga</s> of conceptual fabrication is averted — due to the absence of invalidating valid cognition, there is no inconclusiveness (<s>anaikāntika</s>) either. Due to presence in the similar instance (<s>sapakṣa</s>), there is no contradictory nature of the reason either. If it is accepted that the conventions of existence and non-existence are pervaded by valid cognition, then the establishment of [real] entities would [necessarily] follow, since the establishment of such a pervaded-pervader relation through negative concomitance alone, without any positive concomitance, is impossible.

body.text: vyatirekaniścayo 'pi naivānvayaścayaṃ vinā sambhavati / yat sat tat kathamasaditi tannivṛttyā vyatirekī bhavituṃ śaknoti, sambandhābhāvāt / ato niyatameva pramāṇābhivyaktānvayaḥ sadbhāvavyavahāraśca svīkarttavyaḥ /
body.translated_text: The certainty of negative concomitance (<s>vyatireka</s>) too is impossible without the certainty of positive concomitance (<s>anvaya</s>). How can what is existent, through the exclusion of 'how can what is existent be non-existent,' become negatively concomitant, since there is no [established] connection? Therefore, it is necessarily the case that positive concomitance manifested by valid cognition and the convention of existence must be accepted.

body.text: yadi sa svīkriyate tadā kvacittadeva saditi sadavyavahārapramāṇaṃ yat yat sattānuvidhāne prasiddhaṃ tadevāsmākaṃ vastuni prasiddhamiti cet? tannaiva yujyate / evaṃ sadvyavahārapramāṇavyāptamapi pramāṇamātreṇa paramārthatayā naiyatyena sadviṣayitvena naiva setsyati, vyāpakasaṃnidhānena vyāpyaviśeṣaniścayasya karttumaśakyatvād anyatrāpi sambhavācca / anyathā vṛkṣeṇāpi śiṃśapādiviśeṣā niścayeṇa jñāsyanta iti, kimatenāsti pratikūlam? evaṃ tāvad vṛkṣastvaśeṣaviśeṣasādhāraṇatvānna tena devalādiviśeṣā nirṇetuṃ śakyāḥ / pramāṇaṃ hi naiva tāvad bhāvātikrānte 'parasminnapi sambhavati /
body.translated_text: If that is accepted, then [you say] 'whatever is well-known as conforming to existence somewhere — that something is existent — that very [valid cognition] of the convention of existence is well-known in our [system] as [applying to] real entities'? That is not tenable. Even though valid cognition is pervaded by the convention of existence, by valid cognition alone, the invariable restriction to having an existent object in the ultimate sense will not be established, because the mere presence of the pervader cannot determine a particular pervaded — since it is possible elsewhere too. Otherwise, even the particular species such as <s>Śiṃśapā</s> and the like would be known with certainty through [the universal] 'tree' alone. What is contrary to this? Thus, 'tree-ness,' being common to all particular species, cannot determine the particular species such as <s>Devadāru</s> and the like. For valid cognition does not apply to anything beyond entities.

body.text: itthamabhāvapravṛttatvāt pramāṇahānireva syāt / sarvapramāṇāni bhāvābhivyañjakāni tadvyāptapramāṇabalabhāvivyavahārapravartakānyapi pramāṇāvajñātavastumātre pravṛttatvād vṛkṣādivat kutaḥ sādhāraṇānīti cet? naitad yujyate, saṃvṛtikajagadarthaviṣayīṇyapi pramāṇani bhavantītyetad bahudhā pūrvaṃ carcitam / anyathā sarvapramāṇāni paramārthaikaviṣayīṇi bhaveyuḥ, tataśca sarve tattvadarśinaḥ syuḥ, tattvadarśināṃ kṛte āryamārgabhāvanāyāścāpi nairarthakyam, vaktṛṇāmapi tattvaviṣeye kaścana vivādo na syāt, sarveṣāṃ tattvadarśitvāt teṣu saṃśayābhāvāt / pramāṇalakṣaṇaśāstrāṇāṃ praṇayanamapi nirarthakaṃ syāt, mohanivartanaphalatvāteṣām, tattvajñānārthameva taiḥ sarveṣāṃ mohāvakāśo dūrīkriyata iti /
body.translated_text: Since [valid cognition] operates thus in the domain of non-existence, there would be the abandonment of valid cognition. [If you say:] 'All valid cognitions manifest entities, and even those that operate in conventions of existence pervaded by them [operate] only in the domain of entities apprehended by valid cognition — so why are they common, like [the universal] tree?' — that is not tenable. That valid cognitions are also directed at conventional worldly purposes — this has been discussed extensively earlier. Otherwise, all valid cognitions would be directed solely at the ultimate; from that, everyone would be a seer of truth; for seers of truth, even the cultivation of the noble path would be pointless; among speakers too, there would be no dispute about the nature of reality, since all would be seers of truth and there would be no doubt among them. Even the composition of treatises defining valid cognition would be pointless, since their purpose is the removal of delusion — through them, the scope for everyone's delusion regarding the knowledge of truth is eliminated.

body.text: lakṣaṇakārairlakṣaṇeṣu parasparavirodho bhinnasiddhāntapraveśo vā na kariṣyate, tattvasyaikasvabhāvatvāt / ato vyavahārapramāṇaṃ yannaiva paramārthaviṣayi tadapi vyavahārapramāṇaṃ sambhavatyeva / naiva hi sarvapramāṇāni paramārthatvena vyāptāni / aparamārthaviṣayitve 'pi iṣṭārthaprāpakatvena svapnādivad vyavahārapramāṇaṃ vyavasthāpyate / tadviṣayeṣu 'paramārthā' iti saṃjñāpradāne 'pi nāsti vivādaḥ / dehadhāriṇo ye vastusvabhāvasya yathāvat parijñānena saṃsārakārāto mumukṣavasteṣāmavidyā viṣayebhyo vinivṛttavabhāvā, te ca [viṣayāḥ] samyagjñānagocarā jāyante / abhīṣṭārthakriyāsādhakarthaprāptimātreṇa puruṣā naiva muktāḥ syuḥ sarvasya muktiprasaṅgāt / ataḥ avisaṃvādi jñānaṃ pramāṇamiti yaduktaṃ tat pramāṇasādhāraṇalakṣaṇam / sadvyavahāravyāptamapi tanna samyagarthaviṣayitvena sidhyati / ataḥ kathaṃ tasmin samyag vastu aviparītatayā setsyati / asmin bādhakapramāṇābhāvarupo vyavahāro 'pi sidhyati /
body.translated_text: The definers of [valid cognition] would not introduce mutual contradiction or the entry of different doctrines in their definitions, since the truth has a single nature. Therefore, conventional valid cognition (<s>vyavahāra-pramāṇa</s>), which is not directed at the ultimate, is indeed possible as conventional valid cognition. Not all valid cognitions are pervaded by ultimate [truth]. Even when not directed at the ultimate, conventional valid cognition is established by virtue of being a means of attaining one's desired purpose — like dreams and the like. There is no dispute even if the name 'ultimate' is given to its objects. Those embodied beings who desire liberation from the prison of <s>saṃsāra</s> through the proper knowledge of the nature of reality — for them, <s>avidyā</s> (ignorance) has the nature of being withdrawn from its objects, and those [objects] become objects of right knowledge. People are not liberated merely by attaining purposes accomplished by effective action, since [in that case] the absurd consequence of everyone's liberation would follow. Therefore, the statement 'non-deceptive cognition is valid cognition' is the general definition of valid cognition. Even though pervaded by the convention of existence, it is not established as having a correct object. Therefore, how could the real entity in that be established as non-inverted? In this [case], the convention that has the form of the absence of invalidating valid cognition also succeeds.

body.text: ye tāvat paramārthataḥ svaparobhayāhetukato 'nutpannāsteṣāṃ samyaktayā niḥsvabhāvatvāt, khapuṣpavat / yāni tāvat svato vā parato vā aviparītayā sadvastūni, tāni sarvāṇyapi tathaiva / atra nāsti pramāṇāsiddhatvamapi, yato ye tāvat sāṃkhyādayaste hetuṃ satkāryaṃ vyavasthāpayanti / svata eva vastūni jāyanta iti bruvāṇā naiva yuktisaṅgatāḥ / na hi sad vā asad vā vastu svataḥ svahetau niṣpadyate / ityevaṃ vastuḥ yadyātmānamutpādayatīti niyatameva tatraikatarasyāsiddhatvam / na hyatra asiddhastāvadutpadyate, tadānīṃ tasyāsiddhatvādeva / phalataḥ ko hi nāma kasyotpādakaḥ syāt / vandhyāputrādayaḥ khalvasiddhasvabhāvā nātmasvabhāvamutpādayituṃ kṣamāḥ /
body.translated_text: Those that are in the ultimate unborn from self, from other, from both, or without cause — for them, properly, [their] essencelessness [is established], like a sky-flower. Whatever things are genuinely [existent] from themselves or from others — all of those [are treated] in precisely the same way. Here there is no 'unestablished valid cognition,' because the <s>Sāṅkhyas</s> and others establish the reason as 'the pre-existence of the effect in the cause.' Those who say 'things arise from themselves alone' are not at all in conformity with reasoning. For neither an existent thing nor a non-existent thing is produced from itself in its own cause. Thus, if a thing produces itself, then certainly one of the two [alternatives] is unestablished there. For what is unestablished does not arise — at that time, due to its very unestablished-ness. Consequently, who indeed could be the producer of what? The son of a barren woman and the like, having an unestablished intrinsic nature, are incapable of producing their own intrinsic nature.

body.text: svabhāvata
body.translated_text: Even what is [already]

body.text: siddho 'pi naivotpādakaḥ / tadātmanā siddho 'pi viśeṣābhāvāt kastāvat kasyotpādakaḥ syāt / yastāvat siddhaḥ, sa naivāsiddhasvabhāvayuktaḥ, atiprasaṅgāt / upakāryopakārakatvaṃ tāvadutpādyotpādakasvabhāva eva vastuni yujyate / yadi sa svabhāvena siddhastadā tasmin aṇumātramapi upakāryasvabhāvasyābhāvāt kathaṃ sa utpādyaḥ syāt / aviśeṣaṇīyatve 'pi yadyutpādyatvamahetukatāyāmupakalpyate tadā sajjñānamapi tathaiva kiṃ na parikalpyate / abhinnatvādādhyātmikāyatanādīni tathaiva na parikalpayitavyāni / ata eva vidvadbhiḥ "ābhyātmikāyatanāni na svata utpannāni, sattvāt, sajjñānavat" ityasmin prasaṅge prāṅgārthamaviditvā kecana [prayoge] asmin dṛṣṭāntāsiddhiṃ, kecicca viruddhahetutvaṃ nirupayanti, tatra teṣāmajñānasyaiva doṣaḥ / ityaṃ pareṣu parasparavirodhaṃ pratipādayiṣayā pareṣu siddhāni sajjñānādīni tāvadudāhriyante / svatastāvat saṃsiddhavastuni ko 'pi asvīkṛtiprasaṅgo naivāpāditaḥ /
body.translated_text: established [in its own] intrinsic nature is not a producer. Even though established in that very form, due to the absence of any distinction, who could be the producer of what? What is established is not endowed with an unestablished nature, due to the fault of over-extension. The relation of beneficiary and benefactor is tenable only in entities that have the nature of what is to be produced and what produces. If that [entity] is established by its own intrinsic nature, then since there is not even an atom of the nature of what-is-to-be-produced in it, how could it be something to be produced? Even if production is attributed when there is no distinction, in the absence of a cause — then why is existent cognition not likewise attributed? Due to non-difference, the internal sense-bases (<s>ādhyātmikāyatana</s>) and the like should not be so attributed either. Therefore, the learned — when some, without understanding the meaning of the <s>prasaṅga</s> 'the internal sense-bases do not arise from themselves, because they exist, like existent cognition,' point out the fault of an unestablished example, and others point out the fault of a contradictory reason — the fault is theirs alone, due to ignorance. Thus, with the wish to demonstrate mutual contradiction in the opponents' [position], what is established for the opponents, such as existent cognition and the like, is cited as examples. No <s>prasaṅga</s> of non-acceptance is imposed upon what is established from one's own side.

body.text: sajjñānamapi pareṣu nāsiddham, ato dṛṣṭāntāsiddhiḥ hetorviruddhatvamapi na staḥ / nityaikaparyāyasvabhāvāyāḥ svasantateḥ siddhayarthaṃ tathāvidhahetudṛṣṭāntāsiddheḥ / aparataśca parasparāpratibaddhābhidhānaṃ tāvadabhidhānābhilāṣamātrameva, na tu svasantatervastudharmatāyāḥ prasādhanam / yadi sa siddhaḥ syāttadā tadvirodhābhidhānamucitam, tatra hetudṛṣṭāntayoraprasiddhatvāt tadabhidhānaṃ tāvadapratibaddhameva / pariniṣpannabhāvātmakatve 'pi yadi tadupakāraḥ svīkriyate tadā tadbhinnaḥ sa upakāro na svata utpadyate, arthāntarabhūtasyopakārasya utpannatvāt / yadyabhinnastadopakārasyāpi tathaiva siddhatvāt sa kathamiva setsyati / ato 'sminnapi hetvabhidhānamāvaśyakam /
body.translated_text: Existent cognition is not unestablished for the opponents either; therefore, neither the unestablished-ness of the example nor the contradictory nature of the reason exists. Because such a reason and example are not established for proving a stream of one's own [nature] having a permanent, unitary, sequential intrinsic nature. Furthermore, a statement that is unconnected with one another is merely a wish to speak, not a means of establishing the entity-nature of one's own stream. If that [stream] were established, then a statement of contradiction with it would be appropriate; but since the reason and example are not established there, that statement is simply unconnected. Even if [the entity] has the nature of a perfected reality (<s>pariniṣpanna</s>), if its benefit is accepted, then that benefit, being different from it, does not arise from itself, since the benefit, being a different entity, has [already] arisen. If [the benefit] is non-different, then since the benefit too is established in the same way, how could it be established [as needing to arise]? Therefore, a statement of the reason is necessary even in this [case].

body.text: api ca, yadi kāryakāraṇabhāvo 'yaṃ vṛkṣadrumavat paryāyatayocyate tadā na tathā lokaprasiddhiriti / ato 'vaśyamevāsya pravṛtterbhinnaṃ kāraṇamiti svalpamapi hetūparśanamāvaśyakam / yadi kāryakāraṇaikatvamabhyupagamyate tadā tadupadarśanamasambhavam / yadi hetvabhivyaktau vipariṇāme vā sati phalaṃ bhavatīti nirdiśyate tadā evamayaṃ pṛthagvyasthitaḥ saddhetureva / naivaṃ cintanaṃ yujyate, yato hi sa yadi abhivyaktervipariṇāmasya vāvabhāso niścayena tadbhinnastadā kevalādanyasmādutpattirevābhyupagatā syāt / yadi nāsti bhinnastadā kāryakāraṇaviplavadoṣaḥ prasaktaḥ syāt /
body.translated_text: Moreover, if this cause-effect relation is stated as being synonymous, like "tree" and "<s>druma</s>" (both meaning tree), then that is not how it is conventionally understood. Therefore, it is necessarily the case that a cause different from the arising itself must be indicated — even a minimal indication of a cause is required. If the identity of cause and effect is accepted, then the demonstration of that is impossible. If it is stated that the effect occurs when manifestation (<s>abhivyakti</s>) or transformation (<s>vipariṇāma</s>) of the cause takes place, then this [cause] stands as a distinct, existent cause. Such thinking is not tenable, for if [the cause], being the appearance of manifestation or transformation, is certainly different from that [effect], then origination from something completely other would be accepted. If it is not different, then the fault of the confusion of cause and effect would follow.

body.text: ekasmin yugapad vyaktāvyaktādiviruddhadharmayogaḥ kathamiva yujyeta / ataḥ parasparaviruddhatvād bhedābhedapakṣo 'pi naiva samīcīnaḥ / parasparaparihārasthitalakṣaṇadharmasya itarapratiṣedhakatvād anyatrāsiddhatvācca anubhayapakṣakalpanamapi naiva yuktīmat /
body.translated_text: How could there be the conjunction of mutually contradictory properties such as manifest and unmanifest in a single [thing] simultaneously? Therefore, since they are mutually contradictory, the position of both identity and difference (<s>bhedābheda</s>) is also not correct. Since a property whose characteristic is mutual exclusion negates the other, and since [the conjunction] is not established elsewhere, the supposition of a position of neither [identity nor difference] is also not reasonable.

body.text: api ca, yadyabhīṣṭe taddhetau abhīṣṭaṃ vastu ātmanaḥ purvasvabhāvamaparityajya abhivyaktādyavasthāṃ prāpnoti tadā avasthāvikṛtiprasaṅgaḥ / phalataḥ ekapratītyapekṣaghaṭādīnāmavabhāso 'navabhāsaśca syātām / vārdhakye 'pi balyāvasthādayaḥ spaṣṭaṃ pratibhāseran / yadi parityajyeti pakṣastadā niraṃśasvabhāvatvāt kaścidapyanvayasvabhāvo na syāt / paścād vyaktāvasthāyāmapi dravyāntarasyotpādānnaiva svata utpādaḥ, nāpi kācidabhivyaktiḥ pariṇāmo vā syāditi /
body.translated_text: Moreover, if in the desired cause, the desired thing reaches the state of manifestation and the like without abandoning its previous nature, then the unwanted consequence of modification of states [would follow]. As a result, things like pots dependent on a single cognition would both appear and not appear. Even in old age, the states of childhood and the like would clearly appear. If [one adopts] the position that [the previous nature] is abandoned, then since [the thing has] a nature without parts, there would be no continuity of nature whatsoever. Even in the later state of manifestation, since another substance arises, there is no self-origination (<s>svata utpāda</s>), nor any manifestation or transformation.

body.text: api ca, vyaktamapyanābhāsitaṃ saditaralakṣaṇatvād itarābhyāmabhivyaktipariṇāmābhyāṃ prabhāvitatvāt parikalpitameva / na ca tadanyarupeṇa viparivartanīyam, viruddhatvāt / ekameva vastu tattvaparicchedakāle taditaravyāvṛttyā paricchidyate / anyadapi itaravyāvṛttyā paricchidyate / etadaviparītatvena paricchede sati na tat paricchedayogyaṃ syāt / yasya paricchedakāle yo vicchedyo na bhavati, tadabhāvastena saha parasparaparihārasthitalakṣaṇo bhavati / ye parasparaparihārasthitalakṣaṇāste ekasmin dharmiṇi naiva yuktarupāḥ, yathā - ekasmiścitte mūrttamūrttatvaviśeṣaṇāni / tattvānyatvayoḥ tatsadṛśayorvā kathamekasmin yogaḥ sambhavet / yadi viruddhadharmāṇāmapyekatvaṃ tadā sarveṣāmekadravyatvaṃ prasajyeta / ataśca bandhanamuktyorjātimaraṇayośca yaugapadyaṃ syāt / yadyevaṃ nāsti tadā nāmamātraṃ khalvekatvam / nāstyatra kaścana vivādaḥ / ataḥ yo hi vastubhedaḥ prāgavasthāvilakṣaṇaḥ parikalpyate, sa eva anyastattvavilakṣaṇa iti / yaścānyaḥ sa kathaṃ tasyeti?
body.translated_text: Moreover, even what is manifest but not [yet] appearing is merely imagined, since it has the characteristic of being other than what exists, and because it is brought into being by the other two — manifestation and transformation. And it cannot be transformed into another form, because of contradiction. A single thing, at the time of determining its true nature, is ascertained through its exclusion from what is other than itself. [And] what is other too

body.text: atha yaścāsya svabhāvaḥ paścādupalabhyate, sa pūrvamapi paramārthato vidyata iti? tadā sa tadānīṃ kathaṃ nopalabhyate / athānābhāsasvabhāvatvāt pūrvaṃ nopalabhyata iti cet? tadā haitāvapi tasya tathaivānupalabdhiprasaṅgaḥ / iṣyamāṇe 'pi copalabdhisvabhāve prāgvat paścādapi anupalabdhaḥ syāt / yadi tadanīṃmāvṛtatvādanupalabdha iti cet? tadā paścādapi āvaraṇaśaṅkāsadbhāvāt tathaivānupalabdhiprasaṅgaḥ / dugdhādīnāṃ śatadhā vināśe 'pi yā hi dadhyādirupeṇa upalabdhilakṣaṇaprāptiḥ, sā nāstyupalabdhibādhikā / api ca, yaḥ kaścid dṛḍharupeṇa bhāvasvabhāvastatsya kathamanyathā vikārānubhavaḥ syāt / yadi sa tāavadadṛḍhasvabhāvastadāpi bhaṅguratvānniranvayaṃ vinaṣṭaṃ syāditi tasyāpyanyathā vikārānubhavo naiva syāt /
body.translated_text: Now, [one might ask:] is the nature that is later apprehended also present from the beginning in the ultimate sense? Then why is it not apprehended at that time? If [one says] it is not apprehended earlier because it has the nature of non-appearance — then the same unwanted consequence of non-apprehension [would apply] even later. And even if apprehension is accepted,

body.text: ato 'bhivyakteḥ pariṇāmasya cāyujyamānatvād yā hi tābhyāṃ svata utpattiparikalpanā, sāpi tāvannaiva yujyate / yadi ākasmikī tavat svata utpattistathāpi yaddhi vastūnāṃ deśakālasvabhāvaniyatattvam, tasya kiṃ kāraṇaṃ syāt / nirapekṣeṣu tāvad vastuṣu tathāvidhā naiyatyāmbhāvanā naiva yuktimatī / yadi hi parasāpekṣatvaṃ tadā parata utpattiḥ syāt, na hi upakārābhāve apekṣā nomopapadyate sāpi paścānniṣetsyata iti / apekṣāyā api tāvat sadā saṃnihitasvabhāvatvāt sarvadaivotpattiprasaṅgaḥ / ityevaṃ vyavahāre 'pi tāvat svata utpādo 'sambhava eva /
body.translated_text: Therefore, since both manifestation (<s>abhivyakti</s>) and transformation (<s>pariṇāma</s>) are untenable, the supposition of self-origination through these two is also not tenable. If self-origination is accidental, even then, what would be the cause of the regularity of things with respect to place, time, and nature? For things that are independent,

body.text: parato 'pi naiva [utpādaḥ] / yadi tataḥ [parataścet] utpādaḥ, tadā sa [parākhyaḥ pratyayaḥ] nityo vā bhaved, anityo va / nityāttāvad vyavahāre 'pi notpādo yuktiyuktaḥ, kramākramābhyām arthakriyāyāstatrānu papannatvāt / apratīhatasāmarthyahetuto 'pi na bhavati kadācitkakāryotpattiḥ, nāpi cāvikalahetuto 'pi kādācitkakāryotpattiḥ [sambhavati] / phalataḥ kathaṃ nāma tasmāt kramaśo 'rthakriyā sampasyate? parairanādheyaviśeṣasya [kvacidapi] apekṣāyā anupapannatvāt / sahakārisambaddhasvabhāvamanusaratīti cet? sahakāriṇāmapi sarvadā tathaivānusaraṇaprasaṅgaḥ / nānusaratīti cet? nityatāyāstasya bhaṅga āpadyate / ato nāsti tasya sahakārikāraṇāpekṣā / nityahetusamāśritasya phalasyāpi nānyapratyayāpekṣā, asattvāt / asattve 'pi tatpratibaddhātmabhāvasya prāpyamāṇatvād buddhiparikalpitā apekṣā tāvad vyavasthāpyate, kintu tadabhinirhārāya yo hi apratisāmarthyavān hetuḥ, sa eva tasyānupakārakatvāt [sā] tadapekṣitā bhavati, na tvanyān [apekṣate] /
body.translated_text: Origination from another (<s>parata</s>) is also not [established]. If origination [is from another], then that [cause called] 'other' would be either permanent or impermanent. From a permanent [cause], origination is not reasonable even in convention, since efficacious activity through sequence or simultaneity is not tenable there. And even from a cause of unimpeded capacity,

body.text: ato nityatvena yadabhīṣṭaṃ vastu sadaivopakaroti tadapratihatasamarthyaṃ hetuṃ parityajya kathamanyān apekṣiṣyate? kāryāṇi hi sahakārikāraṇānyapekṣante, tathāpi ye tāvadīścaradayo hetavaḥ, yadi te 'pratihatasāmarthyavantastadā kathamapekṣāmarhanti, yena tebhya utpattimasvīkurvadbhirbalena "naivotpādyante" ityevam ātmabalopadarśanaṃ kariṣyate, nānyatra / ato naiva tāvad akrameṇa kramotpattiriti / evameva kāryāṇi yadi hetudharmān nānusaranti tadā tadabhinnatvaprasaṅgaḥ syādeveti / ato 'vaśyamubhayorbhedo 'bhyupeyaḥ /
body.translated_text: Therefore, if the desired thing that is permanent always serves [as a cause], then abandoning the cause of unimpeded capacity, how would it depend on other [conditions]? For effects do require cooperative causal conditions; but if those causes such as <s>Īśvara</s> and the like have unimpeded capacity, then how can they require [cooperation]? And if

body.text: akramādapi hetoḥ kramiṇaḥ kāryasyotpādo na virudhyatīti cet? naitad yujyate, yataḥ 'kāryāṇi sarvān hetudharmān nānuvidadhate' ityevaṃ tatkathanaṃ syāt / kinyu kāryāṇi tāvat kāraṇānvayavyatirekānuvidhāyīni bhavantyeva / etāvanmātrameva ca kāryakāraṇabhāve hetutvaṃ nāma / kimapi kāryaṃ nityasya vastano vyatirekaṃ naivānuvidhatte, nityasya tāvad vyatirekābhāvādeva / anyathā tadanityameva syānna nityamiti /
body.translated_text: If [one says] that the production of a sequential effect from a non-sequential cause is not contradictory — this is not tenable. For one could then say that "effects do not follow all the properties of their causes." But effects do indeed follow the presence and absence (<s>anvaya-vyatireka</s>) of their causes. And this alone is the [basis of the] cause-effect [relationship].

body.text: nāpi anvayānuvidhānamapi / avikale 'pi kadācit kāryotpādābhāvāt yad yatra anvayavyatirekau nānuvidhatte, na tat tatkāryaṃ yujyate, atiprasaṅgāt /
body.translated_text: Nor is there even the following of co-occurrence (<s>anvaya</s>). Since sometimes, even when [the cause is] unimpaired, the effect does not arise — what does not follow the co-occurrence and co-absence in a given [context] cannot reasonably be an effect of that [cause], because of over-extension.
