body.translated_text: "Blessed One, one who sees two extremes — this is called the view of annihilationism and eternalism. 'Conditioned things are impermanent' — if, Blessed One, one sees thus, this would be an annihilationist view, this would not be right view. '<s>Nirvāṇa</s> is permanent' — if, Blessed One, one sees thus,

body.text: ācāryeṇāpyuktam -
body.translated_text: The master [<s>Nāgārjuna</s>] too has stated:

children.translated_text: For one who accepts [real] existence, the view of eternalism and annihilationism
follows, since own-nature would be either permanent or impermanent.

body.text: ityādi //
body.translated_text: And so forth.

body.text: ataśca sapakṣe sadbhāvānna viruddho 'pi hetuḥ, yato hi vipakṣe yasya sadbhāvaḥ, sa eva viruddhaḥ, na tu yasya sapakṣe sadbhāvaḥ, sa viruddha iti / māyādayastāvat vastutvenānupapannāḥ, jñānajñeyābhyāṃ vilakṣaṇasvabhāvatvātteṣām, iti pūrvaṃ nirdiṣṭameva / na hi jñānajñeyābhyāṃ bhinno vastunaḥ svabhāvaḥ / anutpannasvabhāveṣvākāśapuṣpādiṣvadarśane 'pi pratītyasamutpādasvabhāvastāvat samyaktayā yujyata eveti ye kathayantītyanenāpi [kathanena] naiva [hetoḥ] viruddhatvaṃ sādhayituṃ śakyate 'sambaddhatvāt, vyāpakapravṛteḥ vyāpyasādhane 'śakyatvācca /
body.translated_text: And therefore the reason is not contradictory, since it exists in the similar case (<s>sapakṣa</s>). For only that which exists in the dissimilar case (<s>vipakṣa</s>) is contradictory, not that which exists in the similar case. Illusions and the like are indeed untenable as real things; from both knowledge and the knowable,

body.text: māyādiṣu hi mithyātvena [tatra] naiva pratītyasamutpādaḥ sidhyati, dṛṣṭāntavikalatvāditi yatkathanaṃ tadapyasambaddhameva / yadi paramārthasvabhāvamadhikṛtya māyādīnāmanutpannatvaṃ kevalamabhidhīyate, tattu, tadā svīkāryameva / yato 'smābhirapi paramārthata utpattimabhyupagamya naiva hetornideśaḥ kṛtaḥ, sa tu kevalamubhyasiddhapratibhāsamādāyaiva / na hi siddhāntāpekṣayā dharmihetvādīnāṃ nirdeśaḥ kriyata iti tu pūrvaṃ nirdiṣṭameva / yadi māyādayo vyavahāreṇāpyanutpannā ityabhyupagamyate tadedaṃ lokasyāpi nirvartakatvād asmābhirasyāṃ nivṛttau prayatno naivāstheyaḥ / ko 'pi svasthamanāḥ puruṣo yadi 'yathā māyādīnāṃ pratyayā mantrauṣadhyādayaśca dṛśyate, tathā teṣāmutpattirnaiva dṛśyate' ityevaṃ kathayati, tattu teṣāṃ [kathanaṃ] viduṣāṃ kṛte 'tyantaṃ hāsyāspadamapamānakaraṃ ceti / itthaṃ nāstyasiddhatvamapi hetoḥ /
body.translated_text: The statement that in illusions and the like, dependent origination (<s>pratītyasamutpāda</s>) is not established because of their falsity, due to the deficiency of the example — that too is simply incoherent. If it is stated that only the non-arisenness of illusions and the like is spoken of with reference to their ultimate nature,

body.text: yathoktaṃ bhagavatā -
body.translated_text: As stated by the Blessed One:

children.text: yaḥ pratyayairjāyati sa hyajāto na tasya utpādu svabhāvato 'sti /
children.translated_text: That which arises through conditions is indeed unborn; its origination does not exist by own-nature.

children.text: yaḥ pratyayādhīnu sa śūnya ukto yaḥ śūnyatāṃ jānati so 'pramattaḥ //
children.translated_text: That which depends on conditions is declared empty; one who knows emptiness is heedful.

body.text: sāgaramatinirdeśasūtre 'pyuktam -
body.translated_text: In the <s>Sāgaramati-nirdeśa-sūtra</s> too it is stated:

children.text: pratītya yad yad bhavati tattannasti svabhāvataḥ /
children.translated_text: Whatever arises in dependence — that does not exist by own-nature.

children.text: niḥsvabhāvā hi te bhāvāḥ kadācit sambhavanti na //
children.translated_text: For those entities that are without own-nature never come into being.

body.text: ācāryeṇāpyuktam -
body.translated_text: The master [<s>Nāgārjuna</s>] too has stated:

children.text: pratītya yad yad bhavati tattacchāntaṃ svabhāvataḥ /
children.translated_text: Whatever arises in dependence — that is quiescent by own-nature.
Therefore, that which is arising is quiescent, and origination itself is [quiescent].

body.text: punaśca
body.translated_text: And again:

children.translated_text: That which is dependent origination (<s>pratītyasamutpāda</s>) — we declare that to be emptiness (<s>śūnyatā</s>).
That is a dependent designation (<s>prajñaptir upādāya</s>); that itself is the middle path (<s>madhyamā pratipad</s>).

body.text: yadi vināśādayo hi vikalpāḥ paramārthata utpāttau bādhitā ityucyate, tadapi naiva yuktiyuktam / yā ca bādhābhidhīyate, kāsau? yadi mithyātvena sidhyantītyucyate, tadā vayamapyabhyupagacchāmaḥ / ataḥ saṃvṛtireva sā ityucyate / yadi yuktyā te prasidhyanti tadā paramārthata eva bhaveyuḥ, na tu saṃvṛtyā / yadi prasiddhā tāvad bādhā nirākṛtaivetyucyate, tadapi naiva yujyate, na hi pramāṇabādhitā mithyāsvabhāvā api māyādayo loke 'prasiddhāḥ / ato vastusthitaṃ bhrāntaṃ vijñānamapi māyādivalloke prasiddhamityucyamānamapi na yujyate / na hyekasmin vividhaprakārake viruddhajñāne tathaiva māyādisvamiyucyamānamapi na yujyate / na hyekasmin vividhaprakārake viruddhajñāne tathaiva bhāyādisvabhāvaḥ sambhavati, loke 'pi ca tannaiva jñānasvarupeṇa prasidhyati / māyādīnāṃ jñānasvabhāvatve 'pi jñānasya tadabhinnatayā gṛhītāmithyākāratvenāvabhāsitatvāt tadapi tadvanmithyaiva / anyathā satyāsatyasvabhāvayostāvat ko hi sambandhaḥ syāt / ato nāsti bhrāntiḥ / asti bādhāvirodha ityucyate, tadapi na yujyate, yadi nāstyātmanā virodhastadā kathaṃ sa pramāṇena sādhayituṃ śakyate /
body.translated_text: If it is said that constructs such as <s>vināśa</s> (destruction) are <s>bādhita</s> (invalidated) in their arising from the standpoint of <s>paramārtha</s> (ultimate reality), even that is not logically sound. And what is this <s>bādhā</s> (invalidation) that is spoken of — what is it? If it is said that they are established as <s>mithyātva</s> (falsity), then we too accept that; therefore it is said that this is merely <s>saṃvṛti</s> (conventional). If they are established through reasoning, then they would exist in the ultimate sense alone, not conventionally. If it is said that the established invalidation is simply refuted, even that is not tenable, for even <s>māyā</s> (illusion) and the like, though of false nature and invalidated by <s>pramāṇa</s> (valid cognition), are not unestablished in the world. Therefore, even saying that erroneous <s>vijñāna</s> (consciousness), which is fixed on entities, is established in the world like <s>māyā</s> and the like, is not tenable. For in a single cognition of diverse and contradictory kinds, a nature like that of <s>māyā</s> is not possible, and even in the world, that is not established in the form of cognition. Even if <s>māyā</s> and the like were of the nature of cognition, since cognition appears as having a false aspect grasped as non-different from it, that too would be false just like it. Otherwise, what connection could there be between natures that are real and unreal? Therefore, there is no <s>bhrānti</s> (error). If it is said that there is no contradiction with invalidation, even that is not tenable — if there is no contradiction intrinsically, then how can it be established by <s>pramāṇa</s> (valid cognition)?

body.text: yadyastyāmani virodhaḥ, sa ca pramāṇaiḥ sidhyatyapītyucyate tadā sādhananirbharaḥ saḥ kathamasvīkāryaḥ syāt / na sa virodho 'vabhāsata ityucyate cet, tadāsya visarjanaṃ pūrvamevāsmābhiḥ kṛtam /
body.translated_text: If it is said that there is intrinsic contradiction, and that it is established by <s>pramāṇas</s> (valid means of knowledge), then how could what is dependent on proof be unacceptable? If it is said that the contradiction does not appear, then its dismissal has already been accomplished by us previously.

body.text: api ca, antarjñeyavādināṃ matānusāraṃ yadadvayajñāne ākāradvayaṃ sāgaraparvatabhūmijalādikaṃ tadaṃśatayopacaryate, tadekasmin kathaṃ viruddhāvabhāso 'nuvidhīyate / ato 'ntarjñeyavādibhirapyavaśyaṃ kathañcid bhrāntaṃ jñānamabhyupeyameva / anyathā sarve 'pi tattvavedino jāyeran, na ca prativādibhiḥ saha vivādā api jāyeran / kathaṃ cāriṣṭanīlākṣatākāmalādibhirupahatanetrāṇāṃ dehādayo viruddhasvabhāvadveye pratibhāseran / na ca satyātmakasya jñānasya pratibhāsamārnairmithyākāraiḥ saha kaścanāpi sambandhaḥ, satyāsatyoḥ parasparaviruddhatvāt / na hi bhavatāṃ mate virodho dṛśyata ityataḥ sarveṣāṃ pratyakṣatastattvadarśitvasambhavād muktyatthināṃ kṛte tattvabhāvānāyāḥ pratyatno nirarthaka eva syāt /
body.translated_text: Moreover, according to the view of the <s>antarjñeyavādins</s> (proponents of internal objects), in non-dual cognition the twofold aspect — oceans, mountains, earth, water, and so forth — is figuratively designated as parts of it. How then is contradictory appearance to be accounted for within a single [cognition]? Therefore, even the <s>antarjñeyavādins</s> must necessarily accept that cognition is somehow erroneous. Otherwise, all beings would be knowers of reality, and there would be no disputes with opponents. And how could those whose eyes are afflicted by cataracts, jaundice, and similar conditions perceive bodies and the like as having a dual nature of contradictory character? There is no connection whatsoever between cognition that is of a real nature and false aspects appearing within it, since the real and the unreal are mutually contradictory. Since, in your view, contradiction is not perceived, it would follow that all beings directly perceive reality, and the effort to bring about realization of <s>tattva</s> (truth) for those seeking liberation would be entirely pointless.

body.text: yadyevaṃ cintyate yad 'bhrānte vijñāne vividhāvabhāsānāṃ viruddhatve 'pi virodho naiva vyavasthāpyate, vastuvisayatvātteṣāmati / vastubalapravṛttānumānadvārā vastutvena svīkṛtānāmeva virodho 'bhidhīyate, na tu mithyātvena svīkṛtānām / yadyevaṃ na syāt tadā tadanumānaṃ vastubalapravṛttameva na syāt / phalato vijñāne bhrāntānāṃ mithyākārāṇāmapyavabhāsaḥ syāt / tatra tāvattattvānyatvādivirodho 'pi nābhidhīyate ' - yadyevaṃ vicāryate tadā sāṃvṛtakāryakāraṇabhāvasya kathaṃ virodhaḥ pratipādyate, mithyābhūte tasmin vastubalapravṛttānumānaviṣayatvāsambhavāt sa viruddha iti nābhidheya eva /
body.translated_text: If one thinks thus: 'Even though the diverse appearances in erroneous <s>vijñāna</s> (consciousness) are contradictory, contradiction is not established, because they have real objects as their domain. Contradiction is predicated only of those accepted as real through <s>vastubalapravṛttānumāna</s> (inference proceeding from the force of reality), not of those accepted as false. If it were not so, then that inference would not proceed from the force of reality. Consequently, even false aspects would appear in erroneous consciousness. And regarding those, contradiction such as identity and difference is not predicated' — if this is considered, then how is contradiction to be demonstrated for conventional <s>kāryakāraṇabhāva</s> (causal relation), since, being false, it cannot be the object of inference proceeding from the force of reality, and therefore it should not be stated to be contradictory at all?

body.text: yadi [virodhaḥ] kriyate tadāvaśyamasmākamevesṭasiddhiḥ, na tu yuṣmākam / yato hi bhavatāṃ tathāvidhena virodhena mithyātvasiddhireva syānnatvavabhāsanirākṛtiḥ, mithyātvasyāpi prasiddhayavirodhāt / yadi sa mithyātvena prasādhyate tadāsmākameva pakṣaḥ sthāpitaḥ syād, yato vayamapi kāryakāraṇadeśakālahetupratyayaviśeṣāṇāṃ satyāmapyapekṣāyāṃ [taṃ] pramāṇabādhitaṃ ca mithyā caiva manyāmahe, ata eva [saḥ] saṃvṛtau vyavasthāpyate / tathāvidhavirodhakaraṇena bhavadbhiranyeṣāṃ vastugrahanivṛttiḥ kathaṃ nāma na svīkriyate, kintu nirdoṣābhidhānāttāvad bhavatāmeva bādhā syāt asmākaṃ tu pramāṇānāmapravṛttirapi nāsti, anyathā kathaṃ nāma saṃvṛtau sādhayituṃ śakyaḥ syāt /
body.translated_text: If [contradiction] is maintained, then it is necessarily our position that is established, not yours. For through such contradiction, what would be established for you is merely <s>mithyātva</s> (falsity), not the negation of appearance, since there is no contradiction with the establishment of falsity itself. If it is established as falsity, then our very thesis would be confirmed, for we too regard the specific conditions of cause and effect, place, time, and causal factors as both dependent on <s>pramāṇa</s> (valid cognition) and also false — and precisely for that reason it is established in the <s>saṃvṛti</s> (conventional). How is it that through establishing such contradiction you do not accept the cessation of others' grasping at entities? Rather, since [your position] is stated without fault, the invalidation would apply to you alone. For us, there is not even non-operation of <s>pramāṇas</s> (valid means of knowledge) — otherwise, how could anything be established in the conventional?

body.text: yathaiva kāryakāraṇabhāvaḥ sidhyati tathaiva samyaktvena abhyupagatavatāṃ mithyāropanivṛttaye kevalaṃ vayaṃ pramāṇāni prayuñjamahe, nānyatra / pramāṇānāṃ prayoge satyapi naiva pratyakṣabādhā pravartate / pramāṇaistāvat kevalaṃ vastutattvasya yathāsthitireva svīkriyate, na tu prasiddhivirodho 'pi / anyathā naiva tat pramāṇaṃ syāt / yo hi vastūnāṃ paramārthataḥ, prajñaptasvabhāvaḥ, sa eva pramānairbādhyate / abhrāntatvaṃ hi pratyakṣalakṣaṇam / abhrāntapramāṇena yo hi bādhyate, tasya naiva viṣayatvaṃ yujyate, atiprasaṅgāt / ato nāsyasyāṃ pratijñāyāṃ pratyakṣabādhā / yadhevaṃ na syāttadā spaṣṭāvabhāsitayā bāhyārthasya pratyakṣasiddhe 'pi na sa pratyakṣaviruddhaḥ syāt / phalata ekānekasvabhāvavirahitatve 'pi na sa niḥsvabhāvaḥ sidhyatītiḥ sidhyatīti syāt /
body.translated_text: Just as <s>kāryakāraṇabhāva</s> (causal relation) is established, so too we employ <s>pramāṇas</s> (valid means of knowledge) solely for the removal of false superimposition by those who have correctly understood, and for no other purpose. Even when <s>pramāṇas</s> are employed, <s>pratyakṣabādhā</s> (perceptual invalidation) does not arise. By <s>pramāṇas</s>, the reality of entities is simply accepted as it stands, without any contradiction with what is established. Otherwise, it would not be a valid means of knowledge at all. What is conceptually designated as the nature of entities in the ultimate sense — that alone is invalidated by <s>pramāṇas</s>. For non-erroneousness is the defining characteristic of <s>pratyakṣa</s> (direct perception). That which is invalidated by a non-erroneous <s>pramāṇa</s> cannot rightly be its object, due to overextension. Therefore, there is no perceptual invalidation of this thesis. If it were not so, then even when an external object is established by perception through clear appearance, it would not be contradicted by perception. Consequently, even though devoid of a nature that is either one or many, it would follow that it is not established as <s>niḥsvabhāva</s> (without intrinsic nature).

body.text: taimirikādiṣu keśamaśakādīnāmavabhāse 'pi pratyakṣato virodhānna kenāpi teṣāṃ mithyātvam asvīkriyate / ataḥ svānurūpakāryakāranabhāvena anādikālikaparamparāagatānāṃ sarveṣāṃ janmanāṃ deśākālahetuviśeṣāpekṣitatve 'pi māyotpādavat saṃvṛtāveva vyavasthā kriyate /
body.translated_text: Even in the case of those with <s>timira</s> (cataracts) and the like, though hairs and flies appear [before their eyes], no one fails to accept their falsity on account of perceptual contradiction. Therefore, all births that have come through beginningless succession in accordance with their own corresponding <s>kāryakāraṇabhāva</s> (causal relation) — even though dependent on specific conditions of place, time, and cause — are established in <s>saṃvṛti</s> (the conventional) alone, like the production of <s>māyā</s> (illusion).

body.text:
ye khalu yathāprasiddhaṃ vyavasthāpayanti, teṣāṃ yadā samakālikāsamakālikavyavasthāyāṃ nāsti virodhastadā akṣaṇikatvādidoṣā api teṣu naiva prarvatante, alīkeṣu virodhasyāpravṛtteḥ / māyāsvapnādisadṛśeṣu dharmeṣu paramārthatastāvat kṣaṇikākṣaṇikatvādayo naiva hi yujyate, yathoktaṃ prajñāpāramitāyām -
ye rūpasya nityatve 'nityatve vā ācaranti te nācaranti prajñāpāramitāyām tat kathamiti? tad rūpaṃ yadā nāsti tathā sat tadā kathaṃ tannityamanityaṃ vā syāt /"
body.translated_text: Indeed, for those who establish things as they are commonly known, when there is no contradiction in the arrangement of what is simultaneous and what is not simultaneous, faults such as <s>akṣaṇikatva</s> (non-momentariness) do not apply to them, since contradiction does not operate with respect to what is unreal. With regard to <s>dharmas</s> (phenomena) that are like <s>māyā</s> (illusion), dreams, and the like, categories such as <s>kṣaṇikatva</s> (momentariness) and <s>akṣaṇikatva</s> (non-momentariness) are not tenable in the ultimate sense, as stated in the <s>Prajñāpāramitā</s>: 'Those who practice with respect to the permanence or impermanence of <s>rūpa</s> (form) do not practice the <s>Prajñāpāramitā</s>. How so? When that <s>rūpa</s> does not exist as such, how could it be either permanent or impermanent?'

body.text: evaṃ tāvat sarvajñatāparyantaṃ vistareṇābhidhātavyam /
body.translated_text: In this manner, it should be elaborated extensively up to and including <s>sarvajñatā</s> (omniscience).

body.text: katipayeṣvanyeṣu [sutreṣu] yā khalu saṃskārāṇāṃ kṣaṇikatā deśitā, sā prasādasaṃskārebhyo mānasamudvignaṃ kṛtvā kramaśo nairātmye praveśāyaiva deśitā /
body.translated_text: The <s>kṣaṇikatā</s> (momentariness) of <s>saṃskāras</s> (conditioned formations) that is taught in certain other [sūtras] was taught precisely for the purpose of generating mental urgency from complacent dispositions, and thereby gradually leading [beings] into <s>nairātmya</s> (selflessness).

children.translated_text: Nothing whatsoever arises in this way, nor is there any cessation.
The teaching of cessation and arising is for the purpose of the path.
Through arising, destruction is known; through destruction, <s>anityatā</s> (impermanence) [is known].
Through entry into <s>anityatā</s> (impermanence), one engages in the <s>saddharma</s> (true doctrine).

body.text: yadi māyādivadaṅkurotpādādiṣu bījādīnāṃ sāmarthyamabhyupagamyata iti cintyate tadā vastunaḥ svīkṛtireva syāt, yato hyevaṃ yāni sāṃvṛtikāni bījākhyāni tāni sarvābhidhānasamatikrāntaśaśaśṛṅgādibhyo vinivṛttānyevābhidheyāni / yadyevaṃ nāsti tadā kathaṃ bhavadbhirlokāgavirodhaparihāraḥ kartuṃ śakyeta /
body.translated_text: If it is thought that, just as with <s>māyā</s> (illusion) and the like, the capacity of seeds and so forth in the arising of sprouts and so on is accepted, then that would amount to accepting the reality of entities. For those conventional things called seeds are to be designated as distinct from <s>śaśaśṛṅga</s> (hare's horns) and the like, which transcend all designation. If this is not so, then how could you resolve the contradiction with worldly convention and scripture?

body.text: vayaṃ tu yattāvat sarvasāmarthyavirahalakṣaṇebhyaḥ śaśaśṛṅgādibhyo vinivṛttaṃ tadeva vastviti kathayāmaḥ / 'yadi bhavantastathāvidhamapi saṃvṛtisaditi nāmnābhidhātumabhilaṣante tadā saharṣaṃ bravantu, saṃvṛtiparamārthaśavdairabhidhīyamānānāṃ vastūnām arthakriyākāritvābhedādi'tyevaṃ cintyate? tadapi naiva yaktum, yato hyevaṃ svapnādau gajāśvagnibhūmivṛṣabhādayo mithyābhāvā ye vividhārthakriyāṃ kurvāṇāḥ parasparabhinnaśarīrānugatā dṛśyante te yathaiva bhinnadeśakālavasthāsu dṛśyante tathaiva kiṃ sarvābhidhānasamatikrāntaśaśaśṛṅgādibhyo vinivṛttakāyāḥ santi? na vā? te yadyekāntena vinivṛttakāyāstadā tevāmapi vastutvaprasaṅgaḥ syāt /
body.translated_text: We, however, say that whatever is distinguished from <s>śaśaśṛṅga</s> (hare's horns) and the like — which are characterized by the complete absence of all capacity — that alone is an entity. If it is thought: 'If you wish to designate even such [things] by the name "conventionally existent," then say so gladly — there is no difference in <s>arthakriyākāritva</s> (causal efficacy) between entities designated by the terms <s>saṃvṛti</s> (conventional) and <s>paramārtha</s> (ultimate)' — even that is not tenable. For thus in dreams and the like, the various false entities such as elephants, horses, fire, earth, bulls, and so forth, which are seen performing diverse <s>arthakriyā</s> (causal functions) and possessing mutually distinct bodies, are seen in different places, times, and conditions — are they or are they not distinct in body from <s>śaśaśṛṅga</s> (hare's horns) and the like, which transcend all designation? If they are entirely distinct in body, then even those [hare's horns] would absurdly have the status of entities.

body.text: yadi te vinivṛttakāyā ityucyeta, tarhi kathaṃ bhavantaḥ prasiddhivirodhasya parihāraṃ kariṣyanti? yadyucyeta yathāvabhāsaṃ tatsvabhāvo nāvatiṣṭhatītyataḥ pratītyasamutpannatvājjñānasvabhāvatvena vastutaḥ santīti? etadapi naiva yujyate, yato hi tadā jñānamātrasvabhāvatvātte kāyādiviśeṣānanugatatvādatyantaviruddhasvabhāvenāvabhāsiṣyante / anyasyānyasvabhāvenāvabhāso naiva yuktarūpaḥ, tattvānyatvayorviruddhatvāditi pūrvamevāveditam / yadi jñānasvabhāvastāvad śuddhasphaṭika iva niraṃśaḥ kkacanāpyanavasthito nīlādivividhasvabhāveṣvanavabhāsamāna ityabhyupagamyate, tadā svapnādiṣu gajāśvādīni vastuni tatsvabhāvatvena na samudbhaviṣyanti, tadviruddhakārayogāt / yadyevaṃ nāsti tadā tathāvabhāso naiva śakyarūpaḥ /
body.translated_text: If it is said that they are distinct in body, then how will you resolve the contradiction with what is established? If it is said that the nature does not persist as it appears, and therefore they exist as real by virtue of being <s>pratītyasamutpanna</s> (dependently arisen) and of the nature of cognition — even this is not tenable. For then, being merely of the nature of cognition, they would not possess the specific characteristics of bodies and so forth, and would appear with an utterly contradictory nature. The appearance of one thing with the nature of another is not logically proper, since identity and difference are contradictory — this has been stated previously. If it is accepted that the nature of cognition is like a pure crystal, partless, not located anywhere, and not appearing in diverse natures such as blue and so forth, then in dreams and the like, entities such as elephants and horses would not arise as having that nature, due to the connection with contradictory effects. And if this is not so, then such appearance would not be possible at all.

body.text: ata eva vayaṃ jñānasvabhāvātītaṃ viparītākāreṇāvabhāsitaṃ mithyātvāllaukikamabhyupagacchāmastathā parikalpitasvabhāvenocyamānameva vastutvena bhrānto viṣaya iti kathayāmaḥ, na tu jñānasvabhāvatvena / so 'pi tadabhinnatmakatvenāvabhāsitatvānnasti satyasvabhāvena siddhaḥ / evaṃ vastvātmanā prasiddhamapi pramāṇena yathāvat sfuṭamavabhāsite 'pi paramārthatayā vastusvabhāvatvena na vyavasthāpayāmaḥ, yathā - tṛṇapuruṣaṃ puruṣatvena / ataḥ paramārthato vastuvapuṣābhūtaṃ yanmithyā tasmin pāramārthikasarvadoṣavirahitaśaśaśṛṅgadibhyo nivṛttamanivṛtaṃ vā cittaṃ naiva praviśatītyucyeta tadevaṃ yathoktaḥ saṃvṛtisvabhāvaḥ pramāṇena mithyāsvabhāvatvanokto 'pi na tathaiva cintanīyaḥ, yathā - māyāsvapnādyabhinno vastusvabhāvaḥ pramāṇena suspaṣṭīkṛtaḥ ayamapi paramārtha iti prajñapyate tadā saharṣaṃ prajñapyatāmutsavaścānubhūyatām, parantu prajñaptimātrakathanena naiva vastūni bhinnasvabhāvatvenopādīyante / ataḥ pratījñā parityajyatāmiti kathanamivaitad /
body.translated_text: For precisely this reason, we accept what appears in an inverted aspect, transcending the nature of cognition, as <s>laukika</s> (worldly/conventional) on account of its <s>mithyātva</s> (falsity); and we say that it is an erroneous object spoken of as an entity through <s>parikalpitasvabhāva</s> (imagined nature), not through the nature of cognition. Even that [entity] is not established with a real nature, since it appears as non-different from [cognition]. Thus, even what is established as an entity, though clearly manifested by <s>pramāṇa</s> (valid cognition) as it truly is, we do not establish as having entity-nature in the ultimate sense — just as one does not [establish] a straw-man as a real man. Therefore, if it is said that regarding what is ultimately unreal and false in its entity-nature, the mind neither enters nor does not enter with respect to [its distinction from] <s>śaśaśṛṅga</s> (hare's horns) and the like, which are free from all ultimate defects — then the conventional nature described above, though stated by <s>pramāṇa</s> to be of false nature, should not be conceived in that way. Just as the entity-nature that is non-different from <s>māyā</s> (illusion), dreams, and the like is clearly elucidated by <s>pramāṇa</s> — if this too is designated as <s>paramārtha</s> (ultimate), then let it be designated gladly and let the celebration be enjoyed! However, by mere designation alone, entities are not apprehended as having distinct natures. Therefore, saying 'abandon the thesis' is like this.

body.text: ācāryaḥ khalvatyantagambhīrasāgare paramārthanaye praveṣṭumasamarthānāṃ śāśvocchedādyaparadarśanānāṃ malaviśuddhayarthaṃ bālapṛthagjanānāṃ ca pravṛttyarthaṃ ye paramārthanukūlāṃ yathāprasiddhāṃ puṇyajñānasambhārādyarthakṛyāṃ kurvanti, tānevātra paramārthataḥ saditi kathayāmāsuḥ, na tvatyantaniyataparamārthajñānārthamiti jñātavyam / [yato hi] te naiva santi paramārthataḥ saditi tu pūrvamevāveditam
body.translated_text: The <s>Ācārya</s> (Master) indeed, for the purification of the defilements of those who hold views such as <s>śāśvata</s> (eternalism) and <s>uccheda</s> (annihilationism) and who are unable to enter the extremely profound ocean of the ultimate method, and for the engagement of ordinary <s>bālapṛthagjanas</s> (childish common beings) — those who perform <s>arthakriyā</s> (causal functions) such as the accumulation of <s>puṇya</s> (merit) and <s>jñāna</s> (knowledge) in accordance with what is commonly established and in conformity with the ultimate — it is they alone whom [the masters] declared to be 'ultimately existent' in this context. It should be understood that this was not for the purpose of absolutely fixed ultimate knowledge, for it has already been stated previously that they do not ultimately exist.

body.text: etadarśamaktaṃ vārtike - "yathāvaktu tathaiva" iti / āryaśrīmālāsiṃhanādasūtre 'pi - "yadanityaṃ tanmithyā moṣadharmakaṃ ca, yanmoṣadharmakaṃ tadasatyam" ityuktam / āgame 'uyuktam - "etaddhi bhikṣavaḥ paramaṃ satyaṃ yaduta amoṣadharmaṃ nirvāṇam, sarvasaṃskārāśca mithyā moṣadharmāṇaḥ' iti /
body.translated_text: This has been stated in the <s>Vārtika</s>: 'Just as it is said, so it is.' In the <s>Āryaśrīmālāsiṃhanādasūtra</s> as well: 'What is impermanent, that is false and of deceptive nature; what is of deceptive nature, that is unreal.' And in the <s>Āgama</s> it is said: 'This indeed, O <s>bhikṣus</s> (monks), is the supreme truth, namely, <s>Nirvāṇa</s>, which is of non-deceptive nature; and all <s>saṃskāras</s> (conditioned formations) are false and of deceptive nature.'

body.text: paramārthato niḥsvabhāvatve 'pi vastuno yadi niyatadeśakālādyavabhāso bhavatīti kathaṃ na śaśaśṛṅgādayo 'pyavabhāsanta iti cet? bhavadbirapyasyottaraṃ dātavyaṃ syāt, yato hi keśādivanmithyāvabhāse 'pi kimiti keśādīnāmeva mithyāvabhāsaḥ, na śaśaśṛṅgādīnām / yadi timirādihetupratyayādīnāṃ pratīniyatasāmarthyena tathā pratiniyatatvamityucyeta tadā asadvastuni kathaṃ nāma hetupratyayādīnāṃ pratiniyatasāmarthyamiti kathayituṃ śakyate / yadi taddarśanena tathā bhavatīti cet? tadā tathaiva apareṣvapi pratiniyatahetupratyayatvena pratiniyatasāmarthye 'pi kimiti naiva tathā vyavasthā svīkriyate / iyanmātreṇa vastutve 'pi naiva prasaṅgaḥ, tathā sati taimirikadṛṣṭakeśādīnāmapi vastutvaprasaṅgaḥ syāditi pūrvamevāveditam /
body.translated_text: If, despite things being without own-nature in the ultimate sense, there is an appearance of determined place, time, and so forth for entities, then why do rabbit's horns and the like not also appear? — if such is the objection, you too would have to give an answer to this, for even in the case of a false appearance like hair and so forth, why is there a false appearance only of hair and the like, and not of rabbit's horns? If it is said that this determinacy is due to the specifically determined capacity of causes and conditions such as <s>timira</s> (eye disease) and the like, then how can one speak of a specifically determined capacity of causes and conditions with regard to a non-existent entity? If it is said that it is so because it is seen to be so — then why is the same arrangement not accepted in other cases as well, where there is specifically determined capacity through specifically determined causes and conditions? By this alone there is no implication of real entityhood, for it has already been stated that in such a case, there would be the absurd consequence that the hair and the like seen by one afflicted with <s>timira</s> would also possess real entityhood.

body.text: yadyevaṃ na syāttadā taimirikairadhyālambitānāṃ mithyākeśāṃdīnāṃ hetupratyayā api kathaṃ nāma niyatāḥ syuḥ / taimirikakeśādīnāṃ jñānasvabhāvenāpi satyatvaṃ naiva yujyata iti pūrvameva nirdiṣṭam /
body.translated_text: If it were not so, then how could the causes and conditions of the false hair and the like apprehended by those afflicted with <s>timira</s> (eye disease) be determinate? It has already been pointed out that even by the nature of cognition, the reality of the hair seen by one with <s>timira</s> is not tenable.

body.text: api ca, yadi jñānasvabhāvaḥ satyatvena siddhaṃ syāttadā keśādayo na tato bhinnā iti teṣāmapi satyatvenāvabodhaḥ syāt, kintu tadasiddhamiti pūrvamevābhihitam / keśādayastu mithyātvena lokena pramāṇena ca siddhā eva / ato jñānamapi keśādimithyāsvabhāvenābhinnatvāt tathaiva mithyāmātramiti kathaṃ keśādīnāṃ tatsvabhāvatvena satyatvaṃ syāditi /
body.translated_text: Moreover, if the nature of cognition were established as real, then since hair and the like are not different from it, they too would be cognized as real; but that has not been established, as was already stated. Hair and the like are indeed established as false by the world and by <s>pramāṇa</s> (valid means of knowledge). Therefore, since cognition too is not different from the false nature of hair and the like, it is likewise merely false — so how could the hair and the like be real by virtue of being of that nature?

body.text: yathā sarvaṇi vastūni paramārthato 'nutpannāni tathaiva saṃvṛtāvapyutpannāni bhavituṃ na śaknuvanti, tathā hi - ye tāvat paramārthato 'nutpannāsteṣāṃ saṃvṛtāvapi notpādaḥ, yathā - śaśaśṛṅgādaya iti ye bruvanti teṣāṃ māyādibhiranaikāntikatvam, sādhyavaiparītye sati heturapi sandigdhavipakṣavyāvṛttikaḥ / na hi dṛṣṭamātreṇeṣṭasiddhiḥ, prameyādīnāmubhayapakṣavyāptisambhavāt / ataḥ paramārthato 'sato yadi saṃvṛtāvapyasattvaṃ tadā saṃvṛtisatyasyaiva vināśaprasaṅgaḥ, phalataḥ ko 'pi viparyayo na syāditi /
body.translated_text: Those who say that just as all entities are unoriginated in the ultimate sense, so too they cannot be originated even in the conventional — namely, that those which are unoriginated ultimately have no origination even conventionally, like rabbit's horns and the like — against them, [the reason is] inconclusive due to illusions and the like, and since the <s>sādhya</s> (what is to be proved) is reversed, the reason also has uncertain exclusion from the counter-positive. For the desired conclusion is not established merely by observation, since objects of knowledge and the like may pervade both sides. Therefore, if what is non-existent ultimately is also non-existent conventionally, then there would be the absurd consequence of the destruction of <s>saṃvṛtisatya</s> (conventional truth) itself, and consequently no error whatsoever would exist.

body.text: siddhe 'pi prasaṅge vyāpterasiddhatvād heturanaikāntikaḥ / saṃvṛtāvapi adṛṣṭotpadāḥ śaśaśṛṅgādayo na tathāvidhakarmaṇāṃ sañcayābhāvāna tu paramārthasvabhāvarahitatvād, aniyatavastūnāṃ saṃvṛtisvabhāvo 'pi hetupratyayasamūhanirbhara iti svīkārāt / na hetupratyayanirbharatāmātreṇa vastutvaprasaṅgaḥ māyādimithyāvastūnāṃ hetupratyayasamūhabhāvābhāvābhyāṃ pravṛttinivṛttidarśanāt / na hi darśanamātreṇa vastūnāṃ tathābhāvaḥ sanniti nirdiṣṭam / catuṣkoṭirahitatvād vidvadbhirvastūnāṃ tattvato 'nupapannatvaṃ sādhitam / ato niḥsvabhāvatāyāṃ spaṣṭataḥ siddhatve 'pi pramāṇamārgasya jñānābhāvad ye 'nyato dūṣitān nirākartumabhilaṣante, tebhyastāvat pramāṇatattvaṃ darśayiṣyate / ye paramārthataścatuṣkoṭikotpādarahitāste niḥsvabhāvā e, yathā gagananalinam /
body.translated_text: Even if the implication is established, the reason is inconclusive because the pervasion is not established. Rabbit's horns and the like, which are not seen to originate even conventionally, are so not because they lack ultimate own-nature, but because there is no accumulation of the appropriate kind of <s>karma</s> (action); for it is accepted that even the conventional nature of indeterminate entities is entirely dependent on the assemblage of causes and conditions. There is no implication of real entityhood merely from dependence on causes and conditions, since the activity and cessation of illusory false entities and the like are seen through the presence and absence of an assemblage of causes and conditions. It has been stated that things are not truly so merely because they are seen. Since things are devoid of the four alternatives (<s>catuṣkoṭi</s>), the wise have demonstrated that entities are ultimately untenable. Therefore, even though the absence of own-nature is clearly established, those who wish to refute the objections raised by others without knowledge of the path of <s>pramāṇa</s> (valid means of knowledge) — to them, the truth of <s>pramāṇa</s> will be shown. Those which are devoid of origination through the four alternatives ultimately are without own-nature, like a sky-lotus.

body.text: vivādādhikaraṇāśca sarve padārthāstatsadṛśā eva, evaṃvādinaṃ kaścit 'kathaṃ nāma ekasmādekasyānutpattibodhaḥ' iti pṛcchatīti cet? na hi pramāṇanivṛttyā vastusvabhāvanivṛttiḥ, tasya tadutpādakatvatadātmakatvābhāvāt / yadi kecit 'tadanaṅgīokārāt kaścit tatkhaṇḍayatīti 'kathayantīti cet? tadayuktam / yadi kecana' īśvarādinā ekena jagad utpadyata iti kathayantīti cet? etadapi na yuktam / yadyekamādekasyotpattiriti tadā sā nityād vā anityād vā bhavet / na nityāt, tasya anutpannāvasthāto 'bhinnatvāt pūrvāparakālavad madhye 'pi utpādakatvavirodhāt / yadi sa utpādayatīti cet? pūrvāparakāle 'pi tadvadutpattiprasaṅga, utpattisvabhāvānusaraṇāttasya / nānusaratīti ced? nityatāyā hānisadbhāvāt kramayaugapadyābhyāṃ tasyotpādakatvaṃ vistareṇa nirākriyate / na hi kadācinnityādutpattiryuktimatī /
body.translated_text: And all entities that are the subject of dispute are exactly like that. If someone asks such a proponent, 'How can there be cognition of the non-origination of one thing from another?' — the cessation of <s>pramāṇa</s> (valid means of knowledge) does not entail the cessation of the own-nature of entities, since [pramāṇa] is neither the producer nor the essential nature of that [entity]. If some say that someone refutes it because they do not accept that — that is not reasonable. If some say that the world is produced by a single entity such as <s>Īśvara</s> (God) — that too is not reasonable. If one thing arises from one thing, then that arising would be either from something permanent or from something impermanent. Not from something permanent, because [being permanent] it is not different from its state of not having produced, and just as it is contradictory for it to be a producer in the earlier and later times, so too in the middle. If it is said that it does produce — then there would be the absurd consequence of production in the earlier and later times as well, since it follows its nature of producing. If it is said that it does not follow — since there would be the loss of permanence, its capacity to produce is refuted in detail through both sequential and simultaneous [arguments]. For production from something permanent is never logically tenable.

body.text: na cānityādapi / pūrvakālasamakālapaścātkāleṣu ca sāmānyenotpatternirākṛtatvāt / na hi nityānityābhyāṃ vyatiriktastasya kaścanotpādaka iti /
body.translated_text: Nor [is there production] from something impermanent either, since production in general has been refuted in the earlier, simultaneous, and later times. For there is no producer of it that is different from both the permanent and the impermanent.

body.text: ye cānyaiḥ [vādibhiḥ] ekasvabhāvā īśvarādayo jagato 'sya hetavo manyante, tebhyaścāpi [hetubhyaḥ] ekasvabhāvādekasya phalasyotpattistairnāṅgīkriyate, vividhasvabhāvavato jagatastata utpattisvīkārāt / ata ekasmādekasyotpattirna bhavatīti kathanakāle bhrāntatayā īśvarādikaṃ yannirdiśanti, tattu arthasthiterajñānamevodghoṣayanti / na hi īśśvarādayo hetutvena astitvabhājo bhavanti, paraistasya nityasvabhāvatvenopajñapitatvāt / nityastāvat sarvasāmarthyaśūnya iti ca pūrvameva prasādhitatatvāt /
body.translated_text: And those who, along with other [disputants], consider entities of a single nature such as <s>Īśvara</s> (God) to be the causes of this world — even they do not accept the production of a single effect from a cause of a single nature, since they accept the production from that [cause] of a world possessing manifold natures. Therefore, when it is said that one thing does not arise from one thing, those who erroneously point to <s>Īśvara</s> and the like are merely proclaiming their ignorance of the actual state of affairs. For <s>Īśvara</s> and the like do not possess existence as causes, since they have been posited by others as having a permanent nature. And it has already been established that what is permanent is devoid of all capacity.

body.text: yadi punaḥ paraiste [īśvarādayaḥ] kevalamanityatvenopakalpyante, tadāpi tasmādekasyaiva phalasyotpattirnaiva yuktimatī, yato hi tato yadi bhinnasantānavartināṃ phalānāmutpattirbhavati, tadā tasya anyasajātīyakṣaṇasya pratisandhānābhāvād dvitīya eva kṣaṇe samucchedaḥ syāt / yadyevaṃ tadā tataḥ sadā vijātīyaphalānāmutpattikāle sarveṣāṃ pūrvasajātīyakṣaṇānāṃ paścādvartini kṣaṇe pratisandhānābhāvād ye tāvadanityasvabhāvā īśvarādisaṃjñakā jagato hetutvenopajñāpyante, te ke?
body.translated_text: If, however, others conceive of them [<s>Īśvara</s> and the like] as merely impermanent, even then the production of a single effect from that is not logically tenable. For if effects belonging to different continua arise from it, then since there is no reconnection of a moment of the same class, there would be annihilation in the very second moment. If so, then at the time when effects of different classes are always produced from it, since there is no reconnection in the subsequent moment for all prior moments of the same class — who then are those called <s>Īśvara</s> and the like that are posited as causes of the world while being impermanent in nature?

body.text: yadi te prāthamakṣaṇikasvabhāvatvādekasyaiva kṣaṇasya svabhāvenābhidhīyante, tadapi naiva yuktam, hetorabhāvena tasyotpatterasambhavāt athavā sampūrnameva jagat tadvadahetukameva syāt / yato hi pūrvamapi paścādapi taddhetutvena [sarvathā] kimapi nāstīti / yadyevaṃ tadā tasya kṣaṇamātrasvabhāvahāniprasaṅgaḥ, tasyānādikālikatvamapyasmābhiḥ pūvameva pratiṣiddham /
body.translated_text: If they are described as being of the nature of a single moment because of being momentary in nature, even that is not tenable, since in the absence of a cause, the origination of that [effect] is impossible; or else the entire world would be without a cause just like that [momentary entity]. For neither before nor after does anything exist as its cause [in any way]. If so, then there would be the absurd consequence that its nature of being merely momentary would be lost; and its beginninglessness has already been refuted by us previously.

body.text: yadi tasyāparo 'nyo hetuḥ parikalpayate, tadā sa eva kathaṃ na tasya phalaṃ vā tadutpanno veti kalpyate / kiṃ tadabhāve sa na sidhyatīti, kimarthaṃ sa kalpyata iti / abhinnasantāne vidyamāno sa heturanādikālāt tasyāmeva santatau pravṛtta eveti, naivānyasantāne vidyamānaḥ sannutpattikāraka iti kalpyate tadā tasmin paramārthato 'samakālatvam, anyatra ca sajātīyakṣaṇotpattirapi naiva yujyata iti pūrvaṃ bahuśo nirdiṣṭam / ataccāpi hetubhedasya abhinnakārake prasaṅgaśca paścāt pratipādayiṣyate / etaśca tato 'nekaphalotpattirapi jñātavyā /
body.translated_text: If another, different cause is imagined for it, then why is that very thing not conceived as either its effect or as produced from it? If without it, that [effect] is not established — then for what purpose is it imagined? If a cause existing within the same continuum has been operating in that very continuum since beginningless time, then it is not to be conceived as one existing in another continuum that could produce origination. In that case, there would be no simultaneity in the ultimate sense, and the origination of a moment of the same class elsewhere is also not tenable, as has been stated many times before. And that too — the absurd consequence that a difference in causes would have the same producer — will be demonstrated later. And from this, the production of multiple effects from that should also be understood.

body.text: yadyante cakṣurādayastāvat phalasyaikasya niyatotpādakā iti manyante, tadā andhavadhiratvaprasaṅgaḥ durnivāra eva syāt, yato hi cakṣurādīnīndriyāṇi yadā svavijñānamutpadayanti tadā sajātīyānyakṣaṇāni notpādayanti / phalato dvitīyasmin kṣaṇe sarveṣāmandhabadhirāditvaprasaṅgaḥ syāt / samuha eva tāvad vijñānaphalamutpādayati, ato naikasmādekasya phalotpattiḥ, cakṣuḥśrotramanaskārādibhiścakṣurvijñānādīnānutpādasya [bhūyasā] dṛśyamānatvāditi cettadapi naiva yuktam / yadyevaṃ tadā hetubhedo bhedaniyāmako naiva syāt / yo hi ghaṭādīnāṃ paṭādibhyo bhinnaḥ svabhāvaḥ, sa khalu hetubhedenaiva kṛtaḥ, na tu prakṛtyā janita iti / yadyevaṃ na syāttadā ahetukānyeva tāvad vastūni syuḥ / tatra hetubhede 'pi yadi phalabhedo na syāttadā hetorbhedābhedābhyāṃ phalasya bhedābhedau na kṛtau syātām, vyabhiciritatvāt / bhinnābhinnābhyāṃ vastuno 'bhāvāt sarveṣāmeva ahetukatvaprasaṅgaḥ / itthaṃ naiva te samūhād vyatiriktāḥ sidhyanti, naiva ca te samūhāt pṛtham kartuṃ śakyante / parantu parasparabhinnasvabhāvāt pratyekasmādutpattisāmarthayavato yadi phalamudbhuyate tadā abhinnameva kathaṃ nāmodbhūyate / yadi sarva evaikaphalotpādane samarthāḥ, na tvanekaphalotpādana ityevaṃ cettadapi na yuktam / yadyevaṃ tadā sajātīyaphalapratīsandhānābhāvād dvītiye tāvat kṣaṇe cakṣurādisantānānoccheda eva syāt / yadi teṣu sajātīyakṣaṇotpāde sāmarthyamityucyate tadā tadanyadeva tāvad vastu syāttataśca sāmarthyameva hetuḥ syānna na khalu vastu /
body.translated_text: If they think that the sense faculties such as the eye and the like are the determinate producers of a single effect, then the absurd consequence of blindness and deafness would be quite unavoidable. For when the sense faculties such as the eye produce their own <s>vijñāna</s> (consciousness), they do not produce moments of the same class. Consequently, in the second moment there would be the absurd consequence of blindness, deafness, and so forth for all. If it is objected that the aggregate itself produces the effect of consciousness, and therefore one effect does not arise from one [cause alone], since it is [mostly] observed that visual consciousness and the like are not produced without the eye, ear, mental attention, and so forth — even that is not tenable. If so, then the difference in causes would not be a determiner of difference [in effects]. For the distinct nature of pots and the like from cloth and the like is indeed brought about by the difference of causes alone, and not generated by nature. If this were not so, then things would simply be without causes. In that case, if even with a difference in causes there were no difference in effects, then the difference and non-difference of the effect would not be brought about by the difference and non-difference of the cause, due to deviation. Since an entity that is both different and non-different does not exist, there would be the absurd consequence that everything is without a cause. Thus they are not established as distinct from the aggregate, nor can they be separated from the aggregate. But if an effect arises from each one individually, which has the capacity to produce from its own mutually distinct nature, then how could the effect arise as non-different? If all are capable of producing a single effect but not of producing multiple effects — even that is not tenable. If so, then due to the absence of reconnection of an effect of the same class, there would be the destruction of the continuum of the eye and the like in the very second moment. If it is said that they have the capacity to produce moments of the same class, then that would be an entirely different entity, and it is the capacity itself that would be the cause, and not the entity at all.

body.text: punaśca, sambandho 'pi naiva setsyati, samarthasyopakārābhāvāt / upakurvantyeveti cet, samarthāntarasya tatrāpekṣitatvādanavasthākhyastāvad doṣa eva syāt / yadi te svabhāvabhūtaṃ samarthamuparkurvantīti manyate tadā phalamapi tathaiva kiṃ na kurvantīti / ime samarthāstu vastusvabhāvenābhinnā eva / ato ye yataḥ sāmarthyāt sajātīyaphalamutpādayanti, tata eva ca carkṣurvijñānādisāmānyamapyutpādayanti / ataḥ kathaṃ nāma phalaṃ bhinnaṃ syāt /
body.translated_text: Furthermore, the connection too would not be established, since what is capable would provide no benefit. If it is said that they do benefit — since another capacity would be required for that, there would be the fault called infinite regress. If one thinks that they benefit through the capacity that is their own nature, then why does the effect not do the same? These capacities are not at all different from the own-nature of the entity. Therefore, those which produce an effect of the same class from whatever capacity, from that very [capacity] they also produce the general visual consciousness and the like. So how could the effect be different?

body.text: yadi phalamekaṃ samūhanirbharam, anyacca [phalaṃ] ekaikahetunirbharamityataḥ [phalaṃ] bhinnaṃ syāditi cintyate, tadapi naiva yuktam / samūho 'pi tāvadekaikahetusāpekṣa iti samūhanirbhratvamapi [vastutaḥ] ekaikanirbharatvameva / ataḥ phalasya sajātīya vijātīyatayorbhedo naiva syāt /
body.translated_text: If it is thought that the effect is different because one effect depends on the aggregate while another effect depends on each individual cause — even that is not tenable. The aggregate too depends on each individual cause, so dependence on the aggregate is in reality dependence on each individual [cause]. Therefore, there would be no difference between the effect being of the same class or of a different class.

body.text: hetubhedastrāvat [phalasya] bhedako na bhaviṣyatītyevaṃvidhasya prasaṅgasya ko hyarthaḥ? yadi khaṇḍaśo notpādayatītyarthastadā vastusvabhāvasya niraṃśatvād aśaṃtaścotpādasyāsvīkṛtatvāt kathaṃ nāma prasaṅgaḥ syāt, tallakṣaṇasyānupapannātvāditi /
body.translated_text: What is the point of such an absurd consequence that the difference of causes would not differentiate [the effect]? If the meaning is that [the cause] does not produce partially, then since the own-nature of an entity is without parts, and since production in parts has not been accepted, how could there be an absurd consequence, since the defining characteristic of that is not established?

body.text: yadi viśeṣako [bhedako] na bhavatītyevamartho gṛhyate tadā asiddhamevaitat / hetubhistāvadanekebhyo vijātīyaphalebhyo viparītameva jantaya ityabhidhānamapi naiva yuktam, yato hyekasya aṃśata utpatterasambhavāditi prasaṅgo naivocyate, parantu bhavanto ye vastuṣu parasparaṃ vyatirekaṃ viśeṣaṃ vā manvate, sa vividhairhetubhireva kriyate / yadi vividhahetūnaṅgīkṛtyāpi phalamekavidhameva svīkṛyate tadā bhrāntisadbhāvād vastūnāṃ tāvad bhedo vividhahetubhirakṛta eva syādityevaṃ prasaṅgo nūnamabhidhānīyaḥ syāt / yaścānekavijātīyanivṛttilakṣaṇasya phalaviśeṣasyābhilāpaḥ, so 'pyasambaddha eva, yato hi ye viśeṣātmakatvena viśeṣaphalamutpādayanti, te yadi vijātīyanivṛttyaiva sajātīyalakṣaṇotpattito 'pi nivartante, tadā tebhya utpadyaṃ sajātīyaṃ phalaṃ vijātīyaṃ ca naiva parasparanivṛttaṃ syād, bhitranivṛttihetorabhāvāt /
body.translated_text: If the meaning taken is that there is no differentiator, then this is simply unestablished. It is also not tenable to say that from multiple causes, the opposite of effects of different classes is [produced in] beings, since the absurd consequence is not stated because of the impossibility of partial production of a single thing, but rather because you who consider entities to have mutual distinction and differentiation hold that this is brought about by various causes alone. If, despite accepting various causes, one accepts that the effect is of only one kind, then since error exists, it must surely be stated as an absurd consequence that the differentiation of entities is simply not brought about by various causes. And the statement about the specific effect characterized by the exclusion of multiple different classes is also irrelevant, since if those which produce a specific effect by virtue of being of a specific nature also cease from producing what is of the same class by the very exclusion of what is of a different class, then the effect of the same class and the effect of a different class arising from them would not be mutually excluded, due to the absence of a cause for mutual exclusion.

body.text: yadi hetavaste nivṛttisvabhāvatvāt svayaṃ sajātīyaphalanāṃ bhedakā api bhaviṣyantītyucyate, tadā tathaiva te sāmānyaphale 'pi kathaṃ na bhedakāḥ? yato hi tatra sarve ekaikā hetavo bhavanti / ye tāvadekotpādakasvabhāvā eva te tato viparītaṃ kamapyanyaṃ notpādayituṃ śaktāḥ, yato hi te utpādakasvabhāvanivṛttyā anyārtha iva bhavanti, nānye utpādakasvabhāvā iti / punaste parasparanivṛttasvabhāvāḥ kintu naiva te utpādakasvabhāvanivṛttāḥ / nānyasmin tadutpādakasvabhāva iti naivaṃ kathyate, kintu ye ekenotpādyasvabhāvāste nānyeneti kathyate /
body.translated_text: If it is said that the causes, being of the nature of cessation (<s>nivṛtti</s>), will themselves become differentiators of effects of the same class (<s>sajātīya-phala</s>), then in the same way, how are they not differentiators with respect to the general effect (<s>sāmānya-phala</s>) as well? For therein all individual causes exist. Those that have only one productive nature (<s>utpādaka-svabhāva</s>) are not capable of producing anything else contrary to that, because through the cessation of their productive nature they become as if serving another purpose, and are not of another productive nature. Moreover, they are of mutually ceased natures, yet they have not ceased from their productive nature. It is not said that 'in another there is that productive nature,' but rather what is said is that those that have one nature to be produced are not [produced] by another.

body.text: api ca, te svasvabhāvanaivotpādayanti, na tvanyasvabhāvena, atadātmakatvāt, te ca yathāsvaṃ bhinnā api / svasvabhāvenotpādayantītyasmin kathane ko virodhaḥ? ekasvabhāvasyābhāvo naiva tasya svabhāvo bhavituṃ śaknoti, akārakatvāttasya /
body.translated_text: Furthermore, they produce only through their own nature, not through another's nature, because they are not of the nature of that [other]. And they, though individually distinct, what contradiction is there in the statement that they produce through their own nature? The absence of one nature cannot become its [actual] nature, because of its non-efficacy.

body.text: tenaiva tatphalaṃ niṣpādanīyamiti yaduktaṃ tatra kā yuktiriti cet sāṃkhyaireva tatsamādhānaṃ vidheyamiti śobhanaṃ pratibhāti / yato hi te khalu bhinnabhinnasvabhāvaṃ jagaditi pratipādayanti / atasteṣāṃ yattatra grahaṇaṃ tannivṛtyarthameva ācāryeṇa bhinnavastunirdeśakānāṃ kṛte vyavahāravaśāduktam tāni [vastūni] pratītyasamutpannatayā naiva paramārthata ekārthāni nāpi ca bhinnarthānīti manvānāṃ kṛte naiva kimapyuktamiti / teṣāṃ tāvadanusāraṃ tu māyāsadṛśatvāt sarveṣu teṣu na kimapyekaṃ vastu bhinnamabhinnaṃ vā sidhyati /
body.translated_text: If it is asked, 'what reasoning is there for the statement that the effect must be accomplished by that very [cause]?' — it appears fitting that the resolution should be provided by the <s>Sāṃkhyas</s> themselves. For they indeed maintain that the world has a nature that is both different and non-different (<s>bhinna-abhinna</s>). Therefore, what the <s>Ācārya</s> (master) stated regarding this was said for the sake of refuting that [position], spoken conventionally for those who designate distinct entities — nothing whatsoever was said for those who consider that those [entities], being dependently originated (<s>pratītyasamutpanna</s>), are ultimately neither identical nor different. Following their [view], since all those are like <s>māyā</s> (illusion), no single entity whatsoever is established as either different or non-different.

body.text: api ca, yadi vastuṣu paramārthataḥ svabhavadvayam, ekaścotpādakalakṣaṇaḥ, aparaśca svabhāvalakṣaṇastadā nivṛtte 'pyasmin svabhāvenaivotpādakalakṣaṇastāvannivartata ityuttaraṃ khalu samīcīnaṃ syāditi /
body.translated_text: Furthermore, if entities ultimately had a dual nature (<s>svabhāva-dvaya</s>), one being the characteristic of production (<s>utpādaka-lakṣaṇa</s>) and the other being the characteristic of intrinsic nature (<s>svabhāva-lakṣaṇa</s>), then the reply that 'even when this [productive nature] has ceased, the characteristic of production ceases only by its own nature' would indeed be appropriate.

body.text: yasmin samaye sarva evotpādakasvabhāvastasmin samaye yadi te parasparanivṛttasvabhāvā api tadā utpādakasvabhāvato nivṛttatvāt kathaṃ nāmotpādakāḥ syuḥ / teṣāmayameva svabhāvo yat svabhāvabhede 'pi ekamutpādayanti viruddhasvabhāve 'pi ca sati naiva parīkṣāyogyā iti yadi bhavadbhirucyate tadā pādau prasārya tathātāparīkṣātaḥ parāṅmukhabuddhayo ye vyavahāramātramanusaranti te sukhenāsituṃ śaknuvanti / ye tu tathātāparīkṣāyāṃ pravṛtabuddhayasteṣāṃ kṛte tathaiva sukhāsanaṃ naiva yuktarūpam / yadyevaṃ na syāttadā īśvarādistāvadekaḥ sannapi svabhāvabhede 'pi ca sati krameṇa yugapad vā vicitrasyāsya jagato heturupeṇa naiva kathamapi viruddho bhaviṣyati, tatsvabhāvasya tathaiva svabhāvasiddhatvāt / svabhāvabhede 'pi nāsti parīkṣāyogya ityabhidadhatāṃ kṛte kiṃ nāmottaraṃ dattaṃ syāt? tenaiva phalamutpādanīyamiti pratipādayatāṃ tatra kā yuktiriti ye kathayanti teṣāṃ kṛte agnyādikamapekṣyotpadyamāno dhūmastāvad śakramūrdhato 'uputpadyata iti kathanaṃ yathā ahetukatve yuktyā prasaṅgatayocyate, tathaivātra kimiti nocyate? vyavahāre 'pi ekasamūhāntargato yadyekaphalasyotpādako bhavettadā naiva viruddhaḥ, kintu samūhāntargatastu viruddha evetyevaṃ kathayadbhiḥ saha nāsti kaścana bhedaḥ /
body.translated_text: At the time when all have a productive nature, if they also have mutually ceased natures at that [same] time, then how could they be producers, since they would have ceased from their productive nature? If you say 'this is their very nature — that despite the difference of nature, they produce one thing, and even when there are contradictory natures, they are not fit for examination' — then those who, stretching out their legs, turn their minds away from the examination of <s>tathatā</s> (suchness) and follow mere convention, can sit comfortably. But for those whose minds are engaged in the examination of <s>tathatā</s>, such comfortable sitting is not appropriate. If it were not so, then <s>Īśvara</s> (God) and such, being singular yet having different natures, would in no way be contradicted as causes of this variegated world, whether sequentially or simultaneously, since their nature would be equally established as such. For those who declare that despite the difference of nature there is nothing fit for examination — what answer could be given to them? For those who maintain that 'the effect must be produced by that very [cause]' and who ask 'what reasoning is there for this?' — just as the statement that 'smoke arising in dependence on fire and such actually arises from the top of <s>Śakra</s> (Indra's [head])' is said as an absurd consequence establishing causelessness by reasoning — why is it not said in this case as well? Even in convention, if something included within one aggregate is a producer of one effect, then it is not contradictory; but if [it is included] within [another] aggregate, it is indeed contradictory — with those who speak thus, there is no difference at all.

body.text: atrāpi agnyādibhireva phalamutpādanīyam, na tu śakramūrdhādyanyairiti ye kathayanti, tatra kā yuktiḥ / samuho 'pi bhinnaḥ svabhāvataścotpanna ityevamabhidadhānaiḥ saha ko virodha iti vaktavyaṃ syāt / tatra yathā ekasamūhamāśrityotpadyamānaṃ phalaṃ samūhāntareṇāpyutpadyate tadā tenotpādyasya svabhāvasyāniyatatvād ahetuka ityucyate, tathaiva ekasminneva samūhe vijñānādayo yadā ekahetumapekṣyāpi tadvilakṣaṇahetuta utpadyante tadā kimityahetukatāyāḥ prasaṅgo noktaḥ syāt /
body.translated_text: In this case too, those who say 'the effect must be produced by fire and such, not by others such as the top of <s>Śakra</s> (Indra)' — what reasoning is there for that? One should ask: what contradiction is there with those who say that the aggregate too is distinct and arises from [its own] nature? Just as when an effect arising in dependence on one aggregate is also produced by another aggregate, it is said to be without a cause (<s>ahetuka</s>) because the nature of what is to be produced is undetermined — in the same way, when within a single aggregate, consciousnesses (<s>vijñāna</s>) and such arise from a cause that is dissimilar in character even while depending on one cause, why is the absurd consequence of causelessness not stated?

body.text: hetoryathātmakena prayogeṇa nirduṣṭāt svabhāvaviśeṣād hetubhedo bhedakaśca viruddhāveva syātām / yato hi cakṣurādinā bhinnasvabhāvena cakṣurvijñānādīnāṃ phalānāmutpattikāle sākṣād bhedābhāve 'pi pratītisvabhāvād rūpādayaḥ pṛthagviṣayatvena niyatā bhavanti, tadvikāreṇa ca tathotpadyante / te cānvayavyatirekābhyāṃ samantarapratyayena ca pratītisvabhāvāḥ syuḥ, na tu cakṣurādayastathā niyatāḥ santi / viśeṣeturapi tatsadṛśa eva / indriyeṇa ca viṣayagrahaṇaṃ pṛthaktayā niyatam / ityevamandriyāṇi viṣayāśca na pratītisvabhāvāḥ / indriyeṣu samanantarapratyaye cāpi nāsti viṣayagrahaṇasvabhāvaḥ, viṣayeṇa ca samantarapratyayena cāpi pṛthaktayā viṣayagrahaṇaṃ naiva niyatam / evaṃvidhayā niyatavyavasthayā niścayena hetubhedo bhedaka eva syāt / bheda eva bhinnaviśeṣa ityasau vicāro yadi vyavahāratayā bālapṛthagjanānāṃ pravṛttyarthamevocyate tadā tu sutarāṃ yajyate, na tu paramārthataḥ /
body.translated_text: Through the application of the cause as it actually is, from a flawless particular nature, the difference of causes and the differentiator would indeed be contradictory. For when effects such as visual consciousness (<s>cakṣur-vijñāna</s>) arise from [causes] of different natures such as the eye (<s>cakṣus</s>) and so forth, even though there is no direct difference [in the effect], due to the nature of dependent arising (<s>pratīti-svabhāva</s>), forms (<s>rūpa</s>) and such are determined as distinct objects, and through their modification [the effects] arise accordingly. These would have the nature of dependent arising through positive and negative concomitance (<s>anvaya-vyatireka</s>) and through the immediately preceding condition (<s>samanantara-pratyaya</s>), but the eye and such are not so determined. The distinguishing cause too is similar to that. And the apprehension of objects by a sense faculty is determined separately. Thus, the sense faculties and objects are not of the nature of dependent arising [in the same way]. In the sense faculties and the immediately preceding condition there is no nature of object-apprehension, and by the object and the immediately preceding condition separately, object-apprehension is not determined. Through such a determined arrangement, the difference of causes is certainly a differentiator. If the examination that 'difference is itself a distinct particular' is stated conventionally for the purpose of guiding ordinary childish persons (<s>bāla-pṛthagjana</s>), then it is all the more fitting, but not ultimately.

body.text: atha ye tāvad bhedāstee aprajñaptimātrātmakā vā nivṛttiviśeṣeṇa prajñaptisvabhāvātmakā vā? yadi prathamaḥ pakṣastadā vijñānasya ālambanādasvabhāvādabhinnatvena tathaivānekatvaprasaṅgaḥ / ālamanādisvabhāvo 'pi vijñānavannaiva tāvadekatvanivṛttaḥ syāt / vijñānamapi pratitisvabhāvato nāsti bhinno 'tastathaiva rūpādibhyastasyānutpattiprasaṅgaḥ /
body.translated_text: Now, are those differences merely of the nature of non-designation (<s>aprajñapti-mātra</s>), or are they of the nature of designation (<s>prajñapti-svabhāva</s>) through the distinction of cessation? If the first alternative, then since consciousness (<s>vijñāna</s>) would be non-different from its object (<s>ālambana</s>) which lacks intrinsic nature, there would be the absurd consequence of multiplicity in the same way. The nature of the object and such, like consciousness, would not be free from unity. And consciousness, not being different from the nature of dependent arising (<s>pratīti-svabhāva</s>), would in the same way entail the absurd consequence of non-arising from forms (<s>rūpa</s>) and such.

body.text: tathaivābhinne 'pi rūpādibhya utpadyata ityucyata iti cedekasmin ekadā parasparaviruddhāvutpādānutpādau kathaṃ nāma na viruddhau syātāmityayaṃ doṣo naiva yujyatāmiti vicārya ye viśeṣān vijñānato bhinnārthatvena kalpayanti teṣāṃ tadā vijñānamahetukaṃ syād anyasminneva tadā cakṣurādīnāṃ yogāt / phalataḥ sadā sattvena prasaṅga iti /
body.translated_text: If it is said that '[consciousness] arises even from what is non-different, namely forms and such' — then how would the mutually contradictory [states of] arising and non-arising at one [and the same entity] at one time not be contradictory? This fault should not be accepted. For those who, having examined this, posit particulars as having a nature different from consciousness — for them, consciousness would be causeless, since the eye and such would be connected with something else entirely. And there would be the absurd consequence of [the effect] always existing, since [it would already be] existent as a result.

body.text: yadi prajñaptisvabhāva iti dvitīyapakṣaḥ svīkriyate tadāpi vijñānasyāhetukatvaṃ prasajyata eva, prajñatyātmakatve cakṣurādīnāmupayogābhāvāt / prajñaptyātmakatve kasyāpi yogo naiva bhavatītyataḥ sarveṣāmahetukatvaprasaṅgaḥ / phalataḥ paramārthato 'nekebhya ekasya phalasyotpattirnaiva sarvathā yujayata iti /
body.translated_text: If the second alternative is accepted, namely that [the differences] are of the nature of designation (<s>prajñapti-svabhāva</s>), even then the causelessness of consciousness would follow, because the eye and such would have no utility when [things] have the nature of mere designation. When [things] have the nature of designation, no connection whatsoever obtains for anything; therefore there would be the absurd consequence of causelessness for everything. As a result, the arising of a single effect from many [causes] is ultimately not tenable in any way.

body.text: naikasmādanekasyāpi [utpādaḥ], pūrvadatrāpi hetubhedasyābhedakatvaprasaṅgāt / itthaṃ cakṣuryadisvaviśeṣatayā tajjātīyakṣaṇasyotpādakatvāt svavijñānamutpādayatiti, tadā hetubhedābhāve 'pi phalasya bhinnatvāt phalasya tāvad bhedābhedau kathaṃ nāhetukāviti / yena khalu kāraṇena tatra phalāntarotpattimattve nāstyanyaḥ [kaścana] viśeṣaḥ, niraṃśatvāt sarvavastūnām, ato hettuatāvat svabhāvapracyuto bhūtvā phalaṃ notpādayatīti, tathāpi tasmin hetvātmakatve bhedābhāvāt tannirvṛte phale 'pi tāvad bhedo na syāt /
body.translated_text: Nor [is there] the arising of many from one, because even here there would be the absurd consequence that the difference of cause is not a differentiator, as stated before. Thus, if the eye produces its own consciousness because of being the producer of a moment of its own kind through its own particularity, then even without difference of cause, since the effect is different, how would the difference and non-difference of the effect not be causeless? For there is no other distinguishing [factor] when [each cause] has the capacity to produce a further effect, since all entities are partless. Therefore, even though the cause, having departed from its own nature, does not produce the effect, still, when [the effect] is of the nature of the cause, since there is no difference, there would be no difference in the effect that results from it either.

body.text: ekasmādanekasya anekasmādekasyotpattiryā kathyate, kiṃ sā naiva dṛśyate? [arthāt dṛśyata eva], atastasyāḥ parihāraṃ kartuṃ śakyata ityabhidhānaṃ tāvannaiva yujyate / vayamapi sā ādṛśyeti na sādhayāmaḥ / darśanamātraṃ tu naiva tāvat pramāṇamapi, svapnavanmithyābhāsamānatvāat / yad yathā dṛśyate tattathaiva sadityabhiniviśamānānāṃ kevalaṃ mithyākalpanānāṃ nirākaraṇāya svapna iva sādhyamānatvānnāsti tāvad virodho 'pīti /
body.translated_text: As for the arising of many from one and of one from many that is spoken of — is it not seen? [Indeed it is seen.] Therefore, the statement that 'it can be refuted' is not at all tenable. We too do not prove that it is 'not seen.' But mere seeing is not itself a <s>pramāṇa</s> (means of valid cognition), because it appears falsely like a dream. Since what is being established is like a dream — for the purpose of refuting the mere false conceptualizations of those who insist that 'whatever is seen in whatever way, that exists exactly in that way' — there is no contradiction at all.

body.text:
api ca, cakṣurvijñānādīnāṃ vastūnāṃ yānyanekasmādutyadyamānāni dṛśyante, teṣāṃ pāramārthikaḥ svabhāvastāvadekatvena naiva kathamapi siddhaḥ, sadā vibhinneṣvākoraṣvavabhāsamānatvāt / vividho 'pi svabhāvo yadyekaḥ syāttadā sarveṣāmevaikadravyatāprasaṅgaḥ syāt / yaccaikasya tāvadasiddhiḥ, sā saṃghātātmakatvādasiddhaiva / ekasya cānekaṣāṃ ca vastūnāṃ paramārthata utpattistāvat kutra samavalokyate?
anerkasmādanekasyotpatiriti dvitīyo 'pi pakṣo naiva yuktaḥ / ekaikasya phalasya stāvadanaikairhetubhiḥ kriyamāṇatvādayamapi pakṣastāvadanekasmādekasyaivotpattipakṣaḥ syāt / asya [pakṣasya] doṣo 'pyasmābhiḥ pūrvamevokta iti /
body.translated_text: Moreover, the entities such as visual consciousness (<s>cakṣur-vijñāna</s>) that are seen arising from many [causes] — their ultimate nature is in no way established as one, since they always appear in distinct manifestations. If a manifold nature were also one, then there would be the absurd consequence that everything is a single substance. And the non-establishment of [something being] one — that is non-established precisely because of being of the nature of an aggregate (<s>saṃghāta</s>). Where is the arising of one entity from many, or of many entities, seen ultimately? The second alternative — arising of many from many — is also not tenable. Since each individual effect is produced by multiple causes, this alternative too would be [reducible to] the alternative of arising of one from many. The fault of this [alternative] has already been stated by us previously.

body.text: yadhekasmin phale ekaikasya hetoryogaḥ kriyate, tadā pakṣo 'yam 'ekasmādekasyotpattipakṣaḥ' syāditi / asminnapi pakṣe yaddūṣaṇaṃ tat pūrvamevoktam / ato nāstyayamasiddho heturapi koṭīnāṃ catuṣkaṃ vihāya nāstyanyo 'pi kaścanotpattipakṣaḥ / sarveṣāṃ nityavastūnāṃ nirākaraṇamapi pūrvameva kṛtam / ato nāstyanaikāntikatvamapi hetoḥ / sapakṣe sattvād viruddho 'pi heturnāsti / ācāryo 'pi saṃvṛtau kāryakāraṇabhāvasthitiṃ svīkṛtya yathā vyavahāre ekasmādanekasya cānekasmādekasya cotpattiḥ prasidhyati tathā dṛśyata eveti kathayāgāsa / cakṣurādibhiranvayavyatirekābhyāṃ cakṣurvijñānādīnāmutpattiviśeṣaṃ jñātvā bālāpṛthagjanānāṃ pravṛttyarthaṃ kāryahetvorbhedakāle yadi heturbhinnastadā kāryabhedo 'pi sutarāṃ syādityuktavān, na tu paramārthadaśāyām, paramārthato 'siddhatvāttasya, yathā vicāritaṃ prāgeva / ekasmād hetoranekaphalānāmutpattirayuktetyādikaṃ yaduktam, teṣāṃ sameṣāṃ samādhānamapi pṛthakpṛthasmāmiḥ pūrvameva kṛtam /
body.translated_text: If the connection of each individual cause with one effect is posited, then this alternative would be 'the alternative of arising of one from one.' The refutation of this alternative too has been stated previously. Therefore this is not an unestablished reason (<s>asiddha hetu</s>), and apart from the four alternatives (<s>koṭī-catuṣka</s>), there is no other alternative of arising whatsoever. The refutation of all permanent entities has also been accomplished previously. Therefore there is no inconclusiveness (<s>anaikāntikatva</s>) of the reason either. Since [the reason] exists in the similar instance (<s>sapakṣa</s>), the reason is not contradictory (<s>viruddha</s>) either. The <s>Ācārya</s> (master) too, having accepted the existence of causal relations in the conventional (<s>saṃvṛti</s>), stated that just as in convention the arising of many from one and of one from many is well-known, so it is indeed seen. Having understood the particular arising of visual consciousness and such from the eye and so forth through positive and negative concomitance (<s>anvaya-vyatireka</s>), he stated that when there is a difference of cause in the differentiation of cause and effect, the difference of effect would be all the more [certain] — for the purpose of guiding ordinary childish persons (<s>bāla-pṛthagjana</s>), but not in the ultimate perspective, since that is not established ultimately, as has been examined previously. The resolution of all those [objections] such as 'the arising of many effects from one cause is untenable' has also been individually provided by us previously.

body.text: 'pratītyasamutpannātvād" ityayaṃ yo hetuḥ, sa anaikāntika iti ye kathitavantasteṣāmapyuttaraṃ dattapūrvameva /
body.translated_text: As for those who have stated that the reason 'because of being dependently originated' (<s>pratītyasamutpannatvāt</s>) is inconclusive (<s>anaikāntika</s>) — the reply to them too has already been given.

body.text: yadi vastūni paramārthato na sasvabhāvāni, tadā naiva tāni saṃvṛtāvapi bhavituṃ śakyānīti yaduktam, tasyāpyutaraṃ pūrvaṃ pradattameva / ' ekānekasvabhāvarahitatvāt' iti hetoryadasiddhātvādikamuktam, teṣāṃ sarveṣāmapi samādhānaṃ pūrvācāryaiḥ pūrvaṃ samyaktayā kṛtameva / tathāpi ye tāvat kecana dveṣavaśād dūṣaṇāni prayuñjate, sā teṣāṃ vipratītirevetyabhidhātuṃ śakyate /
body.translated_text: As for what was stated — that 'if entities are ultimately without intrinsic nature (<s>sasvabhāva</s>), then they cannot exist even conventionally' — the reply to that too has been given previously. As for the statements of non-establishment and such regarding the reason 'because of being devoid of a nature that is either one or many' (<s>ekāneka-svabhāva-rahitatva</s>) — the resolution of all of those has been properly accomplished by the earlier <s>Ācāryas</s> (masters). Nevertheless, those who raise objections out of hostility — it can be said that this is simply their misunderstanding.

body.text: yadi te prasaṅgaṃ sādhayanti, tadā naiva hetorasiddhiḥ, vastūnāmekānekasvabhāvarahitatvahetoḥ paraiḥ svīkṛtatvāt / tadabhivyaktadharmasvīkārāttasyāpi [hetoḥ] tāvat sāmarthyataḥ svīkaraṇameva syāditi /
body.translated_text: If they are establishing an absurd consequence (<s>prasaṅga</s>), then the reason is not unestablished, because the opponents themselves accept the reason that entities are devoid of a nature that is either one or many (<s>ekāneka-svabhāva-rahitatva</s>). Since they accept the property manifested by that [reason], acceptance of that [reason] too would necessarily follow through its implicative force (<s>sāmarthya</s>).

body.text: tatra yaistāvat kadācid īśvarādayo nityaikatvasvabhāvena parikalpitāstaisteṣu kramotpādadharmayogo 'pi yataḥ svīkriyate, atastatsāmarthyata ekatvasvabhāvarahitatāpi tairavaśyaṃ svīkṛtā syāt / yato hyekasvabhāvatāyāmanutpādāsthāto 'bhinnatvāt pūrvakālavat paścātkāle 'pyutpādakasvabhāvatā naiva yujyate / yadyutpādaka eva svabhāvaḥ syāttadā pūrvāvasthātaḥ svabhāvasya bhinnalakṣaṇatvādekatvahānireva syāditi /
body.translated_text: In that regard, those who at some point have conceived of <s>Īśvara</s> (God) and such as having the nature of permanent unity (<s>nitya-ekatva-svabhāva</s>) — since they also accept the property of sequential production (<s>kramotpāda-dharma</s>) in those [entities] — through the force of that [acceptance], the absence of a nature of unity would necessarily be accepted by them as well. For when there is a nature of unity, since [the entity] would be non-different from the state of non-production, just as in the earlier state, the nature of being a producer would not be tenable in the later state either. If the nature were indeed productive, then since its characteristic would be different from the earlier state, there would be the loss of unity.

body.text: te [īśvarādayaḥ] tāvadanekatve 'pi naiva yujyante, yato hi tattvatāyāṃ samakālikatvamaparasmiṃśca svaparapratisandhānaṃ tāvannaiva yujyata iti pūrvaṃ prasādhitameva / ye tāvadākāśādīnāṃ trayāṇāmasaṃkṛtānāmekasvabhāvatvaṃ phalapratisandhānābhāvaṃ ca teṣāṃ svīkurvanti, tairapi jñānasvabhāvasya kramodbhūtatvaṃ tāvat svīkriyate, atastatsāmarthyastairapyekasvabhāvarahitataiva svīkṛtā syāt, yato hi pratyekajñānāttajjñeyasvabhāvastāvad bhinna eva syāt / yadi na syāttadābhinnatvāt pūrvavat tajjñāne jñeyasvabhāvo naivopapannaḥ syādata ekasvabhāvastāvannaiva yujyata iti / naiva te 'nekasvabhāvā ityapi pūrvamevāsmābhiḥ prasādhitam /
body.translated_text: Those [<s>Īśvara</s> (God) and others] are not valid even as many, because it has already been established that in reality there can be neither simultaneity nor connection of self and other in another [entity]. Even those who accept the single nature of the three unconditioned [entities] such as space etc. and the absence of connection with results — they too accept that the nature of knowledge arises sequentially. Therefore, by that [logic], they too would have accepted the absence of a single nature, because the knowable-nature from each individual cognition would be different. If it were not [different], then due to non-difference, as before, the knowable-nature in that knowledge would be untenable. Therefore, a single nature is not valid. That they are also not of many natures has been established by us previously.

body.text: ye tāvannityaikasvabhāvāḥ kālapuruṣapradhānabrahmādayaśca vicitrāyā asyā jagadvyavasthāyā hetutvena parikalpyante, te yadi satyāsatyādivividhasvabhāvāṃ vastusāmagrīṃ krameṇa yugapad vā gṛhṇantīti svīkriyate tadā tatsāmarthyata ekatvarahita eva svabhāve te niyamena te niyamena svīkṛtāḥ syuḥ, yato hi vividhasvabhāvasya jagato grahaṇe ekasvabhāvā naiva yujyante / yadi te naiva ekatvena sidhyanti, tadānekatvamapi teṣāṃ sutarāṃ naiva yujyate, saṃghātasvabhāvatvāt /
body.translated_text: Those which are imagined as the cause of this variegated arrangement of the world — eternal, single-natured entities such as Time (<s>Kāla</s>), Person (<s>Puruṣa</s>), Primordial Matter (<s>Pradhāna</s>), <s>Brahmā</s>, etc. — if it is accepted that they apprehend the aggregate of things having various natures such as real, unreal, etc. either sequentially or simultaneously, then by that [logic], they would necessarily be accepted as devoid of unity in nature, because single-natured [entities] are not valid for apprehending a world of various natures. If they cannot be established as having unity, then their plurality is even less valid, because they would have the nature of an aggregate.

body.text: ye tāvat pudgalāmidhaṃ padārthaṃ nityānityatvenānirvacanīyamiti parikalpayanti te 'uyenam ekānekasvabhāvarahitatvena sākṣāt svīkurvantyeva, phalata ekasvabhāvasya tāvannityatve 'nirvacanīyatā naiva yuktimatī / api ca, bhinnabhinnasvabhāvenānubhūyamānasya tāvat kṣaṇikatve 'nirvacanīyatā naiva yujyate / kāyaḥ bhūmiparvatādayo ye 'nityāḥ sāvayavāḥ pṛthaksvabhāvāstān ekadravyatnena parikalpayanti, te 'pi tadavayavadravyaṃ bhinnānekaviṣayavyāpakamiti svīkurvantyata ekatvarahitataiva teṣāṃ svīkṛtā syāt yato hi yadi tasya pratyekasminnavayave nāsti bhinnasvabhāvastadā naiva tasmin vyapakatāpyupapadyata iti /
body.translated_text: Those who imagine the person (<s>pudgala</s>) as an entity that is inexpressible (<s>anirvacanīya</s>) as either permanent or impermanent — they directly accept it as devoid of a single or plural nature. Consequently, inexpressibility is not reasonable when the single nature is permanent. Moreover, for what is experienced as having both different and non-different natures, inexpressibility is not valid in [the context of] momentariness. Those who imagine bodies, mountains, etc., which are impermanent, possessing parts, and of distinct natures, as a single substance — they too accept that the substance of their parts pervades many different objects; therefore, the absence of a single nature would be accepted by them, because if it does not have a different nature in each individual part, then its pervasion across those [parts] would also be untenable.

body.text: niraṃśeṣu tāvadāvṛtanāvṛtatvādiviruddhadharmayogo 'pi naivopapadyate / ye tāvad dehādīnāṃ paramāṇusañcayātmakatvāt tān paramāṇūn pṛthakśaḥ parikalpayanti, te 'pi teṣu saṃyogasaṃghātādīn svīkurvantyevetyatastaistatsāmarthyātteṣāmekatvarahitatāpi
body.translated_text: In partless [entities], the conjunction of contradictory properties such as covered and uncovered is also untenable. Those who imagine the atoms individually, because bodies etc. are of the nature of an aggregate of atoms — they too accept conjunction, aggregation, etc. in those [atoms]; therefore, by that [logic]

body.text: svīkṛtaiva syāditi / yato hi niraṃśasvabhāve [vastuni] yatraiva hi saṃyogādayo 'nubhūyante, tatra tādṛśo nāstyeva kaścana pakṣaḥ [bhāgaḥ], yasmin pakṣeṇa kenacit saha saṃyogaḥ sañcayo vā na bhavanti, tādṛśeṣu [niraṃśeṣu] vistareṇa viṣayavyāptirapi naiva yujyate / na cāvayavinnāmekasvabhāvatvamapi na yujyate, avayavasaṃghātātmakatvātteṣām /
body.translated_text: the absence of a single nature would also be accepted by them. For in an entity of partless nature, wherever conjunction etc. are experienced, there is no part whatsoever in which there is no conjunction or aggregation with some other part; in such partless [entities], pervasion across objects in extension is also not valid. And for part-possessors, a single nature is also not valid, because they are of the nature of an aggregate of parts.

body.text: paramāṇuṣu cāvayavidravyeṣu cobhayeṣu tāvadanekasvabhāvatvamapi na yujyate, yato hi sañcitasvabhāvātmakatvātte yadā naivaikasvabhāvatve yujyante tadā tatparatantratayā vyavasthitatvena teṣāmanekasvabhāvatvamapi naiva sidhyati / itthaṃ yadā kāryaṃ ca kāraṇaṃ cāpi dravyamekānesvabhāvarahitaṃ siddham, tadā tadādhārena kalpitanāṃ guṇakarmasāmānyaviśeṣāṇāṃ saṃghātasya cāpi siddhiḥ sutarāṃ naiva syāt, tatparatantratvātteṣām /
body.translated_text: In both atoms and part-possessor substances, plurality of nature is also not valid, because since they are of the nature of aggregate, when they are not valid as having a single nature, then because they are established as dependent on that [aggregation], their plurality of nature is also not established. Thus, when an entity — whether effect, cause, or substance — is established as devoid of one-or-many natures, then the establishment of qualities, actions, universals, particulars, and aggregates that are imagined on that basis would be even less possible, because they depend on that [substance].
