body.text: evaṃ kādācitkatvasāmarthataḥ samastajñeyānāmekānekasvabhāvaśūnyatvameva svīkarttavyamityanekadhā niveditam / jñānamapi tāvat kāmamekasvabhāvamityupakalpyatāṃ kintu tatsvarūpaṃ vividhasyabhāvagrāhakamiti svīkṛtatvāt tatsāmarthyata ekasvabhāvarahitameva taditi svīkṛtaṃ syāt / yato hi tajjñānaṃ tāvat sākāramityavaśyaṃ svīkarttavyam, anyathā viṣayākāreṇa yo nākāritastasya jñānakāyasya viṣayaġrāhakarūpeṇa vyavasthāpanaṃ nopapannaṃ syāt / yadi sākāratvena svīkriyate tadā tasyaikasvabhāvarahitatvamapi spaṣṭatayā svīkṛtameva syāt, vibhinnātmakatvājjñānakāyasya / vividhatāyā ekatāyāśca parasparaṃ sfuṭo virodhaḥ / ataḥ sarvāṇyeva tāvajjñānāni vibhinnānāṃ vastūnāṃ viṣayitvena svīkriyante / ata eva svayūthyāḥ 'sañcitālambanāḥ paścavijñānakāyāḥ' iti svīkurvanti / ṣaṣṭhaṃ tāvad vijñānaṃ cittacaitasikānapyālambanīkarotīti /
body.translated_text: Thus, it has been demonstrated in many ways that the emptiness of one-or-many natures of all knowables should be accepted on the basis of occasional occurrence and capacity. Even knowledge, though one may wish to imagine it as having a single nature — since it is accepted that its essential nature apprehends various entities — by that [logic] it would be accepted as devoid of a single nature. For that knowledge must necessarily be accepted as having aspects (<s>sākāra</s>); otherwise, for a body of knowledge that is not configured by the aspect of the object, its establishment as apprehending objects would be untenable. If it is accepted as having aspects, then its absence of a single nature would also be clearly accepted, because of the differentiated nature of the body of knowledge. There is a manifest contradiction between diversity and unity. Therefore, all cognitions are accepted as having diverse objects as their content. For this very reason, those of our own school accept that 'the five bodies of consciousness have accumulated objects.' The sixth consciousness also takes as its object mind and mental factors.

body.text: citradarśanakāle citrākāraṃ vijñānamupajāyamāanamanubhūyate, ataḥ sarvajñānāni citrākāratvena prasidhyanti / tatra vividhatāyāṃ [vicitratāyāṃ] svamatasthāpanārtha tāvadanekajñānotpattikalpanamapi nāsti samīcīnam, amūrtatvāttāni tatra prakīrṇarūpeṇa naivopatiṣṭhanti, asthitatvācca vicitratā naivopapadyate / guṇakarmasamavetānāṃ dravyādīnāṃ tāvajjñānena yugapadgrahaṇasvīkārād apare 'pi [siddhāntavādinaḥ] jñānaṃ citrākāratvenaiva svīkurvanti / ye hi dravyaparyāyādiviśeṣaṇaiḥ sarvaṃ vastu tāvanmecakamaṇivadityāmananti, teṣvapi tadviṣayimanaso viṣayatve 'nekavastusvabhāvāḥ svīkriyanta eva / ye tāvaccāturmahābhautikāni vastūnyupakalpayanti, te 'pi jñānamanelavastuviṣayamevābhyupagacchanti / ye ca viṣayaṃ sattvarajastamoguṇātmakamabhyupayanti, te 'pi jñānaviṣayamanekavastusvabhāvaṃ svīkurvanyeva, vastutrayātmakatvasvīkārād viṣayāṇām /
body.translated_text: At the time of perceiving a painting, a cognition of variegated aspect is experienced as arising; therefore, all cognitions are well-known as having variegated aspects. Therein, the imagination of the arising of many cognitions for the purpose of establishing one's own view regarding diversity is also not proper, because being immaterial, they do not abide in a scattered form there, and because without abiding, diversity is untenable. Others [holding different doctrinal positions] too accept knowledge as having variegated aspects, because they accept the simultaneous apprehension by knowledge of substances etc. that are conjoined with qualities, actions, etc. Those who consider all entities to be like a dark gem with the qualifications of substance, mode, etc. — in them too, for the mind that has those as its objects, natures of multiple objects are indeed accepted. Those who imagine entities as consisting of the four great elements — they too accept knowledge as having multiple objects as its content. And those who accept the object as consisting of the three qualities of <s>sattva</s>, <s>rajas</s>, and <s>tamas</s> — they too accept the content of knowledge as having multiple natures, because they accept the objects as having a triple nature.

body.text: ye 'pyatītādiviṣayakaṃ manovijñānamātramanālambanamiti manvate, teṣāmapi mate 'bhidhānākāreṇa yuktatvāttadekākāramiti na yujyate, anekākṣarasvabhāvenāvabhāsitatvāt / svapnādijñānānyapi nīlādivibhinnākārān anubhavantīti tanyekasvabhāvānīti naiva yuktāni / ye khalu vijñānamātrasvabhāvaṃ jagadityāmananti, te bāhyapadārthānāmaviṣayibhūtatvāttat svasaṃvedanasvarūpaṃ paryantaṃ ca jñānamiti svīkurvanti, te 'pyanādikālīnabhrāntavāsānāparipākavaśād rūpādivibhinnaviparītāvabhāsānāṃ sarveṣāṃ vijñānānāmutpattiṃ svīkurvantyato vijñānamekasvabhāvamiti naivābhyupagacchanti / phalato darśaneṣu kasminnapi vijñānaṃ naikasvabhāvamiti sidhyati / yadi tathā na sidhyati, tadā anekasvabhāvo 'pi na sidhyatīti bahuśaḥ pūrvamāveditam /
body.translated_text: Those who consider that mental consciousness alone, having past etc. as its objects, is without an object (<s>anālambana</s>) — in their view too, since it is appropriate in the form of expression, it is not valid that [knowledge] has a single aspect, because it appears with the nature of multiple syllables. Even cognitions in dreams etc. experience diverse aspects such as blue etc.; therefore, they are not valid as having a single nature. Those who consider the world to be of the nature of consciousness only (<s>vijñānamātra</s>) — since external objects do not constitute its content, they accept knowledge as self-awareness (<s>svasaṃvedana</s>) in its essential form and as ultimate. They too accept the arising of all cognitions as having diverse and contrary appearances such as form etc. due to the force of the ripening of beginningless erroneous latent impressions (<s>vāsanā</s>); therefore, they do not accept that consciousness has a single nature. Consequently, in no philosophical system is consciousness established as having a single nature. If it is not thus established, then it is also not established as having a plural nature — as has been frequently stated before.

body.text: ata eva svātantryeṇa sādhako hetirapyayaṃ nāsiddha iti yathoktanayena vādiprativādyubhyeṣu sarve dharma ekānekasvabhāvarahitā eva siddhāḥ / ye va vyavacchedamātrātmakāsteṣu sādhyasādhanānugato dharmeyeva avastubhūtaḥ sidhyatīti pūrvamanekadhā nirdiṣṭam / svaparobhayasiddhāntavādibhirupakalpitadharmiṇyapi sādhyadharmasya yathoktā vyavacchedamātratā dvayorapi siddhaiva /
body.translated_text: For this very reason, this independently proving reason is also not unestablished. As stated, for both proponents and opponents, all <s>dharmas</s> are established as devoid of one-or-many natures. Or, in those [<s>dharmas</s>] that are of the nature of mere exclusion (<s>vyavacchedamātra</s>), only the property that follows proof and what is to be proved — itself being non-substantial — is established. This has been indicated previously in many ways. Even in subjects imagined by holders of one's own, the opponent's, or both positions, the stated mere-exclusion-nature of the property to be proved is established for both.

body.text: punaśca, heturapyayaṃ kathaṃ sidhyati? yadyunupalabdhyeti cet? sāpyaparayānupalabdhyā sidhyatītyanavasthāprasaṅgaḥ syāt / nāpi pratyakṣeṇānupalabdhisiddhirapi, pratyakṣasyāviṣayatvādityapi kathanaṃ nirākṛtameva, yato hi yathoktanayenaiva te hetuṃ sādhayantīti /
body.translated_text: Furthermore, how is this reason established? If through non-apprehension (<s>anupalabdhi</s>)? That too would be established by another non-apprehension, leading to the absurd consequence of infinite regress. Nor is non-apprehension established by perception, because perception does not have [non-apprehension] as its object — this objection too has been refuted, because they establish the reason precisely through the stated method.

body.text: ityevaṃ ye kecidindriyairagamyā ātmādayaste tadvyāptakramikakāryayogādidharmāṇāṃ svīkṛtyā ekānekasvabhāvarahitatvenaiva prasiddhāḥ / yadi dharmyeva tāvadasiddhastadā tadrāhityacintanamapyayuktam, tādṛśānāṃ vastūnāṃ pratiṣedhāya dharmiṇaḥ parīkṣāyāḥ sarvatrānivāryatvāt / atastaddharmā nopalabhyanta iti pūrvameva nirdiṣṭam / anyathā [yadyevaṃ na syāt] tadā tanniṣedhāya bhavatāmapi arthakriyāsāmarthyaviyogalakṣaṇo hetustāvat kathaṃ siddho bhaviṣyatīti codanā kathaṃ na syāt / paraparikalpite dharmiṇi tathāvidhakramikakāryāṇāṃ svīkṛtyaiva tadvyāptadharmāṇāṃ niṣpattestanmatamātrāśritatvād dharmiṇastasya tāvat parikalpitatvameva / anumānena tathā jñāne satyapi nāstyevānavasthāprasaṅgaḥ, svataḥ pramāṇatvāttasya / vyavahāreṇāpi tāvat sādhyavyāptasādhanasya siddhatvāditi pūrvameva samyaguktatvāt /
body.translated_text: Thus, whatever entities like the self etc. are not accessible to the senses — they too, by accepting properties such as sequential causal efficacy etc. that pervade them, are well-known as devoid of one-or-many natures. If the subject itself is unestablished, then thinking about its absence is also not appropriate, because investigation of the subject is unavoidable everywhere for denying such entities. Therefore, it has been stated earlier that their properties are not apprehended. Otherwise, how would the objection not arise that even for you, the reason characterized by the absence of the capacity for causal efficacy is not established for denying them? Since the subject imagined by the opponent [involves] accepting sequential causal effects of that kind, and since the accomplishment of properties pervaded by those depends solely on that [opponent's] view, that very subject is imagined. Even when there is such knowledge through inference, there is no absurd consequence of infinite regress, because that [knowledge] is self-validating (<s>svataḥ pramāṇa</s>). And because it has been correctly stated previously that in convention, the means of proof pervaded by what is to be proved is established.

body.text: rūpādayastāvad dhārmiṇaḥ, ye khalvaparokṣāste 'pi pratyakṣata ekasvabhāvarahitā eva, vividheṣvākāreṣu sarvadā pratibhāsanādaviśeṣeṇa pṛthakśa ekasvabhāvatvenānanubhūyamānatvāt / ekasvabhāvahitatvena siddhe satyanekasvabhāvarāhityamapi sutarāṃ pratyakṣataḥ siddhameva, ekaikasañcitatvadanekasvabhāvasya / na khalu pratyakṣādipramāṇāni vyavahāreṇāsadbhūtānīti pūrvamevoktam /
body.translated_text: Forms and other directly perceptible subjects — they too are devoid of a single nature even from perception, because since they always appear in diverse aspects without distinction, they are not individually experienced as having a single nature. When the absence of a single nature is established, the absence of a plural nature is even more easily established from perception, because plural nature consists of individual [single natures] accumulated together. It has been stated previously that <s>pramāṇas</s> such as perception etc. are not conventionally non-existent.

body.text: yatkhalu paramārthato 'sat, tat saṃvṛtito 'pyasadeva, kriyatāpyaṃśenānanubhāvyatvāt, śaśaśṛṅgavat / yadi pratyakṣamapi tathaivetyucyeta, evaṃ satyasambaddhatvādanaikāntikatvamevāsya hetoriti pūrvameva kṛtottaram / āropitasyātmano yaḥ khalu svabhāvaḥ, so 'pi tathaiva jñeyaḥ, kintu naiva sa paramārthato 'san, marīcikāsu jalajñānādṛśatvāttasya /
body.translated_text: What is ultimately non-existent is also conventionally non-existent, because it is not experienced even partially in any activity, like a hare's horn. If it is said that even perception is like that — in that case, since this reason would be unconnected, it would be merely inconclusive, and this has already been answered previously. The nature of the superimposed self should be understood in that same way — but it is not ultimately non-existent, because it is like the knowledge of water in a mirage.

body.text: āropasvabhāvātmakatvāt sarvapratyakṣāṇāṃ kathaṃ hi tairekānekasvabhāvayuktatvaṃ jñātuṃ śakyata iti cintāyāṃ heturyamatra māyākārāpratyakṣānumānābhyāmanaikāntika eva / yato hi māyākārajñāne tāvad yo 'yaṃ gajādyākārāropastasmin svabhāve paramārthato nabhiniveśo jāyate / tasmiṃstathābhiniveśābhāvāt tat paramārthatastadviviktajñānotpattiheturbhavatītyavaśyaṃ tadviṣayitvena vyavasthāpyate / evaṃ prekṣāvatāṃ pratyakṣasya nirākṛte 'pi bhāntikāraṇe kadācidanyāropākārasvabhāvavataḥ [jñānasya] utpattirbhavatīti paramārthatastatsvabhāve 'nabhiniveśena hetunā niyatena tāvattadviviktaviṣayitvena vyavasthāpyate / tathaivānumānajñānamapi yaddhi sāmānye tāvad vastulakṣaṇe samāropākāram, tadapi vastutathatāyā yathāvajjñānasvabhāvatvāt tadviṣayakaṃ bhavatīti pramāṇasadbhāvādanaikāntika eva hetuḥ / nāsti tadviṣayīti kathanaṃ tāvannaiva yuktm, aścaśṛṅgavad vastūnāmabhyupagamābhāvāt / tarhi kathamiti cet? māyādisvabhāvavaditi, māyādivat pratyakṣatvāt / gṛhīte 'pyekānekasvabhāvarāhitye 'nāptapuruṣaśāstraśravaṇenotpannāropairanirdhāryāpareṇa [prakāreṇa] nirdhārayatāmekānekasvabhāvaviyuktavamanupalabdhyā tāvat kathaṃ setsyati? vividhaprakārādiliṅgaiḥ sarve yadyekasvabhāvarahitatvena sādhyante tadā te 'nekatvasvabhāvarahitā api sidhyanyeva, ekasañcayātmakatvādanekasya / ekastvaṃ vānekatvaṃ vā sarveṣvākāreṣu vyāptam, parasparaparihārasthitalakṣaṇatvāttayoḥ / vyavahāre ghaṭādiviṣayaparicchedena puruṣā atulyasambaddhān vyavahārayogyānatyantaṃ paricchedayanti / tatastulyaviparyayādisvabhāvavicchedena paricchedaḥ / tathaiva / paricchinne 'pyanekavastuvyavahārayogye 'nekadravyajātisaṃghāte tato 'tulyaviparyayaviccedenaiva paricchedaḥ / paricchedo yadi naiva viccinnastadā sa nāstyeva, parasparaparihārasthitalakṣaṇatvāttayoḥ / ye tāvat parasparaparihārasthitalakṣaṇāste sarvatra vyāpinaḥ, ye hi sarvatra vyāpinaste skandhādyanyāpoḍhāḥ, mūrtāmūrtatvādiviśeṣavaditi /
body.translated_text: Since all perceptions are of the nature of superimposition (<s>āropa</s>), the reason presented here in the inquiry 'how can the possession of one-and-many own-nature be known through them?' is indeed inconclusive (<s>anaikāntika</s>) by virtue of the perception and inference of the illusionist (<s>māyākāra</s>). For in the cognition of the illusionist, regarding that superimposition of the appearance of elephants etc., no fixation (<s>abhiniveśa</s>) arises in that own-nature ultimately. Because there is no such fixation in it, that [cognition] ultimately becomes the cause for the arising of knowledge discerning that [nature], and thus it is necessarily established as having that as its object. Similarly, for the discerning, even when the erroneous cause of perception has been refuted, since cognition possessing the nature of some other superimposed appearance sometimes arises, it is established as having an object discerning that, through the invariable reason of non-fixation in that own-nature ultimately. Likewise also inferential cognition — that which has a superimposed appearance with respect to the universal characteristic of a real thing — even that becomes an object of the <s>tathatā</s> (suchness) of reality, because it has the nature of knowledge as it is. Therefore, because <s>pramāṇa</s> (valid cognition) exists, the reason is indeed inconclusive. To say 'there is no object of that' is simply not proper, because there is no acceptance of things as being like a horse's horn. Then how? — Like the nature of illusion (<s>māyā</s>) etc., because of being perceptible like illusion etc. Even when the absence of one-and-many own-nature has been grasped, for those who, through superimpositions arisen from hearing the teachings of unreliable persons, cannot determine [this] otherwise — how will the absence of one-and-many own-nature be established through non-apprehension (<s>anupalabdhi</s>)? If all things are established through various types of inferential marks (<s>liṅga</s>) as lacking the own-nature of oneness, then they would indeed be established as also lacking the own-nature of manyness, because the many is of the nature of a collection of ones. Either oneness or manyness pervades all aspects, because those two are characterized by mutual exclusion. In conventional practice, through the determination (<s>pariccheda</s>) of objects such as pots etc., persons determine things connected with what is dissimilar as fit for practical use, but not completely. Thus determination is through the exclusion of the own-nature of what is similar, contrary, etc. Likewise, even when something fit for the practical use of many things — a collection of many substances and universals — has been determined, determination of that too is only through the exclusion of what is dissimilar and contrary. If determination is never cut off [from anything], then it simply does not exist, because those two [determination and its object] are characterized by mutual exclusion. Those that are characterized by mutual exclusion pervade everything; those that pervade everything are excluded from <s>skandhas</s> (aggregates) etc. as other, just as the distinction of corporeal and incorporeal etc.

body.text: ekānekatve api tathaiva / vyāpakanivṛttyā vyāpyanivṛtterniyatatvānnāsti tāvad heturapi sadigdhavipakṣavyāvṛttikaḥ, apareṣāṃ skandhānāmabhāvāt / vyāpyasya vyāpakasya vā vastunaḥ svato 'siddhatvādasiddha eva sa heturiti kecana / tathaiva dharmiṇyeva kevale vyāpyasadbhāvasidhyarthaṃ vyāpakanivṛtyā vyāpyanivṛttirasiddhaivetyapare / eteṣāṃ sarveṣāṃ [ākṣepāṇāṃ] samādhānaṃ tāvatpūrvamevāsmābhiḥ kṛtam /
body.translated_text: The same applies to oneness and manyness as well. Since the exclusion of the pervaded necessarily follows from the exclusion of the pervader, there is no reason that even has doubtful exclusion from the counter-instance, because there is an absence of the other <s>skandhas</s> (aggregates). Some say that since the real entity — whether pervaded or pervader — is unestablished from its own side, that very reason is unestablished. Likewise, others [say] that for the purpose of establishing the presence of the pervaded in the property-possessor alone, the exclusion of the pervaded through the exclusion of the pervader is itself unestablished. The resolution of all these [objections] has already been given by us previously.

body.text: evaṃ vyāpyavyāpakādisarvavastūnāṃ pūrvaṃ saṃvṛttyāśritatvaṃ prasādhya paścād vyavasthā kṛtetyapi pūrvamāveditameva / atyantaṃ samīpavartini vyāpake niyataṃ vyāpyaviśeṣajñānaṃ naiva bhavatītyapi pūrvameva nirdiṣṭam / ato vyavahāreṇa ekānekasvabhāvamātreṇa sattvaṃ vyāptamiti / tathāpyanena pararmārthasvabhāvo naiva niściyate / ekānekasvabhāvastāvad ghaṭādayaḥ saṃvṛtyāpyavabhāsanta eveti /
body.translated_text: Thus, having first established that all entities — pervaded, pervader, etc. — depend on convention (<s>saṃvṛti</s>), and then having made the determination afterwards — this too has already been stated before. That when the pervader is extremely close, determinate cognition of the specific pervaded does not necessarily arise — this too has been pointed out earlier. Therefore, existence is pervaded merely by the one-and-many own-nature in conventional terms. Even so, no ultimate own-nature is thereby ascertained. Things like pots etc., possessing one-and-many own-nature, do indeed appear even conventionally.

body.text: vyāpyavyāpakabhāvasiddhistu viśeṣato vyavahāradharmiṇamāśrayate, vyāpakanivṛttistu paramārthamāśrayate, ato vivādāspadībhūteṣu sarvadharmiṣu sāmānyena sādhayitumiṣyamāṇatvāt kathamimau dvau [vyāpyavyāpakau] ekasmin dharmiṇyāśritāviti cet? ekasmin dharmiṇyāśritatve 'pi [mithaḥ] sāpekṣatvād bhinnāveveti nāsti doṣaḥ / evameva vyāpyavyāpakabhāvasiddhistu vyāvahārasatyamāśrayate, vyāpakanivṛttistāvat paramārthasatyamevāśrayate, ato viruddhaiva /
body.translated_text: The establishment of the pervaded-pervader relationship depends specifically on the conventional property-possessor (<s>dharmin</s>), while the exclusion of the pervader depends on the ultimate. Therefore, since it is desired to establish [this] generally with respect to all property-possessors that are the subject of dispute, [the objection is raised:] 'How can these two — the pervaded and the pervader — depend on one property-possessor?' Even though they depend on one property-possessor, because they are mutually dependent, they are indeed distinct, so there is no fault. In just this way, the establishment of the pervaded-pervader relationship depends on conventional truth (<s>vyavahārasatya</s>), while the exclusion of the pervader depends on ultimate truth (<s>paramārthasatya</s>), therefore the two are simply incompatible —

body.text:
117
[36-37] yaḥ khalu sādhyaḥ, sādhako vā tau prasajyapratiṣedhasvabhāvau, na vā tathāsvabhāvau? prathame tāvatpakṣe tau naiva bodhyabodhakarupeṇopapannau, niḥsvabhāvatvādasambaddhatvādanupapannatvācca / ye sarvābhilāpavigatalakṣaṇāste na kathañcanāpi bodhyā bodhakāśca, aśvaśṛṅgavat, yathoktāḥ sarve sādhyasādhakādayo 'bhilāparahitalakṣaṇātmakāḥ /
body.translated_text: [36-37] Now, are the provable (<s>sādhya</s>) and the prover (<s>sādhaka</s>) of the nature of an implicative negation (<s>prasajyapratiṣedha</s>), or are they not of such a nature? In the first alternative, those two are not at all established in the form of what is to be cognized and what cognizes, because of their naturelessness, unrelatedness, and untenability. Those that are characterized by the absence of all verbal expression are not in any way objects of cognition or means of cognition, like a horse's horn. As stated, all provable-and-prover relationships etc. are of a nature devoid of verbal characterization.

body.text: ye parasparamasambaddhāste 'pi naiva bodhyabodhakasvabhāvāḥ, himavadvindhyaparvatavat, sādhyasādhakā api parasparamasambaddhāḥ /
body.translated_text: Those that are mutually unrelated are also not of the nature of what is to be cognized and what cognizes — like the <s>Himavat</s> (Himalaya) and <s>Vindhya</s> mountains. The provable and the prover too are mutually unrelated.

body.text: abhinnasvabhāvā api kecana na bodhyabodhakabhāvāpannāḥ, vṛkṣaśākhāvat / sādhyasādhakā apyabhinnāḥ / yadi prasajyapratiṣedhasvabhāvapakṣapātinastadā ekānekasvabhāvarahitāstāvad vastusvabhāvabhūtārthakriyāyogyatvasvīkārādapi na svīkriyanta ityapyayuktīyuktam, vikalpasyāsya paraparikalpiteśvarādiniṣedhe 'pi sarvatra samānatvāt / ato 'vaśyaṃ vyāpakadharmanivṛttyaiva īśvarādīnāṃ nirākaraṇaṃ karttavyam, atyantaparokṣeṣu pratyakṣeṇa niṣeddhuśakyatvāt / atastasmin kathaṃ na sarva vivādā āpateyuriti /
body.translated_text: Even some things of non-distinct own-nature are not fit to be objects of cognition and cognizers — like a tree and its branch. The provable and the prover too are non-distinct. If one adheres to the alternative of implicative negation (<s>prasajyapratiṣedha</s>) as own-nature, then accepting the fitness for real causal efficacy (<s>arthakriyā</s>) as constituting the own-nature of things that lack one-and-many own-nature — even the non-acceptance of that is improper, because this conceptual construction applies equally everywhere, including in the negation of God (<s>Īśvara</s>) etc. as conceived by others. Therefore, the refutation of <s>Īśvara</s> etc. must necessarily be accomplished through the exclusion of the pervading property alone, because what is extremely remote cannot be negated by perception. Therefore, how would all disputes not befall [that position]?

body.text: na tadekaṃ na cānekaṃ viṣayaḥ paramāṇuśaḥ /
body.translated_text: It is neither one nor many; the object [is analyzed] down to the atoms (<s>paramāṇu</s>).

body.text: tathā
body.translated_text: Likewise:

children.text: bhāvā yatra vicāryante na te santi savabhāvataḥ /
children.translated_text: When entities are examined, they do not exist by own-nature.
How so? Because oneness and manyness do not [exist] in them by own-nature.

body.text: ityādibhīrbāhyārthaparikalpanā tāvanniṣedhyate / tatrāpi kathaṃ na vivādāḥ syuriti / yadi niḥsvabhāvatā tatra naiva bodhyata iti cettadā aśvaśṛṅgasyāpi bodhābhāvaḥ kathaṃ nollikhyate / bhavatāmabhilāpalakṣaṇarahitāḥ sarva bhāvā na manāgapi bodhyanta ityādiprayogeṣu vidyata eva sādhyasādhakayorniṣedhasvabhāvaḥ, ataḥ kīdṛśastāvadayaṃ bodhakabhāvaḥ / ataḥ prayogo 'yamātmano hānikara evollikhitaḥ śastraśikṣaṇadoṣābhyupagamavat / ato nāsti prayogakauśalamapi sarvesāṃ vastunāṃ niścetavyaprasaṅgālliṅgasyaiva vastuno bodho na kenāpi svīkriyate, kasyāpi liṅgabodhasya kuisminnapyavaśyameva sambhavāt / ato niyatameva liṅgaṃ pratyakṣeṇa bodhyate, sādhyākārasya niyamenotpādakatvāt /
body.translated_text: Through such [statements], the conceptual construction of external objects is first negated. And how would disputes not arise even there? If <s>niḥsvabhāvatā</s> (naturelessness) is not cognized there — then why is the non-cognizability even of a horse's horn not recorded? In your own formulations such as 'all entities that are devoid of verbal characterization are not cognizable in the slightest' — there does indeed exist the negation-nature of the provable and the prover. Therefore, what kind of cognizing capacity is this? Therefore, this formulation has been recorded as damaging to oneself, like the fault of accepting instruction in weapons [that one then uses against oneself]. Therefore, there is no skill in formulation, because of the absurd consequence that all things would have to be ascertained through inferential marks (<s>liṅga</s>) —

body.text: liṅgaṃ tāvat kalpanayā bodhakatvena vyavasthitamiti yuktam / ato niḥ svabhāvatve 'pi niayatatadākārasya sādhyakāraniścayotpattau hetutvād bodhakatvena kalpanāyāṃ nāsti kaścana doṣaḥ / kevalasya vastubhūtaliṅgasyaiva sarvatra nollekho bhavati, ākāśaniṣedhakasya liṅgasya nitarāṃ kalpitatvādeveti pūrvaṃ nirdiṣṭam / asambaddhatvāditi yadabhihitam, tatrāpi yadi vastubhūtaḥ sambandha evaiko hetutvena kathayitumiṣyate, tadāpi sa heturnāstyanaikāntikaḥ, vastubhūte 'pi [hetau] kutracittathāvidhasya sambandhasyāsiddhatavāt / sa [sambandhaḥ] tāvad dvayāśritatvena parasparaśliṣṭasvabhāvatvena copakalpyate / dvayorniṣpannayoḥ [vastunoḥ] svabhāvaḥ śliṣṭa iti nopapadyate, svasvabhāve vyavasthitatvāttayoḥ / śliṣṭatve satyekatvameva syāt / tacca viruddhameva / ekatve sati naiva dvayāśritvaṃ tāvad yuktam /
body.translated_text: The inferential mark (<s>liṅga</s>) is indeed properly established as a cognizer through conceptual construction (<s>kalpanā</s>). Therefore, even when own-nature is absent, since [the mark] invariably having that appearance is the cause for the arising of ascertainment of the provable appearance, there is no fault whatsoever in the conceptual construction of its being a cognizer. It is only that a real inferential mark alone is never recorded anywhere — because the inferential mark that negates space (<s>ākāśa</s>) is entirely of the nature of conceptual construction, as was pointed out earlier. Regarding the statement 'because of unrelatedness' — even if one wishes to speak of only a real relation as the single ground of reason, even then that reason is not inconclusive, because even in the case of a real [reason], such a relation is somewhere [established] —

body.text: yadi sa sambandhibhyo 'rthāntara iti tadā svasvabhāvavyavasthitatvāt kathaṃ nāma sambaddhasvabhāvaḥ syāt / yadi nāstyarthāntara iti tadā kevalaṃ sambandhināveva syātām / ataḥ sambandhastāvat kalpanāmātrātmaka eva, na tu vastvātmaka iti / yāni hi sambandhodbhūtāni lakṣaṇāni tānyapi kalpanātmakānyeva, kāryakāraṇeyoryugapatsambhavā bhāvāt / ye tāvadasannihitāsteṣu na sambhavati sambandhaḥ /
body.translated_text: If that [relation] is something different from the relata, then since it abides in its own own-nature, how could it be of the nature of being related? If it is not something different, then there would simply be just the two relata. Therefore, relation is merely of the nature of conceptual construction (<s>kalpanā</s>), not of the nature of a real entity. The characteristics that arise from relation are also merely of the nature of conceptual construction, because cause and effect cannot occur simultaneously. Those that are not co-present — for them, relation is not possible.

body.text: api ca, yadā kāryasvabhāvaḥ pariniṣpannaḥ tadā apekṣāvirahānnaiva tasya kūtracinnirbharatvam / ato nāsti tasya kenāpi saha sambandhaḥ / apariniṣpanne 'pi tasmin kāraṇena saha sambandhakāle vidūre sthitatvādasambaddhameva tat syāditi / ataḥ kalpanayaiva bhavanto vastuprayogamanutiṣṭhantīti /
body.translated_text: Moreover, when the own-nature of the effect is fully accomplished, then because of the absence of dependence, it has no reliance on anything whatsoever. Therefore, it has no relation with anything. Even when it is not fully accomplished, at the time of relation with the cause, since it stands far away, it would indeed be unrelated. Therefore, it is through conceptual construction alone that you carry out the practical application of real things.

children.translated_text: Even though the effect does not depend [on the cause], because of the well-known [fact] of [dependence on] its own cause,
Since there is no establishment through dependence on something other than that, conceptual construction again

children.text: hetuṃ badhnāti kāryeṇa kāryaṃ na, tacca kīdṛśam //
children.translated_text: Binds the cause to the effect — [but] not the effect [to the cause]. And what would that [binding] be like?

body.text: tadātmakalakṣaṇasambandho 'pi naiva samīcīnaḥ, dvayāśritatvāttasya / tadātmakatve dvaitaṃ naivopapadyate / dvayābhāve kaḥ kena sambadhyeta sambandhī / ataḥ kalpanāracitamūrtitvāt sarveṣāṃ sambandhānām, abhāve caivānupahatapravṛtterhetorasiddhireva syāt / asambaddhatve sati abhedābhāvāt kathaṃ tādṛśī yaktiḥ, prayujyate / abhede sati tadātmaka eva sambandha iti nirdeśaḥ syāt /
body.translated_text: The <s>tādātmya</s> (identity) relation too is not proper, because it depends on two [things]. If [they are] identical in nature, duality is simply untenable. In the absence of two, who would be related to whom, and what would be the relata? Therefore, since all relations are of a nature fashioned by conceptual construction, in their absence the reason — whose operation is unimpeded — would simply be unestablished. Given unrelatedness, since there is no non-difference, how is such reasoning employed? If non-difference obtains, then it should be designated as an identity relation.

body.text: vastumātra eva tādātmyasambandhaḥ, na tvanyatreti cet? ayuktametad, abhinnaparyāyatvāttādātmyasya / sa tu niḥsvabhāvasyāpi nairātmyasadṛśatvādaviruddha eva / yadyevaṃ na syāttadā 'abhinnatvād' ityapi vaktuṃ na paryeta / tatra 'abhinnatvad' ityayaṃ heturyadi paramārthādhikāreṇocyeta tadā anekāntika eva, yato hi kṛtakatvānityatve yadyapi paramārthato naiva bhinne tathāpi bodhyabodhakavastuṣu tāvat te dṛśyete /
body.translated_text: If [one says] the <s>tādātmya</s> (identity) relation applies only to a mere real entity and not to anything else — this is improper, because identity is synonymous with non-difference. But that is not contradictory even for what lacks own-nature, because it is similar to <s>nairātmya</s> (selflessness). If it were not so, then one could not even say 'because of non-difference.' Therein, if the reason 'because of non-difference' is stated under the purview of the ultimate, then it is simply inconclusive (<s>anaikāntika</s>), because even though <s>kṛtakatva</s> (being produced) and <s>anityatva</s> (impermanence) are ultimately not different, they are nonetheless seen in the objects of cognition and cognizers.

body.text: yadi vyavahāre 'pi tayornāsti bhinnatvamityucyeta tadā asiddhameva, nivṛttiviśeṣopakalpitāyā bhinnatāyāstatra sadbhāvāt / evameva śabdādidharmiṇi yadā akṛtakatvādito nivṛttirniścīyate tadā nityādito 'pi nirvṛtterniścayanāt paramārthato bhinnatāyā abhāve 'pi nivṛttiviśeṣāpekṣayā kṛtakatvānityatvādīnāṃ bhinnavyavasthāyā upakalpanād bodhyabodhakavastuvyavasthā tāvat kriyata eva / itthaṃ yadā vastūni sāmarthyataḥ pratimbivad ekānekasvabhāvavinivṛttāni bhavanti tadā paramārthasvabhāvato 'pi teṣāṃ nivṛttirniyataiva / ato nivṛttiviśesāpekṣayā kṛtakatvaṃ bhinnaṃ vyavasthāpyate, ata eva ca tatra bodhyabodhakabhāvo 'pi sambhavatyeva / punaśca, yathā nityaṃ tāvd vastu arthakriyāsāmarthyavirahād vastusvabhāvena rahitaṃ sādhyate, tathaiva anyatrāpi tatsadṛśatvānna virudhyate /
body.translated_text: If one says that even in convention there is no difference between those two — that is simply unestablished, because difference fashioned by specific exclusions (<s>nivṛttiviśeṣa</s>) does exist there. In just this way, when in the property-possessor such as sound etc., the exclusion from 'being produced' is ascertained, then since the exclusion from 'permanent' etc. is also ascertained — even though difference does not exist ultimately — because the distinct conventional status of being-produced, impermanence, etc. is fashioned with respect to specific exclusions, the establishment of objects of cognition and cognizers is indeed accomplished. Thus, when things, by their own capacity, like reflections, are free from the own-nature of one-and-many, then even from the standpoint of ultimate own-nature, their cessation —

body.text: yadapi atadvyāvṛttiviśeṣeṇānayoḥ kṛtakatvaṃ tad vastu syāt nīlapītādivattasvabhāvatvāditi kathanaṃ tāvadasambaddhameva, kṛtakatvānityatvābhyāmaniyatatvāt / kṛtakatvānityatvayorbhedo vyāvṛttyocyate, kintvetāvatā na tad vastu / yathā nityavastuniṣedhāya arthakriyāsāmārthyarahitatvaṃ niḥsvabhāvatvaṃ ca vyāvṛttikṛtaviśeṣe satyapi naiva vastu, tathaivānyadapi tatsadṛśamiti jñeyam, ato gauṇamevedam / yatkhalu nīlātmakaṃ pītātmakamiti nidarśanaṃ tadapi paramārthe tāvad vastunyasiddhatvādayuktam / ye 'smin asatpakṣatvena doṣamāropayanti, tadapi naiva yuktiyuktam / yato hi nayo 'yamasanniti kathanamātreṇa tāvat paramārthe vastuni na kimapi siddhaṃ bhāvati, amūrtādiśabdaprayoge 'pi kalpyamānamākāśaṃ tāvadasattvānnaiva yuktam /
body.translated_text: The statement that 'the <s>kṛtakatva</s> (being produced) of these two, distinguished by exclusion from what is other than that, would be a real entity, like blue and yellow etc., because of being of that nature' — that is simply irrelevant, because being-produced and impermanence are not invariably [connected in that way]. The difference between being-produced and impermanence is stated through exclusion, but that alone does not make it a real entity. Just as for the purpose of negating a permanent entity, the lack of capacity for causal efficacy (<s>arthakriyā</s>) and naturelessness — even though there is a distinction made through exclusion — are not real entities, likewise other similar [cases] should be understood. Therefore, this is merely figurative (<s>gauṇa</s>). The example 'what is of the nature of blue, what is of the nature of yellow' is also improper, because it is unestablished in an ultimately real entity.

body.text: tatra buddhau pratibhāsamāno yo hi pūrvodito dharmī, so 'pi asatā tāvannayena [asatpakṣeṇa] tathoktaḥ, kintu paramārthe vastuni sa naiva yuktarūpaḥ / vastusaditi vyavaharatāṃ kathanamidaṃ siddhasādhanamiti syāt, ekānekasvabhāvarahitaṃ khalu paramārthaṃ vastu naiva kiñcit, tasya kalpanāviṣayatvenāpi bahirbhūtvāditi / sarve khalu padārthāḥ ekānekasvabhāvābhyāṃ vyāptā iti tu pūrvameva prasādhitam / māyādibhiravyatiriktāḥ paramārthato niḥsvabhāvā hi bhāvāste yadi 'vastu' nāmnā vyavahriyeran, tadā nāsti kaścanāpi doṣaḥ, bhavatkalpitapakṣahānyā tāvattasya dūṣitatvāt / ato nāsti heturanaikāntikaḥ / nāsti viruddhakhyo 'pi [doṣaḥ], pratibimbādisapakṣeṣu sattvāt / ekānekasvabhāvāni pratibimbādivastūni naiva paramārthato yukāni, jñānajñeyādisvabhāvena paramārthato 'siddhatvāditi pūrvamevoktam / [42] evaṃ yathā ekānekasvabhāvalakṣaṇo hetustāvannairātmyaṃ sādhayati tadvadabhāvadharmini dharmivyāvṛttisādhakatvād viruddho 'yaṃ heturiti yaduktaṃ tattu atyantaṃ pramāṇānabhijñatāmātrameva / yadā vastusvabhāvo dharmī sādhayitumiṣyate, tadā tadvyāvṛttisādhakatvena sa heturviruddha ityucyate, kintu yadā sa [dharmī] niḥsvabhāvatvena sādhyate tadā siddhe 'pi vādino mate kathaṃ tāvad viruddho heturbhaviṣyati / niḥsvabhāvatāyāṃ hi sādhayitumiṣṭāyāṃ vastusvabhāvo dharmī naiva sambhavati, ananurūpatvāditi pūrvamevoditam / ataḥ sādhyasādhanābhyāṃ yathokto dharmī avastubhūta eva sammat ityasmāt kāraṇāt tena hetunā tāvad vyāvṛttireva sādhayate / vastusvabhāvasiddhau tu tadviparītasyaiva siddhiḥ syāt /
body.translated_text: Therein, the previously mentioned subject (<s>dharmin</s>) that appears in cognition (<s>buddhi</s>) — it too is so called following the method of non-existence [i.e., the thesis of non-existence]; but in ultimate reality, it is not of the proper form for a real entity. If those who engage in the convention 'the entity exists' say 'this is proving what is already established (<s>siddhasādhana</s>)' — indeed, no real entity whatsoever exists in the ultimate that is devoid of a unitary or manifold intrinsic nature, since that too is beyond the domain of conceptual construction and thus external [to it]. It has already been demonstrated that all categories are pervaded by [the alternatives of] unitary and manifold intrinsic nature. If entities that are ultimately essenceless, non-different from illusions and the like, were conventionally designated by the name 'entity' (<s>vastu</s>), then there would be no fault whatsoever, since [the opponent's] position — fabricated by your own construction — has already been refuted. Therefore, the reason is not inconclusive (<s>anaikāntika</s>). Nor is there the fault called 'contradictory' (<s>viruddha</s>), since [the reason] is present in similar instances (<s>sapakṣa</s>) such as reflections and the like. Reflections and the like, as entities with unitary or manifold intrinsic nature, are not tenable in the ultimate — since they are not established in the ultimate as having the nature of knowledge, the knowable, and so forth, as was stated previously. [42] Thus, just as the reason characterized by the absence of unitary or manifold intrinsic nature proves selflessness (<s>nairātmya</s>), the statement 'this reason is contradictory because it proves the exclusion of the subject from a subject that is non-existence' is merely sheer unfamiliarity with valid cognition. When a subject with the nature of a real entity is desired to be proved, then the reason is called 'contradictory' because it proves the exclusion of that. But when [the subject] is proved as essenceless, even if [the subject] is established in the proponent's view, how could the reason be contradictory? For when essencelessness is the desired thesis, a subject with the nature of a real entity is simply impossible, due to incongruity — as stated previously. Therefore, the subject, as described in relation to the thesis and the proof, is agreed upon as non-real-entity by both. For this very reason, the reason indeed proves exclusion. But if the real-entity intrinsic nature were established, then the opposite [of the thesis] would be established.

body.text: yathāyaṃ heturnairātmyaṃ sādhayati tathaiva abhāvadharmyapīti keṣāñcit kathanamasambaddhameva / yato hi yena kāraṇena tāvannairātmyasya abhāvasya ca dvayordharmayorviruddhahetubhyāṃ siddhirucyate, tau vyāvṛttyāpi naiva bhinnau, paryāyasvabhāvatvāttayoḥ / phalato nirātmakamidaṃ nairātmyāditi kathanamiva syāt / evaṃvidhaṃ tavadabhidhānakauśalaṃ kasya syāt?[na kasyāpītyarthaḥ] / ataḥ sarve niḥsvabhāvāḥ sidhyanti / heturapi bhagavatauvoktaḥ, tathā hi -
body.translated_text: The statement by some that 'just as this reason proves selflessness, so too it proves a subject that is non-existent' is entirely incoherent. For since the establishment of both properties — selflessness and non-existence — is said to come through a contradictory reason, the two are not different even through exclusion, since they are synonymous in nature. Consequently, this amounts to saying 'this selflessness is selfless' (<s>nirātmakam idaṃ nairātmyāt</s>). Who could possess such skill in expression? [The answer: no one.] Therefore, all [entities] are established as essenceless. The reason has also been stated by the Blessed One; thus:

children.translated_text: "Just as in a mirror, a form devoid of unity and otherness

children.text: dṛśayate na ca tannāsti tathā cotpādalakṣaṇam //
children.translated_text: is seen, yet it is not non-existent — so too is the characteristic of origination."

body.text: phalato niḥsvabhāvatāsādhanārthaṃ na ko 'pi heturiti yatkathanam, tasyāpyuttaraṃ dattapūrvameva /
body.translated_text: Consequently, the statement 'there is no reason whatsoever for proving essencelessness' — the answer to that too has already been given.

body.text: yadi vijñānamapi itaradharmāṇāmiva niḥsvabhāvameva syāttadā mithyātvād yogibhiranyadharmāṇāmiva tasyāpi parityāgaḥ kariṣyata eva / yadyevaṃ kariṣyate tadā na ko 'pi yogino bhaviṣyanti, na ca teṣāṃ tattvajñānaṃ bhavaiṣyati, nāpi bhagavatāṃ buddhānāmapratiṣṭhitanirvāṇaṃ naiva ca teṣāṃ tattvajñānaṃ bhaviṣyati / anena khalu hetunā sarvāsāṃ vyavasthānāṃ vilopa eva syāditi yatkathanaṃ tadapi naiva yuktam, yato hi prasaṅgastāvadayaṃ yadi satyābhiniveśaparityāgārthamucyate tadā saharṣamucyatām, kintu tathābhyupagamya naiva prasaṅgaḥ prayuktaḥ, tallakṣaṇasyaivanabhyupagamāt / yadi sarvavidhaprasaṅgaparityāgārthaṃ tāvaducyate, tadā heturayamanaikāntikaḥ sādhyaviparītabādhakapramāṇābhāvāt / yanmithyā tat sarvathā parityājyamityetasya naiva kimapi kāraṇamupalabhāmahe, mithyātve 'pi prayojanavaśānyamāyākāra iva māyādarśanavat / ye hi mithyā svaparārthaṃ naivopayujyante, te yogibhiḥ parityājyā iti kathanaṃ tu yujyate, parantu ye tavat sākṣāt paramparayā vā svaparaprayojanaprasādhakāḥ, kṛpālūnāṃ parahitakaraṇopāyabhūtāsteṣāṃ kathaṃ sarvadā parityāgaḥ kartum śakyate /
body.translated_text: If consciousness (<s>vijñāna</s>) too, like other <s>dharmas</s>, were completely essenceless, then being false, <s>yogins</s> would abandon it just as they abandon other <s>dharmas</s>. If this were done, there would be no <s>yogins</s>, nor would they have knowledge of truth, nor would the blessed <s>Buddhas</s> have the non-abiding <s>Nirvāṇa</s> (<s>apratiṣṭhita-nirvāṇa</s>), nor would they have knowledge of truth. The statement that 'by this very reason, there would be the destruction of all systems' is also not tenable, because if this <s>prasaṅga</s> is stated for the purpose of abandoning attachment to the real, then let it be stated with joy! But having accepted that, the <s>prasaṅga</s> is not really adduced [against us], because we do not accept the very defining characteristic [that would make it a fault]. If it is stated for the purpose of abandoning every kind of <s>prasaṅga</s>, then this reason is inconclusive, because there is no invalidating valid cognition that [establishes] the opposite of the thesis. We find no reason whatsoever for the assertion that 'whatever is false must be entirely abandoned' — for even something false may be [retained] by the force of its purpose, like a magician who retains the [illusion] like the seeing of an illusion. The statement that '<s>yogins</s> should abandon those [things] that are false and serve neither one's own nor others' purpose' is indeed correct. However, those things that directly or indirectly accomplish one's own and others' purposes, and that serve as means for compassionate ones to benefit others — how can their complete abandonment at all times be accomplished?

body.text: ato ye kṣetrapariśuddhinirmāṇakāyādayaste parārthamatyantamāvaśyakāḥ, te sarve viparītaparihāradvārā parityājyā api yāvatsaṃsāramaparityājyā eva / te yadyapi māyākāra iva sarvān mithyābhūtān jānanti, tathāpi parahitopāyabhūtān tān na parityajanti / nāsti teṣu viparyabhūtā āsaktirapi, samyagrūpeṇa teṣāṃ yathābhūtaparijñānāt / yathoktam āryadharmasaṅgītau ḥ
body.translated_text: Therefore, those things such as the purification of the [Buddha-]field (<s>kṣetra</s>), the emanation body (<s>nirmāṇakāya</s>), and the like, which are absolutely necessary for the benefit of others — even though they are to be abandoned through the elimination of inversion, they should not be abandoned for as long as <s>saṃsāra</s> [endures]. Even though they, like a magician, know all [things] as false, they do not abandon those that serve as means for benefiting others. Nor is there any inverted attachment to them, because they fully understand them in their correct nature. As stated in the <s>Ārya-Dharmasaṅgīti</s>:

children.translated_text: "Just as a certain magician endeavors to liberate his magical creation,

children.text: na cāsya nirmite saṅgo jñātapūrvo yato 'sya saḥ //
children.translated_text: yet has no attachment to that creation, since he has previously understood it —
so one who has reached the shore of perfect awakening, knowing the three realms as resembling a magical creation,
girds himself for the sake of the world, since he has previously understood the world as such."

body.text: bhāvo 'pi tāvanna grāhyo na cābhāvo 'pi parityājyaḥ, yato hi śrāvakā api, ye vastusaṃjñinaste 'pio ādimaṃ satyadvayaṃ vivarjayanti, tṛtīyaṃ cāryasatyamabhāvabhūtamapi parigṛhṇanti / kṛpāparādhīnacetaso yogino 'pi parahitārthaṃ vividharūpeṇa gajādimithyānirmāṇādikaṃ sādhayanti /
body.translated_text: Existence (<s>bhāva</s>) too should not be grasped, nor should non-existence (<s>abhāva</s>) be abandoned. For even <s>Śrāvakas</s>, who have the notion of real entities — they too give up the first two [noble] truths and accept the third noble truth even though it has the nature of non-existence. <s>Yogins</s> too, whose minds are dominated by compassion, accomplish various false creations such as elephants and the like for the benefit of others.

body.text: tatra mahākaruṇāparādhīnatayā ye pareṣām aśeṣahitasukhopāyaśālinaḥ prajñālokena vidhvastasakalakleśāndhakārāḥ parahitābhilāṣiṇo matimantaste prahīṇeṣvapi sakalaviparyāseṣu pūrvapraṇidhānavaśatayā yāvat sattvakarmakleśāstāvadākāśaparyantaṃ sthātumevābhilaṣante / itthaṃ sameṣāṃ vastūnāṃ paramārthato niḥsvabhāvatve 'pi hetupratyayasāmagrīpāratantryena māyāvat sambhavantyeva / hetumantaste na bhavanti vastusantaḥ, anvayāsiddhatvānmāyādinā bhrantatvācca / mithyābhūtā hi ye svānurūpahetumantastāvannaiva bhavanti, te vyavahāre 'pyasanta eveti pūrvamevāveditam / ato yathā māyādayaḥ svahetusākalyaparatantratayā prādurbhavanti, tathaiva yagināṃ jñānādayo 'pyavicāraramaṇīyā eva /
body.translated_text: Therein, those intelligent ones who are dominated by great compassion (<s>mahākaruṇā</s>), who possess the means for the complete welfare and happiness of others, whose darkness of all afflictions has been dispelled by the light of wisdom (<s>prajñāloka</s>), who desire the welfare of others — even when all inversions (<s>viparyāsa</s>) have been abandoned, they wish to remain as long as beings [have] <s>karma</s> and afflictions, [remaining] to the very limit of space, by the power of their previous aspirations (<s>praṇidhāna</s>). Thus, even though all entities are ultimately essenceless, they come into being through dependence on the assemblage of causes and conditions, like illusions. Those that have causes are not real entities, due to the non-establishment of positive concomitance and the erroneousness [of perception] as with illusions and the like. Those that are false and have causes appropriate to them are non-existent even in convention — this has already been stated. Therefore, just as illusions and the like come into being through dependence on the totality of their causes, so too the knowledge and the like of <s>yogins</s> are delightful without investigation.

body.text: tatra yogijñānādimāyāhetustāvad yathāvat puṇyajñānasambhārānukūla eva / saṃkṣepato bhagavatām apratisṭhitanirvāṇahetustu karunā prajñā ca / kṛpayā hi tannirvāṇāvabodhe 'pi te naiva tasya sākṣātkāraṃ kurvanti / prajñayā tāvat sarvasaṃkleśahetoḥ sammohasyānavakāśāt saṃsāradoṣagandhenāpyaliptāḥ santo naiva saṃsāre patanti / ataste naivānayordvayoḥ [saṃsaranirvāṇayoḥ] tiṣṭhanti / ataḥ prajñopāyayugnaddhacaryā tāvadapratiṣṭhitanirvāṇahetuḥ / ata eva ca sā bodhasattvānāṃ mārga ucyate / tayā virahitāḥ sattvāstu śrāvakādibhūmisu patanti / yathoktam..........
body.translated_text: Therein, the cause of yogic knowledge and the like, analogous to a magician's [magic], is precisely what is favorable to the accumulations of merit and knowledge. In brief, the cause of the non-abiding <s>Nirvāṇa</s> (<s>apratiṣṭhita-nirvāṇa</s>) of the blessed [Buddhas] is compassion (<s>karuṇā</s>) and wisdom (<s>prajñā</s>). For through compassion, even upon realizing that <s>Nirvāṇa</s>, they do not actualize it directly. Through wisdom, since there is no scope for delusion, the cause of all affliction — being untouched even by the scent of the faults of <s>saṃsāra</s> — they do not fall into <s>saṃsāra</s>. Therefore, they do not abide in either of the two — <s>saṃsāra</s> or <s>Nirvāṇa</s>. Hence, the practice joined with wisdom and method (<s>prajñopāyayugaṇaddha</s>) is the cause of non-abiding <s>Nirvāṇa</s>. Therefore it is called the path of <s>Bodhisattvas</s>. Those beings who are bereft of it fall into the stages of <s>Śrāvakas</s> and the like. As stated...

body.text: "api ca, śāriputra, śūnyatānimittaṃ ca bodhisattvānāṃ mārgaḥ / ye tāvat prajñāpāramitayā virahitāḥ, upāyakauśalyena cāparigṛhītāste yadi bhūtakoṭiṃ sākṣātkurvanti, tadā nūnaṃ śrāvakāḥ pratyekabuddhā eva bhavanti /"
body.translated_text: "Moreover, <s>Śāriputra</s>, emptiness and the signless (<s>śūnyatānimitta</s>) is the path of <s>Bodhisattvas</s>. Those who are devoid of the <s>Prajñāpāramitā</s> (perfection of wisdom) and who are not embraced by skill in means (<s>upāyakauśalya</s>) — if they directly realize the limit of reality (<s>bhūtakoṭi</s>), they will certainly become <s>Śrāvakas</s> or <s>Pratyekabuddhas</s>."

body.text: prabhāsvarādijñānena loko yathāvat samanupaśyati / tadyathā - acintyasāmarthyavattvād yogino yathā vastūnyavabhāsante tathā karatalāmalakavat saṃvṛtiparamārthākārābhyāṃ sarvākāraṃ
body.translated_text: Through the luminous cognition (<s>prabhāsvara-jñāna</s>) and the like, the world is seen as it truly is. Namely — due to the inconceivable power of <s>yogins</s>, in whatever way entities appear to them, they comprehend them completely in all aspects through the two forms of conventional (<s>saṃvṛti</s>) and ultimate (<s>paramārtha</s>) appearance, as clearly as a fruit in the palm of one's hand,

body.text: pratyakṣatayā avabudhyanti / ata eva bhagavān sarvākārajñānatvena vyavasthāpayāmāsa / sarvaprapañcarahitaṃ niruttaraṃ lokottaramaśesadharmanirābhāsaṃ jñānaṃ bhūtārthabhāvanāprakarṣaparyantajaṃ tattvāvabodhakaṃ bhavati, [tathāpi] vyavahāre sarvaṃ nirmāṇavat sadeva bhavati / ato yathā sarvākārajñānādau vastuvyavasthā kṛtā, sā na praṇaśyati, paramārthe 'bhāvāt / ata eva bhagavatyāmuttam - 'yadi bhagavan, sarve dharmā nirmāṇaniva bhavanti tadā bhagavati nirvāṇe ca kimantaram? bhagavān āha - na kimapīti / katham? bhagavataḥ sarvāṇi karmāṇi nirmāṇavad bhavanti / parinirvṛte 'pi bhāvati tathāgato nirmaṇaṃ karoti / nirmaṇasya tāvannodbhavo nāpi parinirvāṇaṃ kimapi bhavati / itthaṃ bodhisattvaiḥ sarvadharmeṣu nirmāṇamivādhimuktiṃ vidhāya prajñāpāramitāyāmācaritavyam / "ityetat pratipāditam /
body.translated_text: through direct perception. Therefore, the Blessed One established [this knowledge] as all-aspect-knowledge (<s>sarvākāra-jñāna</s>). The cognition that is free from all conceptual elaboration (<s>prapañca</s>), supreme, supramundane, [in which] the appearance of all <s>dharmas</s> ceases — born at the culmination of the cultivation of the knowledge of reality — is the awakener to truth. [Yet] in convention, everything exists like a magical creation. Therefore, just as the structure of entities was established in all-aspect-knowledge and the like, it does not perish — [though] in the ultimate, [there is] non-existence. Hence it is stated in the <s>Bhagavatī</s> [Prajñāpāramitā]: 'If, Blessed One, all <s>dharmas</s> are like magical creations, then what difference is there between the <s>Bhagavatī</s> and <s>Nirvāṇa</s>? The Blessed One said: None whatsoever. How? All the actions of the Blessed One are like magical creations. Even after <s>Parinirvāṇa</s>, the <s>Tathāgata</s> creates emanations. Of an emanation, there is neither origination nor any <s>Parinirvāṇa</s> whatsoever. Thus, <s>Bodhisattvas</s> should practice the <s>Prajñāpāramitā</s>, having developed conviction (<s>adhimukti</s>) toward all <s>dharmas</s> as being like magical creations.' This has been taught.

body.text: ye hi rūpādayo bhinnadeśakālāvasthāsu spaṣṭaṃ pratyakṣeṇāvabhāsante te niścayena svabhāvena yuktā ityataḥ pratijñā tāvat pratyakṣeṇa bādhiteti yat pūrvamuktam, tanna sarvathā samīcīnamiti cenna, yato hi bhinnadeśakālāvasthāsvavabhāsitatvamātreṇa pratyakṣāvabhāso naiva yuktaḥ, svapnādyavasthāsvapi tathāvabhāsitatvāt / vastūnaṃ khalu paramārthasvabhāvatayā sādhayitumiṣyante, kintu naiva svabhāvaḥ paramārthatayā siddha iti pūrvamāveditam /
body.translated_text: The previous statement that 'forms and the like, which clearly appear to perception in different places, times, and states, are certainly endowed with intrinsic nature — and therefore the thesis is contradicted by perception' — if [one says] this is not at all correct, [we say:] indeed, merely because of appearing in different places, times, and states, a perceptual appearance is not at all valid, since such appearance occurs even in dream states and the like. We desire to establish the ultimate nature of entities, but the intrinsic nature is not established as ultimate — this was already stated.

body.text: api ca, yadi bhrāntapratyakṣe 'vabhāsitatvat pratyakṣe 'vabhāsitatvamabhyuopagamyate tadā naiva tena bādhā yujyate, timirādyupahatalocaneṣu vidyamāne 'pi dvicandre na tena ekacandrādibādhā yuktimatī / yadyabhrāntapratyakṣe 'vabhāsitatvena tthā [bādhā] abhyupeyate tadā tannaiva sidhyati, arvāgdarśināṃ pratyakṣasya tattvārthe 'bhrāntatvābhāvāt /
body.translated_text: Moreover, if [one argues that] because of appearing in erroneous perception, [something] is accepted as appearing in [valid] perception — then invalidation by that is not tenable, since even the double moon, present for those whose eyes are affected by an eye-disease (<s>timira</s>), does not validly invalidate the single moon and the like. If invalidation is accepted by virtue of appearing in non-erroneous perception, then that cannot be established, because for those of limited vision, perception is not non-erroneous regarding the nature of reality.

children.text: na cakṣuḥ pramāṇaṃ na śrotra ghrāṇaṃ na jihṇa pramāṇaṃ na kāyacittam /
children.translated_text: "The eye is not a valid means of knowledge, nor the ear, nor the nose; nor is the tongue a valid means of knowledge, nor body, nor mind.

children.text: pramāṇa yadyeta bhaveyurindriyā kasyāryamārgeṇa bhaveta kāryam //
children.translated_text: If these sense faculties were valid means of knowledge, for whom would there be any purpose in the noble path?"

children.text: yasmādime indriya apramāṇā jaḍāḥ svabhāvena avyākṛtāśca /
children.translated_text: "Since these sense faculties are not valid means of knowledge, being inert by nature and ethically indeterminate —

children.text: tasmād ya nirvāṇapathaiva arthikaḥ sa āryamārgeṇa karotu karyam //
children.translated_text: therefore, one who desires the path of <s>Nirvāṇa</s> should accomplish [their] purpose through the noble path."

body.text: atastathāgatasyaiva kavalaṃ pratyakṣaṃ paramārthe 'bhrāntam / te naiva kimapi vastu sattvenālambante / yathoktam -
body.translated_text: Therefore, only the perception of the <s>Tathāgata</s> is non-erroneous in the ultimate. They do not apprehend any entity whatsoever as [truly] existent. As stated:

body.text: "subhūte, mohapuruṣāstāvannetrarahitā andhā eva / te rūpavedanāsaṃjñāsaṃskāravijñānata ārabhya sarvākārajñānaparyantaṃ tathāgatacakṣuṣā anupalabdheṣu sarvadharmeṣu sattvenābhiniviśante ".......iti vastaraḥ /
body.translated_text: "<s>Subhūti</s>, foolish persons, devoid of eyes, [are] indeed blind. From form, feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness up to all-aspect-knowledge — regarding all <s>dharmas</s> that are unapprehended by the <s>Tathāgata</s>'s eye — they cling to them as [truly] existent." ...and so on in detail.

body.text: pratijñāyā anumānenābhāsa iti yaduktaṃ tadapi naiva yujyate, yato hi nānumānena kimapi vastu svabhāvataḥ sidhyati, pramāṇabādhitatvāttasyetyuktapūrvam /
body.translated_text: The statement that 'the thesis appears [to be refuted] through inference' is also not tenable, since nothing whatsoever is established as real through inference by its own intrinsic nature — because it is contradicted by valid cognition, as was stated previously.

body.text: dhūmādihetubhiryo hi agnyādīnāṃ loke niścayaḥ, so 'pi tāvadagnirnaiva sadviṣayaḥ, svapne 'pi tathāvidhasya niścayasya sambhavāditi / dhūmāgnyoḥ sattvaniṣedhastāvat kṛtapūrva eva / ato nāsti kimapi / sāṃvṛtikaṃ hi vastu māyāvad hetupratyayasāpekṣam / ato nāsti tena saha kādācitkatvavirodhaḥ / ye tāvadahetukotpādamabhyupagacchanti, teṣāmeva kādācitkatvavirodhaḥ, na tu sahetukotpādamabhyupagacchatām / kādācitkatvamapi tāvadasiddhameva, paramārthato 'nutpādāt /
body.translated_text: The certainty regarding fire and the like in the world through reasons such as smoke — even that fire is not the object of [the convention of] existence [in the ultimate sense], since such certainty occurs even in dreams. The negation of the [ultimate] existence of smoke and fire has already been accomplished. Therefore there is nothing [to object to]. A conventional entity, like an illusion, depends on causes and conditions. Therefore there is no contradiction with its occasionality. Only for those who accept causeless origination does the contradiction with occasionality [arise] — not for those who accept origination with causes. Occasionality too is simply unestablished, because of non-origination in the ultimate.

body.text: yacca trāyastriṃśanagarādikamuktam, tadapyaviruddhameva, vyavahāre sattvāt / vastūnāṃ kūrmaromādivadabhāvasvabhāvatvaṃ yadi naiva pratijñāyate, tadā kathamiti cet? māyāsvapnādivaditi brūmaḥ / tathāgatenāpyuktam -
body.translated_text: What was said about the city of the Thirty-three [gods] and the like — that too is simply non-contradictory, since it exists in convention. If it is asked: 'If it is not maintained that entities have the nature of non-existence like tortoise-hair and the like, then how [do you establish their emptiness]?' We say: like illusions, dreams, and the like. The <s>Tathāgata</s> too has said:

body.text: mahāmate, sarve dharmā niḥsvabhāvā ityapi bodhisattvairnaiva pratijñā kāryā / tadā kimiti cet? ābhāsanirābhāsalakṣanatvād bodhisattvaiḥ sarve dharmā māyāsvapnādivannirdeṣṭavyāḥ /
body.translated_text: "<s>Mahāmate</s>, <s>Bodhisattvas</s> should not even make the assertion that 'all <s>dharmas</s> are essenceless.' Then why? Because of having the characteristic of appearance and non-appearance, <s>Bodhisattvas</s> should describe all <s>dharmas</s> as being like illusions, dreams, and the like."

body.text: vyavahāre tāvad [vastūnam] ābhāsalakṣaṇam, paramārthe tu nirābhāsalakṣaṇamiti sūtreārtho 'bhivyajyate / tadapi -
body.translated_text: In convention, [entities have] the characteristic of appearance; in the ultimate, the characteristic of non-appearance — thus the meaning of the <s>sūtra</s> is expressed. That too —

children.text: sarvaṃ vidyati saṃvṛtyā paramārthe na vidyate /
children.translated_text: Everything exists in convention; in the ultimate, it does not exist.
The essencelessness of <s>dharmas</s> is seen even in the ultimate.

body.text: ataḥ 'sarve dharmā vyavaharamātrāśritāḥ', ityasmin bhagavannirdeśe nāsti kaścana virodhaḥ / bhagavatyāmapyuktam -
body.translated_text: Therefore, in this teaching of the Blessed One — 'all <s>dharmas</s> are dependent on convention alone' — there is no contradiction whatsoever. It is also said in the <s>Bhagavatī</s> [Prajñāpāramitā]:

body.text: 'bodhisattvā mahāsatvāstāvallokkalpanayā anuttarasamyaksaṃbodhau abhisambhotsyante / paramārthatastu bodhyarthamanuṣṭhīyamānāni rūpaṃ vedanā saṃjñā, saṃskārāḥ vijñānāni kānyapi na santyeva / evameva aṣṭādaśa dhātavaḥ, ṣaṭ sparśāḥ, ṣaḍ vedanāḥ, ṣaḍ dhātavaḥ dvādaśa pratītyasamutpādāṅgāni, pāramitā, śūnyatā, smṛtyupasthānāni, samyak prahāṇāni ṛddhipādāḥ, indriyāṇi, balāni, bodhyaṅgāni, āryāṣṭāṅgikamārgāḥ, satyāni, dhyānāni, aparimāṇāni, arūpāṇi, vimuktidvārāṇi, anupūrvasamāpattayaḥ, abhijñāḥ, samādhayaḥ, dhāraṇīdvārāṇi, tathāgatabalāni, pratisaṃvidaḥ, mahākṛpā, āveṇikabuddhadharmāḥ, catvāpi phalāni, mārgajñānāni, anuttarasamyaksaṃbodhirapi naiva svabhāvataḥ sattvena sidhyanti / sarveṣāmeteṣāṃ dharmāṇāṃ lokavyavahārāśrayena kalpitatvāt, na tveteṣāṃ paramārthataḥ sattvam' - iti nirdeśaḥ /
body.translated_text: '<s>Bodhisattvas</s>, great beings, will attain <s>anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi</s> (supreme perfect awakening) through that worldly conceptual construction. But in ultimate truth, form, feeling, perception, formations, and consciousnesses that are cultivated for the purpose of awakening — none of these exist at all. Likewise, the eighteen elements, six contacts, six feelings, six elements, twelve limbs of <s>pratītyasamutpāda</s> (dependent origination), the <s>pāramitās</s> (perfections), <s>śūnyatā</s> (emptiness), <s>smṛtyupasthānas</s> (foundations of mindfulness), <s>samyak-prahāṇas</s> (right efforts), <s>ṛddhipādas</s> (bases of supernatural power), <s>indriyas</s> (faculties), <s>balas</s> (powers), <s>bodhyaṅgas</s> (factors of awakening), the noble eightfold path, the truths, <s>dhyānas</s> (meditations), the immeasurables, the formless [attainments], the gates of liberation, the progressive attainments, the <s>abhijñās</s> (superknowledges), the <s>samādhis</s> (concentrations), the gates of <s>dhāraṇī</s>, the <s>Tathāgata</s> powers, the <s>pratisaṃvids</s> (analytical knowledges), great compassion, the distinctive qualities of a <s>Buddha</s>, even the four fruits, the path-knowledges, and even <s>anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi</s> — none of these are accomplished through intrinsic nature as real entities. Since all these <s>dharmas</s> are constructed through dependence on worldly convention, they do not have reality in the ultimate' — thus is the teaching.

body.text: rūpata ārabhya sarvākārajñānaparyantaṃ ye tāvad dharmāsteṣāṃ na staḥ saṃyogaviyogāvapi / yato hi rūpaṃ adarśnam apratigham alakṣaṇameva asattvāt / sattvānāṃ grahaṇārthaṃ te kevalaṃ tathāgatena lokavyavahārārthaṃ kathitāḥ, na tu paramārthataḥ / lokasaṃvṛtau ye pinaḥ prāptirabhisamayaḥ pañcagatibhedāste 'pi pūrvata eva paramārthato na santi / paramārthe tu karmāpi nāsti karmaphalamapi, saṃkleśo nāsti, nāsti vyavadānamapi / na sta utpādanirodhāvapītyuktam / paramārthatastāvad bhagavān sarvatra saṃkleśavyavadānayorniṣedhaṃ kṛtavān, tathāpi vyavahāre tān aṅgīkṛtavān / teṣāṃ tāvadaniṣedhena svīkaraṇe 'pi nāsti[kaścana] doṣaḥ / anyatra bhagavān spapne sarpaṃ dṛṣṭvā mūrcchā tadabhāve saṃkleśaṃ vyavadānaṃ ca mithyaiveti kathitavān /
body.translated_text: From form up to <s>sarvākāra-jñāna</s> (all-aspect-knowledge), for all those <s>dharmas</s>, there is neither conjunction nor disjunction. For form is invisible, non-resistant, and simply without characteristics, due to its non-existence. Those [dharmas] were taught by the <s>Tathāgata</s> solely for the purpose of grasping by beings, for the sake of worldly convention, but not in the ultimate. Those that exist in worldly convention — attainment, realization, the distinctions of the five destinies — they too do not exist from the very beginning in the ultimate. In the ultimate, there is no <s>karma</s>, no fruit of <s>karma</s>, no defilement, and no purification either. There is neither origination nor cessation — so it was said. In the ultimate, the Blessed One negated defilement and purification everywhere, yet in convention he accepted them. In accepting them without negation, there is no fault whatsoever. Elsewhere, the Blessed One described defilement and purification as merely false, like fainting upon seeing a snake in a dream and [recovering upon its] absence.

body.text: nāsti caturyasatyāpavādadoṣo 'pi, yato hi mahāyānāndanyatra bhagavān teṣāṃ [āryasatyānāṃ] upadeśaṃ kṛtavān / brahmapripṛcchāsūtre tāvaduktam -
body.translated_text: There is also no fault of repudiating the four noble truths, since in other <s>Mahāyāna</s> [texts] the Blessed One taught about them [the noble truths]. In the <s>Brahma-paripṛcchā-sūtra</s> it is said:

body.text: "yaduta duḥkhaṃ samudayo nirodho mārgadho mārgaśceti naiva santyāryāṇāṃ satyāni, kintu brahmān, yadaniṣpannaṃ duḥkham, tadevāryāṇāṃ satyam / yo dyanutpannaḥ, sa evāryāṇāṃ samudayaḥ / yaścānirodho 'nutpannaśca sa evāryāṇāṃ satyam / sarvadharmāṇāmadvayasamatāyāṃ yā khalu mārgabhāvanā, saivāryāṇāṃ satyamiti / ato nāsti paramārthato duḥkhasatyam / tattu śrāvakānadhikṛtya saṃsārodvignamānasānāṃ kṛte pudgalanairātmyapraveśāryaṃ tāvadanityādisvabhāvatvena kevalaṃ nirdiṣṭam, na tu nairātmyadvayanirdeśādhikāreṇeti jñātavyam" /
body.translated_text: "Namely, suffering, origination, cessation, and the path — the noble truths do not exist [ultimately]. Rather, <s>Brahman</s>, that which is unproduced as suffering — that itself is the truth of the noble ones. That which is unarisen — that itself is the origination of the noble ones. That which is non-cessation and unarisen — that itself is the truth of the noble ones. In the non-dual equality of all <s>dharmas</s>, the cultivation of the path — that itself is the truth of the noble ones. Therefore, the truth of suffering does not exist in the ultimate. But it was taught merely as having the nature of impermanence and the like, for the purpose of introducing <s>Śrāvakas</s> to the selflessness of persons, for those whose minds are alarmed by <s>saṃsāra</s> — not from the perspective of the teaching of the non-dual selflessness" — thus it should be understood.

body.text: yaśca tāvajjanyajanakasvabhāvo janeṣvāgopālaṃ prasiddhastena prasiddhivirodhadoṣo 'pīti yaduktaṃ tadapyasambaddhameva, paramārthasvabhāvādīnāṃ sāmānyajaneṣvaprasiddhatvāt / yadi prasiddhastadā te naiva santi sādhāraṇajanāḥ / svapnādivanmithyāsvabhāvasyāpi prasiddhirnaiva susambhavā / prasiddhistāvat pratyakṣāṇumānābhyātiriktatvena naiva pramāṇamiti / sā pramāṇāntargaveti cet? tadā tadvirodhaparihāreṇa tadbādhāyā api parihāraḥ kṛta eva /
body.translated_text: The statement that 'there is the fault of contradicting well-known [convention], since the nature of produced-and-producer is well-known among people from cowherds onward' — that too is simply incoherent, because the intrinsic nature of the ultimate and the like is not well-known among ordinary people. If it were well-known, then those would simply not be ordinary people. Even the well-knownness of a false intrinsic nature, like a dream, is not truly possible. Moreover, well-knownness, being nothing other than perception and inference, is simply not a [separate] valid means of knowledge. If [one says] it is included within valid means of knowledge, then by resolving the contradiction with that, the invalidation by that is also already resolved.

body.text: yaccāvaśyaṃ parotpattyarthaṃ hetuprayogābhilāṣeṇa tato 'vaśyamutpattyabhyupagamāt svavacanavirodha ityuktam, tadapyaviruddhameva, niyatotpattyarthaṃ hetuprayogānnaiva tataḥ paramārthato niyatotpattirabhyupagatā bhavati / tatkimiti cet? utpattimātram, notpattiviśeṣaḥ / paramārthata utpattiniṣedhenātra vastūnāṃ niḥsvabhāvataiva paramārthataḥ sādhayitumiṣyate, na tūtpattimātraniṣedhaḥ / ato yadyapi hetubhyo niyatatayā pāramārthikī utpattirnaiva bhavati, tathāpi bimbāt pratibimbavat sāṃvṛtikī utpattistāvadaviruddhaiva / ato nāsti pratijñāyāḥ svavacanavirodhaḥ /
body.translated_text: The statement that 'since one necessarily desires the employment of a reason for the purpose of another's origination, and since origination is thereby necessarily accepted, there is self-contradiction' — that too is not contradictory, because from the employment of a reason for the purpose of determinate origination, determinate origination in the ultimate is not thereby accepted. Why? [What is accepted is] origination in general, not origination in particular. Here, through the negation of origination in the ultimate, it is desired to establish the essencelessness of things in the ultimate — not the negation of origination in general. Therefore, even though determinate origination from causes does not occur in the ultimate, still, like a reflection from an object, conventional origination is entirely non-contradictory. Therefore, there is no self-contradiction of the thesis.

body.text: yacca bhagavatā - "cakṣurvijñānasamaṅgī nīlaṃ vijānāti no tu nīlam" - ityuktam, tadapi indriyaviṣayavyavahāramabhyupetyaivaktamiti / anyatra tu - "na cakṣuḥ pramāṇaṃ na śrotra ghrāṇam" ityādinā ṣaḍindriyāṇāṃ pramāṇatvaṃ pratiṣiddhameveti pūrvameva nirdiṣṭam /
body.translated_text: The statement by the Blessed One — 'one possessing eye-consciousness cognizes blue, but not [the concept of] blue' — that too was said having accepted the conventional usage of sense-faculties and objects. Elsewhere, however, through [the statement] 'the eye is not a valid means of knowledge, nor the ear, nor the nose' and so forth, the validity of the six sense-faculties has been negated — as was already pointed out.

body.text: āryaprajñāpāramitādiṣvapi rupādiviṣayāṇāṃ pratiṣedho vihita eva / lokasaṃvṛtau tu sarva [dharmāḥ] saṃvidyanta evetyevaṃvidhaṃ bhagavān svābhiprayaṃ suspaṣṭaṃ prakaṭitavān / upalambhavatāṃ tāvannāsti suvidhuddhā prajñāpāramitetyapyuktavān / upalambhānupalambhayorbodhisattvebhyo heyopādeyatvamapi [kramaśaḥ] nirdiśyata eva / bhagavatyāmapyuktam - kiyatā bhagavan, upalambhaḥ, kiyatā ca tāvadanupalambho bhavatīti? bhagavān āha - yāvad dvayatā tāvadupalambhaḥ, yadadvayaṃ tadevānupalambhaḥ / apṛcchāt - kiyatā bhagavan dvayatā? bhagavān āha - yāvat sūbhūte, nāma rūpaṃ śrotraṃ ghrāṇam ityat ārabhya yāvad buddhatvam anuttarasamyaksaṃbodhiḥ buddha iti tāvad dvatetyupadideśa / punaśca, yāvad dvayasaṃjñā, naiva tāvadānulomikī kṣāntirityapyuktavān / āryadharmasaṃgītau 'pi - sarvadharmā naivopalabhyante, teṣāmadarśanādityuktam / ato vyāvahārikacakṣurādīnābhisandhāya draṣṭṛtvato jñātṛtvaparyantamātmaprasiddhestaddṛṣṭiniṣedhāryaṃ pudgalanairātmyapraveśābhiprāyeṇa cakṣurādīnāṃ nirdeśaḥ kṛtaḥ / ata eva cānābhāsina ākāśetpalasya nīlatvādivadime nīlādirūpāṇāṃ ye sāṃvṛtikā ābhāsāste 'pi na santyatyantābhāvarūpāḥ /
body.translated_text: In the <s>Ārya-Prajñāpāramitā</s> and other [texts] too, the negation of objects such as form and the like has been carried out. But in worldly convention, all <s>dharmas</s> do indeed exist — thus the Blessed One clearly revealed his intention. He also said that for those who apprehend, there is no thoroughly purified <s>Prajñāpāramitā</s>. The abandonability and adoptability of apprehension and non-apprehension respectively is also taught to <s>Bodhisattvas</s> in sequence. It is also said in the <s>Bhagavatī</s>: 'To what extent, Blessed One, is there apprehension, and to what extent non-apprehension?' The Blessed One said: 'To the extent that there is duality, there is apprehension; that which is non-dual — that itself is non-apprehension.' [<s>Subhūti</s>] asked: 'To what extent, Blessed One, is there duality?' The Blessed One said: 'To the extent that, <s>Subhūti</s>, there is name — form, ear, nose, and so forth, up to Buddhahood, <s>anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi</s>, Buddha — to that extent there is duality,' — so he taught. And furthermore, he also said: 'As long as there is the notion of duality, there is no conforming patience (<s>ānulomikī kṣānti</s>).' In the <s>Ārya-Dharmasaṅgīti</s> also: 'All <s>dharmas</s> are simply unapprehended, because they are unseen' — so it was said. Therefore, with reference to the conventional eye and other [faculties], and for the purpose of introducing [beings to] the selflessness of persons through negating the view [that posits a self] — from the self-evident capacity of being a seer up to being a knower — the teaching of the eye and other [faculties] was given. For this very reason, just as the blue color and the like of an unreflecting sky-lotus [are unreal], these conventional appearances of blue and other forms are also not of a nature of absolute non-existence.

body.text: 'yat kiñcit samudayadharmakaṃ tat sarvaṃ nirodhadharmakam' ityamunānumānena samyaktayā kṣaṇikatvena sthitasya vastudharmiṇaḥ siddhirninirdaṣṭeti yaduktaṃ tadapyutpādavināśadharmiṇo jñānena nairātmyapraveśārthaṃ śrāvakānadhikṛtya pudgalanairātmyamabhipretya coktam, na tu bodhisattvānāmadhikāreṇa gambhīratattvālāpamapekṣya proktamiti / yato hi bhagavatā saṃskārāṇāmutpādavināśasvabhāvasya samyaganudarśanaṃ taduddeśaṃ ca prajñāpāramitāyāmiva nirmitasadṛśamityuktam / saṃskārāsaṃskārakoṭidvayayogastāvadanuttarasamyaksaṃbodherupāya ityupadiṣṭaḥ / āryadharmasaṃgītau hi tathāgatena bhayasthānasya parihārārthaṃ vyavahāre cotpādanirodhau tāvaduktau /
body.translated_text: The statement that 'through the inference — whatever has the nature of origination, all that has the nature of cessation — the establishment of the property-possessor, the real entity established as momentary, has been demonstrated' — that too was said with reference to <s>Śrāvakas</s>, with the intention of [teaching] the selflessness of persons through cognition of what has the nature of arising and perishing, for the purpose of introducing [them to] selflessness — but it was not said from the perspective of <s>Bodhisattvas</s> with reference to the discourse on the profound reality. For the Blessed One said that the correct observation of the nature of arising and perishing of <s>saṃskāras</s> (conditioned things), along with its illustration, is similar to a magical creation, as in the <s>Prajñāpāramitā</s>. The conjunction of the two categories of the conditioned and unconditioned has been taught as the means to <s>anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi</s>. For in the <s>Ārya-Dharmasaṅgīti</s>, the <s>Tathāgata</s> spoke of origination and cessation in convention for the purpose of removing the ground of fear.

body.text: ārcāryeṇāpyuktam -
body.translated_text: The <s>Ācārya</s> [<s>Nāgārjuna</s>] also said:

body.text: utpādavyayakarmaṇābhiprāyārthaḥ pradarśitaḥ /
body.translated_text: The intended meaning was demonstrated through the activity of arising and perishing.

body.text: punaśca,
body.translated_text: Moreover,

children.text: yathā mayā yathā svapno gandharvanagaraṃ yathā /
children.translated_text: Just as by me, just as a dream, just as a city of the <s>Gandharvas</s> —
so is origination described, so is abiding, and so is destruction.

body.text: api ca, āryasāgaranāgarājaparipṛcchāsūtre 'pi -
body.translated_text: Furthermore, in the <s>Ārya-Sāgaranāgarāja-paripṛcchā-sūtra</s> also:

children.translated_text: In the beginning and end there is emptiness; birth, destruction, and abiding likewise.

children.text: sarve dharmāḥ svabhāvena śūnyā nāsanna sat punaḥ //
children.translated_text: All <s>dharmas</s> are empty by own-nature — they are neither non-existent nor existent again.

body.text: ityādikamudāhatam /
body.translated_text: And so forth has been cited.

body.text: yacca tāvat saṃskārāṇāṃ kṣaṇikatvam, tadapi naivopapannamiti nirdiṣṭam / āryasubāhuparipṛcchāsūtre coktam -
body.translated_text: Now, the momentariness of <s>saṃskāras</s> (conditioned things) — that too is not tenable — has been stated. In the <s>Ārya-Subāhu-paripṛcchā-sūtra</s> it is also said:

body.text: "yaduta trayāṇāmatītānāgatapratyutpannānāṃ kālānāṃ parijñānaṃ jāyate / tatrātītāḥ saṃskarāḥ, ye tāvanniruddhāste bhūtakāla ityucyunte / ye hyanāgatā anutpanāste bhaviṣyakāla iti / ye ca pratyutpanne pṛthagutpannāste vartamānakāla ityubhidhīyante / vartamānakālotpannāni skandhadhātvāyatanāni na sthitāni nāpyasthitānīti parijñāyante / kathamiti cet? loko 'yaṃ kṣaṇamātramapi nāvatiṣṭhati / ye tāvat kṣaṇikāsteṣāmutpado 'pyanyaḥ, sthitirapyanyā, vyayo 'pyanyo bhavatī, teṣāṃ kṣaṇikatvāt sthitāsthitatvābhāvācca /" ityādikamabhihitam
body.translated_text: "Namely, the knowledge of the three times — past, future, and present — arises. Therein, those <s>saṃskāras</s> that are past, that have ceased — they are called the past time. Those that are future and unarisen — they are called the future time. And those that have arisen separately in the present — they are called the present time. The <s>skandhas</s> (aggregates), <s>dhātus</s> (elements), and <s>āyatanas</s> (sense-bases) that have arisen in the present time are understood as neither abiding nor non-abiding. How so? This world does not remain even for a single moment. For those that are momentary, their origination is one thing, their abiding another, and their destruction yet another — because of their momentariness and because of the absence of the state of abiding or non-abiding." And so forth was stated.

body.text: ataśca kṣaṇikatā tāvat kalpanāsvabhāvātmikaiva, tadādimadhyāntānāṃ bhinnasvabhāatvādityupadideśa / tathaivācāryeṇāpyuktam -
body.translated_text: Therefore, momentariness is of the nature of conceptual construction alone, since beginning, middle, and end are of different natures — thus it was taught. The <s>Ācārya</s> also said likewise:

children.translated_text: Just as a moment has an end, so its beginning and middle may be conceived.

children.text: trayātmakatvāt kṣaṇasyaivaṃ na lokasya kṣaṇaṃ sthitiḥ //
children.translated_text: Because a moment has a threefold nature, the world does not abide [even] for a moment.

body.text: yacca bhagavatā "dhūmena jñāyate vahniḥ" ityadikamuktam, tadapi sūtrāntareṣu sakalasāmagrīsamavadhānāt samutpadyamānānāmagnidhūmādīnāṃ sāmānyena niṣedhaparakameva / ato naiva tat paramārthamadhikṛtyoktamiti nirdiṣṭameva pūrvam /
body.translated_text: The statement by the Blessed One — 'fire is known from smoke' — and similar [teachings], that too, because of the general negation of things such as fire and smoke that arise from the complete assemblage of causes in other <s>sūtras</s>, is entirely directed toward negation. Therefore, it was not said with reference to the ultimate — as has already been stated.

body.text: āryalaṅkāvatāre 'pyuktam -
body.translated_text: In the <s>Ārya-Laṅkāvatāra</s> also it is said:

children.text: samavāyād vinirmukto buddhayā bhāvo na gṛhyate /
children.translated_text: An entity free from <s>samavāya</s> (co-inherence) is not apprehended by the intellect.
Therefore I declare [it to be] empty, unoriginated, and without own-nature.

body.text: anyacca tatraiva -
body.translated_text: And elsewhere in the same [text]:

children.translated_text: Oneness or manyness, as conceived by the childish —

children.text: samavāyāt pṛthaṅ nāsti na cānyasya pṛthak sthitiḥ //
children.translated_text: apart from <s>samavāya</s> (co-inherence), [it] does not exist; nor does anything else abide separately.

body.text: āryaghanavyūhasūtre coktam -
body.translated_text: In the <s>Ārya-Ghanavyūha-sūtra</s> it is said:

children.text: na skandhā dhātavo naiva sarve dharmā alakṣaṇāḥ /
children.translated_text: There are no <s>skandhas</s> (aggregates), no <s>dhātus</s> (elements) at all; all <s>dharmas</s> are without characteristics.
Even when examined, the <s>paramāṇu</s> (atom) that is so established does not exist.

body.text: punaśca,
body.translated_text: Moreover,

body.text: pṛthivyabādivastūni kalpitāni sukalpakaiḥ /
body.translated_text: Substances such as earth, water, and the like are constructed by skillful constructors.

body.text: api ca,
body.translated_text: Furthermore,

body.text: vicāre sati naivāsti paramāṇośca vastutā /
body.translated_text: Upon investigation, there is no reality whatsoever of the <s>paramāṇu</s> (atom).

body.text: ityādyaktam /
body.translated_text: And so forth has been stated.
